[1157][Para 001] Abnormal position of crypt. Rx: extraction or orthodontic alignment. See options for palatally displaced 3 (…… Palatally displaced maxillary canines, p. 144).
[1158][Para 001] 1° failure of eruption usually affects molar teeth. The aetiology is not understood. Although bone resorption proceeds above the unerupted tooth, they appear to lack any eruptive potential. Refer for advice, usually extraction is only option.
[1159][Para 006] Infraoccluded (ankylosed) primary molars
[1160][Para 005] These occur where the 1° molar has failed to maintain its position relevant to the adjacent teeth in the developing dentition and is therefore below the occlusal level of adjacent teeth. Often due to ankylosis 2° to disruption in normal resorptive/repair cycle of exfoliation. This is usually self-correcting (if the permanent successor is present and not ectopic) and the affected tooth is exfoliated at the normal time. However, where the premolar is missing or ectopic, where the infraoccluded molar moves below the contact of adjacent teeth, or appears in danger of disappearing below the gingival level, extraction may be indicated (monitor carefully and if in doubt get a specialist opinion).
[1161][Para 006] Ectopic eruption of first permanent molars
[1162][Para 005] Most commonly occurs in the upper arch—against the distal of E occurs in 2–5% of children. It is an indication of crowding. In younger patients (<8yrs) many self-correct (‘jump’). If still present after 4–6 months (‘hold’) or in older children, insertion of an orthodontic separating spring may allow the 6 to jump free. More severe impactions should be kept under observation. If the E becomes abscessed or the 6 is in danger of becoming carious then the 1° tooth should be extracted. The resulting space loss can be dealt with later as part of the overall orthodontic Rx plan.
[1163][Para 006] Premature exfoliation
[1164][Para 005] The most common reason for early tooth loss is extraction for caries. Traumatic avulsion is less common. More rarely, systemic disease such as neutropenia or leukaemia may result in an abnormal periodontal attachment and thus premature tooth loss. Alveolar bone loss in a young child is a serious finding and warrants urgent referral.
[1165][Para 009] Abnormalities of tooth number
[1166][Para 022] Anodontia
[1167][Para 004] Means complete absence of all teeth. Rare. Partial anodontia is a misnomer.
[1168][Heading 1] Hypodontia (oligodontia)
[1169][Para 004] Developmental absence of one or more teeth.
[1170][Para 006] Prevalence
[1171][Para 005] 1° dentition: 0.1–0.9%, 2° dentition: 3.5–6.5%.5 In Caucasians most commonly affected teeth are 8 (25–35%), 2 (2%), lower 5 (3%). Affects F >  and is often associated with smaller than average tooth size in remainder of dentition. Peg-shaped 2 often occurs in conjunction with absence of contralateral 2. NB: 3 migrates down guided by the distal aspect of 2. When 2 is absent, peg-shaped, or small-rooted, it is important to monitor the maxillary canine for signs of ectopic eruption.
[1172][Para 006] Aetiology
[1173][Para 005] Often familial—polygenic inheritance. Also associated with ectodermal dysplasia and Down syndrome.
[1174][Para 001] Rx: 1° dentition—none. 2° dentition—depends on crowding and malocclusion.
[1175][Para 001] 8—none.
[1176][Para 057] 2—see …… Management of missing incisors, p. 114.
[1177][Para 001] 5 — (NB: 5 sometimes develop late). If patient is crowded, extraction of E, either at around 8yrs for spontaneous space closure or later if space is to be closed as a part of orthodontic Rx. If lower arch is well aligned or spaced, consider preservation of E, and bridgework later (if Es have no pathology and long roots, they can sometimes be maintained into adulthood).
[1178][Heading 1] Hyperdontia
[1179][Para 004] Better known as supernumerary teeth.
[1180][Para 006] Prevalence
[1181][Para 005] 1° dentition 0.8%, 2° dentition 2%. Occurs most frequently in premaxillary region. Affects  > F. Associated with cleidocranial dysostosis and CLP. Supernumerary ($) in 1° dentition is followed in about 50% of cases by $ in 2° dentition, so warn parent!
[1182][Para 006] Aetiology
[1183][Para 005] Theories include offshoot of dental lamina and third dentition.
[1184][Para 006] Classification
[1185][Para 005] Classification is either by shape or position (Table 3.2) and orientation (e.g. ‘upright, ‘inverted’, etc.).
[1186][Para 036] Table 3.2 Classification of abnormalities by shape and position
[1187][Para 006] Effects on dentition and Rx
[1188][Para 001] No effect. If unerupted keep watch (radiographic review occasionally to exclude cystic change/damage to adjacent teeth—both relatively rare). If erupts—extract.
[1189][Para 001] Crowding. Rx: extract; if supplemental, extract tooth with the worse crown or root form, or the tooth with the most displaced apex.
[1190][Para 001] Displacement. Can cause rotation &/or displacement. Rx: extraction of $ and fixed appliance, but tendency to relapse.
[1191][Para 001] Failure of eruption. Most likely cause of 1 to fail to erupt. Rx: extract $ and ensure sufficient space for unerupted tooth to erupt. May require extraction of 1° teeth &/or permanent teeth and orthodontic appliance. Then wait. Average time to eruption in these cases is 18 months.6 If after 2yrs unerupted tooth fails to erupt despite sufficient space, may require conservative exposure and orthodontic traction.
[1192][Para 016]  Children with hypodontia will often benefit from specialist/multidisciplinary management, coordinating paediatric dental, restorative, and orthodontic management.
[1193][Para 009] Abnormalities of tooth structure
[1194][Para 022] Disturbances in structure of enamel
[1195][Para 004] Enamel usually develops in two phases: first, an organic matrix and second, mineralization. Disruption of enamel formation can therefore manifest as follows:
[1196][Para 006] Hypoplasia
[1197][Para 005] Caused by disturbance in matrix formation and is characterized by pitted, grooved, or thinned enamel.
[1198][Para 006] Hypomineralization
[1199][Para 005] Hypocalcification is a disturbance of calcification. Affected enamel appears white, yellow, or brown and opaque. May become more discoloured post-eruptively. Affected enamel may be weak and prone to breakdown. Most disturbances of enamel formation will produce both hypoplasia and hypomineralization, but clinically one type usually predominates.
[1200][Para 006] Aetiological factors
[1201][Para 005] The following is not an exhaustive list:
[1202][Para 028] Localized causes
[1203][Para 025] Infection (‘Turner tooth’), trauma, irradiation, and idiopathic (…… Enamel opacities, p. 76).
[1204][Para 028] Generalized causes
[1205][Para 001] Environmental (chronological hypoplasia):
[1206][Para 001] Prenatal, e.g. rubella, syphilis.
[1207][Para 001] Neonatal, e.g. prolonged labour, premature birth.
[1208][Para 001] Postnatal, e.g. measles, congenital heart disease, fluoride, nutritional.
[1209][Para 001] Hereditary:
[1210][Para 001] Affecting teeth only—amelogenesis imperfecta.
[1211][Para 001] Accompanied by systemic disorder, e.g. Down syndrome, tuberous sclerosis.
[1212][Para 006] Chronological hypoplasia
[1213][Para 005] So called because the hypoplastic enamel occurs in a distribution related to the extent of tooth formation at the time of the insult. Characteristically, due to its later formation, 2 is affected nearer to the incisal edge than 1 or 3.
[1214][Para 006] Fluorosis
[1215][Para 005] See …… Fluoride, p. 28.
[1216][Para 006] Rx of hypomineralization/hypoplasia depends on extent and severity
[1217][Para 056] Posterior teeth
[1218][Para 025] Small areas of hypoplasia can be fissure-sealed or restored conventionally, but more severely affected teeth may require crowning. Stainless steel (SS) crowns (…… Stainless steel crowns, p. 88) can be used in children as a semi-permanent measure.
[1219][Para 028] Anterior teeth
[1220][Para 025] Small areas of hypoplasia can be restored using composites, microabrasion, or resin infiltration but larger areas may require veneers (…… Veneers, p. 258) or crowns.
[1221][Para 006] Molar incisor hypomineralization (MIH)
[1222][Para 049] See Fig. 3.2.
[1223][Para 001] Aetiology unknown. Prevalence ↑ over the past two decades in developed countries. Prevalence 14.2%.7
[1224][Para 001] Primarily affects 6s, but ~50% also have defects on permanent incisors.
[1225][Para 001] Affected 6s have hypomineralized defects of enamel, varying from discoloration to severe enamel dysplasia with post-eruptive breakdown. Sensitivity i, 2° caries i. Defects may affect anything from one to all 6s.
[1226][Para 001] Yellow/white opacities on buccal surface of affected incisors. Distribution often asymmetrical. No clear chronological pattern. Incisors less prone to enamel breakdown than 6s.
[1227][Para 016] Rx options include intracoronal restoration, SS crowns, microabrasion, vital bleaching, resin infiltrate, or extraction, depending on aesthetics and prognosis (…… Extraction of poor-quality first permanent molars, p. 140). Partial composite veneers can be considered to repair post-eruptive breakdown of incisors.
[1228][Para 023] 
[1229][Para 019] Fig. 3.2 Upper first permanent molar in a patient with molar incisor hypomineralization; the likely Rx would be extraction.
[1230][Para 006] Hypomineralized second primary molars (HSPM)
[1231][Para 005] HSPM is a developmental defect of dental enamel that shares features with MIH. Also known as 1° molar hypomineralization. It may lead to post-eruptive breakdown and 2° caries. Recent studies suggest it is a predictor that MIH may be more likely to occur in the permanent dentition.
[1232][Para 006] Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI)
[1233][Para 005] Many classifications exist, but generally these are classified by the type of enamel defect &/or the mode of inheritance. There are now known to be mutations in at least 15 different genes that are associated with AI8 (commonly affected genes: AMELX, ENAM, AMBN, KLK4, MMP20).
[1234][Para 028] Main types
[1235][Para 001] Hypoplastic—enamel may be thin (smooth or rough) or pitted. Most commonly autosomal dominant inheritance. Enamel-renal syndrome: a rare hypoplastic AI associated with the FAM20A gene. Clinical features may include severely hypoplasic and discoloured enamel, semi-lunar shape of incisal edges, intra-pulpal calcification, hyperplastic dental follicles, delayed eruption, and gingival hyperplasia.
[1236][Para 001] Hypocalcified—enamel is dull, lustreless, opaque white, honey, or brown coloured. Enamel may breakdown rapidly in severe cases. Sensitivity i, calculus ↑ common. May be autosomal dominant or recessive.
[1237][Para 001] Hypomaturation—mottled or frosty-looking white opacities, sometimes confined to incisal third of crown (‘snow-capped teeth’).
[1238][Para 016] Usually both 1° and 2° dentitions and all the teeth are affected. The different subgroups give rise to a wide variation in clinical presentation, ranging from discoloration to soft &/or deficient enamel. It is therefore difficult to make general recommendations, but it is wise to seek specialist advice for all but the mildest forms. Rx: in more severe cases, SS crowns and composite resin can be used to maintain molars and 2° inc, prior to more permanent restorations when child is older.
[1239][Para 042]  Enamel-renal syndrome: a rare hypoplastic AI caused by mutation of the FAM20A gene and associated with nephrocalcinosis. Suspected individuals should be referred for genetic confirmation, and if confirmed, renal investigation. Clinical features may include severely hypoplasic and discoloured enamel, semi-lunar shape of incisal edges, intra-pulpal calcification, hyperplastic dental follicles, delayed eruption, and gingival hyperplasia.
[1240][Heading 1] Disturbances in the structure of dentine
[1241][Para 004] These include dentinogenesis imperfecta, dentinal dysplasias (types I and II), regional odontodysplasia, vitamin D-resistant rickets, and Ehlers–Danlos syndrome—all of which are rare.
[1242][Para 006] Dentinogenesis imperfecta (hereditary opalescent dentine—DI)
[1243][Para 005] This is more common, affecting 1 in 8000. Both 1° and 2° dentitions are involved, although later-formed teeth may be less so. Main types:
[1244][Para 001] I—associated with osteogenesis imperfecta.
[1245][Para 001] II—teeth only.
[1246][Para 016] Affected teeth have an opalescent brown or blue hue, bulbous crowns, short roots, and narrow flame-shaped pulps. The ADJ is abnormal, which results in the enamel flaking off, leading to rapid wear of the soft dentine. Rx: along similar lines as for severe amelogenesis.
[1247][Para 042]  Children with opalescent teeth may also have brittle bone disease.
[1248][Para 042]  Early recognition and Rx of amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta is important to prevent rapid tooth wear.
[1249][Heading 1] Disturbances in the structure of cementum
[1250][Para 004] Hypoplasia and aplasia of cementum are uncommon. The latter occurs in hypophosphatasia and results in premature exfoliation. Hypercementosis is relatively common and may occur in response to inflammation, mechanical stimulation, or Paget’s disease, or be idiopathic. Concrescence is the uniting of the roots of two teeth by cementum.
[1251][Para 042]  Children with developmental dental anomalies will often benefit from specialist/multidisciplinary management, coordinating paediatric dental, restorative, and orthodontic management.
[1252][Para 042]  Prevention is a priority in children with developmental dental anomalies to minimize the risk of 2° caries, tooth surface loss, and periodontal disease.
[1253][Para 009] Abnormalities of tooth form
[1254][Para 014] Normal width 1 = 8.5mm, 2 = 6.5mm.
[1255][Heading 1] Double teeth
[1256][Para 017] Gemination
[1257][Para 005] This occurs by partial splitting of a tooth germ.
[1258][Para 006] Fusion
[1259][Para 005] Fusion occurs as a result of the fusion of two tooth germs. As fusion can take place between either two teeth of the normal series or, less commonly, with a $ tooth, then counting the number of teeth will not always give the correct aetiology.
[1260][Para 008] As the distinction is really only of academic interest, the term ‘double teeth’ is to be preferred. Both 1° and 2° teeth may be affected and a wide variation in presentation is seen. The prevalence in the 2° dentition is 0.1–0.2%.
[1261][Para 006] Rx
[1262][Para 005] Rx for aesthetics should be delayed to allow pulpal recession. If the tooth has separate pulp chambers and root canals, separation can be considered. If it is due to fusion with a $ tooth, the $ portion can be extracted. Where a single pulp chamber exists, sometimes the tooth can be contoured to resemble two separate teeth or the bulk of the crown reduced.
[1263][Heading 1] Macrodontia/megadontia
[1264][Para 004] Generalized macrodontia is rare, but is unilaterally associated with hemifacial hypertrophy. Isolated megadont teeth are seen in 1% of 2° dentitions.
[1265][Heading 1] Microdontia
[1266][Para 017] Prevalence
[1267][Para 005] 1° dentition <0.5%. In 2° dentition, overall prevalence is 2.5%. Of this figure, 1–2% is accounted for by diminutive 2s. Peg-shaped 2s often have short roots and are thought to be a possible factor in the palatal displacement of 3s (…… Palatally displaced maxillary canines, p. 144). 8s also commonly affected.
[1268][Heading 1] Dens in dente
[1269][Para 004] This is really a marked palatal invagination, which gives the appearance of a tooth within a tooth. Usually affects 2s, but can also affect premolars. Where the invagination is in close proximity to the pulp, early pulp death may ensue. Fissure sealing of the invagination as soon as possible after eruption may prevent this, but is often too late. Extraction may be required, other options include RCT (can be difficult), pulpotomy, and apical Rx.
[1270][Heading 1] Dilaceration
[1271][Para 004] This describes a tooth with a distorted crown or root. Usually affects 1s. Two types seen, dependent upon aetiology (Table 3.3).
[1272][Para 008] The traumatically induced type is caused by intrusion of the 1° incisor, resulting in displacement of the developing 2° incisor tooth germ. The effects depend upon the developmental stage at the time of injury.
[1273][Para 008] Rx: depends upon severity and patient cooperation. If mild it may be possible to expose crown and align orthodontically provided the apex will not be positioned against the labial plate of bone at the end of the Rx, otherwise extraction is indicated.
[1274][Para 036] Table 3.3 Types of dilaceration
[1275][Heading 1] Turner tooth
[1276][Para 004] This term is used to describe the effect of a disturbance of enamel and dentine formation by infection from an overlying 1° tooth which therefore usually affects premolar teeth. Rx: as for hypoplasia …… Hypoplasia, p. 70.
[1277][Heading 1] Taurodontism
[1278][Para 004] Taurodontism means ‘bull-like’. May occur in some types of AI. Radiographically an elongation of the pulp chamber is seen, which resembles a bull’s head. Rx: none required, but may complicate endodontic Rx and occasionally extraction.
[1279][Para 009] Abnormalities of tooth colour
[1280][Para 022] Extrinsic staining
[1281][Para 004] By definition this is caused by extrinsic agents and can be removed by prophylaxis. Green, black, orange, or brown stains are seen, and may be formed by chromogenic bacteria or be dietary in origin. Chlorhexidine mouthwash causes a brown stain by combining with dietary tannin. Where the staining is associated with poor OH, demineralization and roughening of the underlying enamel may make removal difficult. Rx: a mixture of pumice powder and toothpaste or an abrasive prophylaxis paste together with a bristle brush should remove the stain. Meticulous OHI can help to prevent staining returning, but recurrence is unfortunately relatively common.
[1282][Heading 1] Intrinsic staining
[1283][Para 004] This can be caused by:
[1284][Para 001] Changes in the structure or thickness of the dental hard tissues, e.g. enamel opacities.
[1285][Para 001] Incorporation of pigments during tooth formation, e.g. tetracycline staining (blue/brown), porphyria (red).
[1286][Para 001] Diffusion of pigment into hard tissues after formation, e.g. pulp necrosis products (grey), root canal medicaments (grey).
[1287][Heading 1] Enamel opacities
[1288][Para 004] These are localized areas of hypomineralized (or hypoplastic) enamel. Fluoride (…… Fluoride, p. 28) is only one of a considerable number of possible aetiological agents.
[1289][Heading 1] Rx
[1290][Para 004] Seven possible approaches:
[1291][Para 006] Approach 1
[1292][Para 005] Acid pumice abrasion technique is effective for some types of diffuse (surface) enamel defects. Two methods available (take pre-operative photos to monitor improvement):
[1293][Para 028] Hydrochloric acid technique (quicker, but great care needed)
[1294][Para 025] A mixture of 18% hydrochloric acid and pumice is applied to the affected area using a wooden stick. Careful isolation with rubber dam, use of a neutralizing agent (e.g. sodium bicarbonate), and protection of the soft tissues/patient is essential. The mixture is rubbed into the surface for 5sec and then rinsed away. These two steps are repeated (max. ten times—removing <0.1mm enamel) until the desired colour change is achieved. The enamel is then polished and a fluoride solution applied.9 Tell the patient to avoid highly coloured foods for 48h.
[1295][Para 028] Phosphoric acid technique (slower but potentially safer)
[1296][Para 025] A number of variations of this technique are in use. A commonly used method is to etch with 30–50% orthophosphoric acid for 1–2min, wash, then use pumice and water slurry with rubber prophy cup for 1min (take care not to overheat the tooth). Wash. Repeat etch and pumice stage ×2, washing between. Dry tooth and apply topical fluoride solution (avoid pigmented varnishes). May be repeated up to ×2, but leave at least 6 weeks before each repeat to check for improvement.
[1297][Para 006] Approach 2
[1298][Para 005] Resin infiltrate is a valid and well supported approach of treating enamel opacities. There are various systems available but commonly the tooth is etched with hydrochloric acid, dried with ethanol, prior to application of a methacrylate-based resin.
[1299][Para 006] Approach 3
[1300][Para 005] Bleaching (…… Tooth whitening, p. 256). The patient should be 18yrs or older.
[1301][Para 006] Approach 4
[1302][Para 005] Veneers (…… Veneers, p. 258). Should not be considered before the gingival position is stable, at least 16yrs old.
[1303][Para 006] Approach 5
[1304][Para 005] Crowns (…… Anterior crowns, p. 260). Should not be considered before the gingival position is stable, at least 16yrs old.
[1305][Para 006] Approach 6
[1306][Para 005] Localized composite restorations in affected areas including composite veneers.
[1307][Para 006] Approach 7
[1308][Para 005] Resin infiltration is a minimally invasive Rx for hypomineralized areas. The low-viscosity, unfilled resin penetrates areas of demineralization within the enamel and improves the appearance of these. The manufacturer’s instructions should be followed for the system being used.
[1309][Para 009] Anatomy of primary teeth (and relevance to cavity design)
[1310][Para 014] 1° teeth differ in several respects from permanent teeth, affecting both the sequelae of dental disease and its management (Fig. 3.3). (The following bracketed numbers refer to the numbered features in Fig. 3.3.)
[1311][Para 023] 
[1312][Para 019] Fig. 3.3 Cross-sections of second deciduous molar showing features of anatomy of primary molars.
[1313][Heading 1] Thinner enamel
[1314][Para 004] (1) Enamel in 1° teeth is ~1mm thick, which is half that of 2° teeth.
[1315][Heading 1] Larger pulp horns
[1316][Para 004] (2) The pulp chamber in 1° teeth is proportionately larger, with more accentuated pulp horns. DE—three pulp horns MB, DB, and palatal. Lower DE—four pulp horns MB, ML, DB, and DL. These features mean that caries will affect the pulp sooner and there is a greater likelihood of pulp exposure during cavity preparation. Aim for only 0.5–1.0mm penetration into dentine, except where caries determines deeper preparation.
[1317][Heading 1] Pulpal outline
[1318][Para 004] (3) This follows the amelo-dentinal junction more closely in 1° teeth, therefore cavity floor should follow external contour of tooth sinuously to avoid exposure.
[1319][Heading 1] Narrower occlusal table
[1320][Para 004] Greater convergence of the buccal and lingual walls results in a proportionately narrower occlusal table. This is more pronounced in D than E therefore, over-extension of an occlusal cavity or lock can lead to weakening of the cusps.
[1321][Heading 1] Broad and flat contact points
[1322][Para 004] (4) This makes detection of interproximal caries more difficult, and means that in 1° molars divergence of the buccal and lingual walls towards the approximal surface is necessary to ensure cavity margins are self-cleansing.
[1323][Heading 1] Bulbous crown
[1324][Para 004] (5) 1° molars have a more bulbous crown form than 2° molars, making matrix placement more difficult.
[1325][Heading 1] Inclination of the enamel prisms
[1326][Para 004] (6) In the cervical third of 1° molars the enamel prisms are inclined in an occlusal direction so there is no need to bevel the gingival floor of a proximal box.
[1327][Heading 1] Cervical constriction
[1328][Para 004] (7) This is more marked in 1° molars, therefore if the base of the proximal box is extended too far gingivally it will be difficult to cut an adequate floor without encroaching on the pulp.
[1329][Heading 1] Alveolar bone permeability
[1330][Para 004] This is ↑ in younger children, thus it is usually possible to achieve local anaesthesia of 1° mandibular molars by infiltration alone, up to 6yrs of age.
[1331][Heading 1] Thin pulpal floor and accessory canals
[1332][Para 004] (8) This may explain the greater incidence of inter-radicular involvement following pulp death.
[1333][Heading 1] Root form
[1334][Para 004] (9) 1° molars have proportionately longer roots than their permanent counterparts. They are also more flared to straddle the developing premolar tooth. The roots are flattened mesio-distally, as are canals within.
[1335][Heading 1] Radicular pulp
[1336][Para 004] (10) This follows a tortuous and branching path, making complete cleansing and preparation of the root canal system almost impossible, although instrumenting canals is often easier than suggested in some texts. In addition, as the roots resorb, a different approach to RCT is needed for the 1° dentition, pure zinc oxide and eugenol being the obturation material of choice.
[1337][Para 009] Extraction versus restoration of primary teeth
[1338][Para 014] Despite a welcome reduction in the prevalence of dental decay, the dilemma of whether to restore or extract a 1° tooth is still all too familiar. In making a decision, a number of factors should be considered, including:
[1339][Heading 1] Age
[1340][Para 004] This will influence the likely cooperation for restorative procedures, the expected remaining length of service of the affected tooth, and the severity of sequelae following early tooth loss (as the earlier the tooth is lost, the greater the potential for space loss).
[1341][Heading 1] Medical history
[1342][Para 004] For patients where recurrent bacteraemia carries ↑ risks (e.g. immunocompromised, risk of endocarditis) it is generally considered that 1° tooth pulp therapy should be avoided, with extraction (taking appropriate precautions where necessary) often being more appropriate. Conversely, in haemophiliacs, extractions should be avoided and 1° teeth preserved, if possible, until their exfoliation. Prevention is particularly important in all such patients.
[1343][Heading 1] Motivation and cooperation of parents
[1344][Para 004] As it is the parents that bring the child to the surgery, we must explain to them the benefits of maintaining the 1° dentition. Unfortunately, a small proportion of the population may regard a dentist that fills 1° teeth with suspicion—after all, everyone knows that baby teeth fall out!
[1345][Heading 1] Extent of caries
[1346][Para 004] In a child with an otherwise caries-free mouth, every attempt should be made to preserve an intact dentition. Where there is extensive caries, restoration of Es and loss of Ds can be an acceptable compromise.
[1347][Heading 1] Pain
[1348][Para 004] If a child is suffering pain from one or more teeth, this needs to be alleviated as soon as possible. If symptom free, then the dentist will have more time to explore the extent of the lesion(s) and the child’s cooperation.
[1349][Heading 1] Extent of lesion(s)
[1350][Para 004] In 1° molars destruction of the marginal ridge indicates a high probability of pulpal involvement.10 If several 1° molars require pulp therapy, and cooperation/motivation is poor, serious thought should be given to extraction rather than restoration.
[1351][Heading 1] Position of tooth
[1352][Para 004] Although early loss of 1° incisors will have little effect, extraction of C, D, or E will, in a crowded case, lead to localization of the crowding. Extraction of Es, particularly in the upper arch, should be deferred, if possible, until the 6 has erupted.
[1353][Heading 1] Presence/absence of permanent successor
[1354][Para 004] Bear in mind the amount of crowding present and the likelihood of spontaneous space closure.
[1355][Heading 1] Malocclusion
[1356][Para 004] If still undecided, it is worth considering the occlusion. In a particularly crowded case, restoration of a decayed tooth may be indicated if further space loss would mean that extraction of more than one premolar per quadrant would be required. Much has been written about compensating (same tooth in opposing arch) and balancing (contralateral tooth) extractions, although this is still an area of some controversy.11 The rationale is that a symmetrical problem is easier to deal with later but if taken to its logical conclusion, gross caries of D| and ⎡E will result in a clearance! In general, loss of Cs in a crowded patient should be balanced to prevent a centre-line shift. Balancing Ds in a child with ↑ risk of caries also has the advantage of removing very caries-prone contacts (i.e. E–D and D–C).
[1357][Para 008] So much for the theory; in practice, it should be remembered that a happy and cooperative patient is more important in the long term. When treating a child under local analgesia, leaving extractions unbalanced and monitoring for centre-line shift may be preferable to prolonging intervention in the dental chair.
[1358][Para 009] Local analgesia for children
[1359][Para 014] Although there is no scientific evidence to suggest that 1° teeth are less sensitive than 2° teeth, clinically it is sometimes possible to complete cavity preparation of minimal cavities without LA, especially on 1° anterior teeth. Adequate management of approximal caries in 1° molars usually requires LA.
[1360][Heading 1] General principles
[1361][Para 001] Explain to patient in terms they will understand what you are trying to do and why.
[1362][Para 001] Use flavoured topical anaesthesia (e.g. 20% benzocaine).
[1363][Para 001] Warm anaesthetic solution to room temperature only.
[1364][Para 001] Use a fine-gauge (e.g. 30-gauge) disposable needle.
[1365][Para 001] Always have a dental nurse to assist.
[1366][Para 001] Hold mucosa taut. Verbal distraction can help at the moment of needle penetration.
[1367][Para 001] Use slow rate of injection or ‘the wand’.
[1368][Para 001] Warn about post-operative numbness and avoidance of self-inflicted trauma (e.g. lip chewing/sucking).
[1369][Heading 1] Choice of anaesthetic agent
[1370][Para 017] First choice
[1371][Para 005] Lidocaine 2% with 1:80,000 adrenaline. Maximum dose = 4.4mg/kg.12
[1372][Para 006] Second choice
[1373][Para 005] Prilocaine 3% with felypressin (0.03IU/mL)—may give slightly less profound anaesthesia. Maximum dose = 6.6mg/kg.
[1374][Para 008] For lidocaine, maximum dosage equates to (i) 2.2mL for a healthy 10kg 1.5yr-old child and (ii) 4.4mL for a healthy 20kg 5yr-old (i.e. 1 × 2.2mL cartridge per 10kg). This may need to be reduced for children with certain medical conditions.
[1375][Para 008] Articaine 4% with adrenaline may be used (maximum dose 7mg/kg) and there is some evidence that lower 1° and 2° molar teeth can be more reliably anaesthetized by infiltration alone. However, articaine is not licensed for children <4yrs of age and greater care is needed to avoid exceeding the maximum dose, as the volume at maximum dosage is less than other LA agents. Some evidence suggests greater risk of prolonged anaesthesia/paraesthesia when articaine is used for ID blocks, so some suggest avoiding the use of articaine for blocks.
[1376][Heading 1] Infiltration injection
[1377][Para 004] Can be used in most circumstances. Infiltration technique as for adults (…… Local analgesia—techniques, p. 628). In children, the malar buttress overlies 6, so it is often advisable to deposit some solution over the more permeable bone mesial and distal to this tooth.
[1378][Heading 1] Block injection
[1379][Para 017] Inferior dental block
[1380][Para 005] Using thumb and forefinger, find the shortest width of the ramus. Penetrate about 1cm into lingual tissues from the internal oblique ridge, on a line between thumb and finger. An aspirating syringe is essential. NB: the mandibular foramen is lower on the ramus in young children (about the same level as the occlusal plane).
[1381][Para 006] Posterior superior alveolar block
[1382][Para 005] This is rarely required in children and carries a significant risk of post-injection haematoma. If necessary due to failure of infiltration for 6, the technique should be modified by depositing solution distal to the zygomatic buttress and massaging it backwards towards the posterior superior alveolar foramen (maxillary molar block).13
[1383][Heading 1] Alternative techniques
[1384][Para 017] Intraligamentary injection
[1385][Para 005] These purpose-designed syringes have an ultra-short needle and a ‘gun’ or ‘pen’ appearance. This makes it helpful for children with a needle phobia, or as a more acceptable alternative or adjunct to an IDB. In addition, as the lips and tongue are not anaesthetized it is useful for young or disabled children, in whom there is a greater risk of post-operative soft tissue trauma.
[1386][Para 006] Jet injection
[1387][Para 005] In this technique, a jet syringe (e.g. Syrijet® or Injex®) is used to inject LA solution under pressure through mucosa and bone to a depth of about 1cm. It is useful for producing soft tissue analgesia prior to conventional LA injection or for infiltration analgesia, and for some patients who will not contemplate LA using a needle, but is not widely used.
[1388][Para 006] Computer-controlled delivery (e.g. The Wand®, Single Tooth Anesthesia (STA®) system)
[1389][Para 005] Allows carefully controlled slow delivery via a line and needle resembling an IV-giving set. Especially useful for direct palatal analgesia, intraligamental analgesia, and for anxious patients.
[1390][Para 009] Restoration of carious primary teeth
[1391][Para 014] Making an accurate pre-operative ∆ (including appropriate radiographs) and Rx plan is essential. This will enable Rx to be provided as efficiently as possible (…… Treatment planning for children, p. 58).
[1392][Heading 1] Local anaesthesia
[1393][Para 035] See …… Local analgesia for children, p. 82.
[1394][Heading 1] Isolation
[1395][Para 004] Ideally, a rubber dam should be used routinely for restorative procedures. It not only protects the airway, but also improves moisture control and visibility, and aids in patient management. It is essential for all root canal and pulp therapy for permanent teeth, and is advisable for restoration of 1° teeth. If placement of a rubber dam is not possible, plastic disposable salivary ejectors are better tolerated than the metal flange type.
[1396][Heading 1] Instruments
[1397][Para 017] Burs
[1398][Para 005] High-speed: pear-shaped bur numbers 330 and 525, and short fissure bur number 541. Slow-speed: a selection of pear-shaped and round burs are most useful. For access use a small bur and for caries removal use the largest round bur which fits into the cavity.
[1399][Para 006] Handpiece
[1400][Para 005] A miniature-head handpiece is invaluable. Some children are apprehensive of the aspirator tip, making use of a high-speed, water-cooled handpiece difficult; others find the vibration of the slow-speed handpiece distressing, and may confuse it with pain. In these cases distraction or counting (i.e. ‘I will count to three each time, then I will stop’) can help. Occasionally it is possible, but time-consuming, to complete cavity preparation with hand instruments.
[1401][Heading 1] Material selection for intracoronal restorations
[1402][Para 017] GIC
[1403][Para 005] This has advantages of adhesion and fluoride release, but is more technique sensitive and less wear resistant than amalgam. Useful in non-load-bearing Class III and V cavities, temporization of 1° teeth in young, pre-cooperative children, or teeth near to exfoliation.
[1404][Para 006] Resin-modified GI cement (RMGIC)
[1405][Para 005] This has been demonstrated to have excellent performance in 1° teeth.
[1406][Para 006] Compomer
[1407][Para 005] A modified composite-type material with some of the properties of GIC. More technique and moisture sensitive than amalgam, but studies suggest similar longevity.
[1408][Para 006] Composite resin
[1409][Para 005] Early studies suggested poor performance in 1° teeth, but modern materials placed with good isolation (i.e. rubber dam) perform as well, or better than amalgam, but take longer to place.
[1410][Para 042]  Plastic, intracoronal restorations perform best in 1° molars with small Class I and II cavities. SS crowns (…… Stainless steel crowns, p. 88) give superior longevity where lesions are more extensive.
[1411][Para 006] Amalgam
[1412][Para 005] Because of concerns about toxicity and environmental pollution, plus the availability of alternative materials, amalgam is less frequently used.
[1413][Para 042]  The European Parliament agreed on 14 March 2017 to the final version of its Regulation on Mercury, the EU’s instrument to ratify the Minamata Treaty of 2013. This stipulates that amalgam is not to be used for the Rx of 1° teeth, in children <15yrs, or in pregnant or breastfeeding women, except when strictly deemed necessary by the practitioner on the ground of specific medical needs of the patient (from 1 July 2018).
[1414][Para 008] However, many clinicians outside the EU still consider amalgam to be an acceptable and durable material for Class I and II restorations in 1° molars.
[1415][Heading 1] Principles of cavity design
[1416][Para 017] Outline form
[1417][Para 005] Should include any undermined enamel. Extension for prevention is now outmoded, but any suspect adjacent fissures should be included. Do not cross transverse marginal ridges unless they are undermined.
[1418][Para 006] Caries removal
[1419][Para 005] Caries should be excavated from the ADJ first. If necessary, you may need to re-establish outline form to improve access to ensure the ADJ is caries free. Then progress to carefully removing caries from floor.
[1420][Para 006] Resistance form/retention form
[1421][Para 005] While not as crucial with adhesive materials, ensuring reasonable resistance form is of value in load-bearing situations.
[1422][Heading 1] Reasons for failure of restorations in primary teeth
[1423][Para 001] Recurrent caries, often due to failure to adequately complete caries removal because of flagging patient cooperation or failure to use adequate LA. If unable to finish cavity it is better to place a temporary dressing (GIC often best) and try again at another visit.
[1424][Para 001] Cavity preparation does not satisfy the mechanical requirements of the filling material.
[1425][Para 001] Inadequate moisture control, especially true of GICs, compomers, and composites.
[1426][Para 001] Presence of occlusal high spot.
[1427][Para 016] There are many others, but these are the most common.
[1428][Heading 1] Useful tips
[1429][Para 001] Let the child participate by ‘looking after’ the saliva ejector or cotton wool.
[1430][Para 001] If the child is nervous give them some control by asking them to signal, e.g. by raising their hand, if they want you to stop.
[1431][Para 001] If the child’s cooperation runs out before the cavity is completed, try and ensure all caries is removed from the ADJ and place a dressing of either zinc oxide or GIC. This should suffice for several visits, until you are ready to try again.
[1432][Para 001] LA is easier to give in the maxilla, so most advocate starting with an upper tooth.
[1433][Para 001] Don’t try to do too much at one visit—plan Rx at a pace the child can accept.
[1434][Heading 1] Communication
[1435][Para 004]  It is important to explain to the child what you are doing, and why, in terms they can understand.
[1436][Para 008] It may be helpful to describe some of the instruments we use in ways that can make them seem less threatening to a child (‘childrenese’) (e.g. see Table 3.4).
[1437][Para 036] Table 3.4 Unthreatening alternatives for dental terms (‘childrenese’)
[1438][Para 009] Plastic restoration in primary molars
[1439][Para 014] See …… Anatomy of primary teeth (and relevance to cavity design), p. 78 for anatomy of 1° molars and effect upon cavity design. Have all necessary instruments and filling materials ready so that appointment is kept as short as possible.
[1440][Para 001] Explain and show child (and parent) what you are going to do.
[1441][Para 001] Appropriate LA (…… Local analgesia for children, p. 82). Waiting for the LA to work is sometimes a good opportunity to deliver/reinforce preventive advice,
[1442][Para 001] In a small cavity, gain access with a high-speed handpiece and pear-shaped bur. The outline can then be established and caries removed.
[1443][Para 001] Approximal caries—cut down through the marginal ridge to allow access for caries removal. Ideally should just extend into embrasures and walls of box should converge occlusally (i.e. the box is wider at the base than at occlusal level) (Fig. 3.4).
[1444][Para 023] 
[1445][Para 019] Fig. 3.4 Adequate depth and width.
[1446][Para 001] In larger cavities, an excavator or large round bur can be used to start caries removal from the walls. Any undermined enamel should be cut back.
[1447][Para 001] If caries is deep, stop and re-assess whether pulpotomy (…… Primary molar pulp therapy, p. 93) is required. If outline form extends beyond acceptable limits, consider an SS crown, especially in Class II cavities.
[1448][Para 001] Check retention and that walls are caries free.
[1449][Para 001] Wash and dry cavity.
[1450][Para 001] Line with hard-setting calcium hydroxide if using amalgam.
[1451][Para 001] Check occlusion.
[1452][Para 016]  Reinforce good aspects of the child’s behaviour with praise and possibly a sticker/badge/toothbrush.
[1453][Para 009] Stainless steel crowns
[1454][Para 014]  SS crowns are the most durable restoration for 1° molars with extensive caries and those where pulp Rx has been performed.
[1455][Para 042]  SS crowns are preformed metal crowns made from high-grade SS and do contain small traces of nickel. They are therefore not suitable for patients with a known nickel allergy.
[1456][Heading 1] Indications
[1457][Para 001] Badly broken down 1° molar.
[1458][Para 001] After pulp therapy in 1° molars.
[1459][Para 001] As interim measure for 2° molars, where crowns are required but the patient is too young.
[1460][Para 001] Temporary coverage during preparation of cast crown for premolar or 2° molar.
[1461][Para 001] Developmental anomalies.
[1462][Para 001] Severe tooth loss due to bruxism/erosion.
[1463][Para 006] Instruments
[1464][Para 005] High-speed tapered diamond bur and diamond occlusal wheel. Straight handpiece and a stone. Slow-speed handpiece and burs as required. Crown scissors, dividers, selection of suitable crowns, and Adam’s pliers. Johnstone contouring pliers (no. 114) and Abel pliers (no. 112) can also be useful, but are not essential.
[1465][Para 008] There are two principal methods for placement:
[1466][Heading 1] Conventional technique
[1467][Para 004] SS crowns rely for retention only on a tight adaptation at the gingival margin of the preparation, therefore taper of preparation walls is not critical (Fig. 3.5).
[1468][Para 001] LA and if possible rubber dam.
[1469][Para 001] Measure M–D length with dividers to aid crown selection.
[1470][Para 001] Remove caries.
[1471][Para 001] Occlusal reduction (~1mm), roughly following cuspal planes.
[1472][Para 001] Approximal reduction (~20° from vertical) using tapered diamond, without producing a ledge at gingival margin.
[1473][Para 001] Remove buccal and lingual bulbosities only sufficient to seat crown (often little/no reduction required).
[1474][Para 001] Select crown. Correct size will be a ‘click’ fit.
[1475][Para 001] Check height and occlusion. Minor prematurity is not a problem. If extensive blanching of surrounding tissues or over-extended, trim crown. Usually not necessary.
[1476][Para 001] Use pliers to adapt contact points and crimp margins. Smooth trimmed margins with stone.
[1477][Para 001] Cement with zinc polycarboxylate or GIC.
[1478][Para 016] Technique for 2° molars (Fig. 3.6) is similar but more careful adjustment is necessary.
[1479][Para 023] 
[1480][Para 019] Fig. 3.5 Preparation for stainless steel crown.
[1481][Para 023] 
[1482][Para 019] Fig. 3.6 The same tooth as in Fig. 3.2 following placement of a stainless steel crown.
[1483][Heading 1] ‘Hall’ technique
[1484][Para 004] Taught as the gold standard for restoring 1° molars with distal or mesial caries. No conventional preparation or caries removal is normally carried out, and is referred to by advocates as a ‘biological’ technique (as opposed to ‘conventional’). After simply removing any loose debris, a crown is cemented over the carious, unprepared molar, with the child ‘biting’ the cement-filled crown down into place. The technique has several potential advantages, and it may allow effective Rx for children who might otherwise be unable to accept ‘conventional’ interventions. LA is not usually required and it is quicker than conventional SS crown placement. Advocates of the technique suggest that it achieves a coronal seal, cuts off carious lesions from substrate, and protects the pulp from chemical, thermal, and mechanical insults. It is recommended that its use is restricted to asymptomatic teeth with no evidence of pulpal inflammation/necrosis/periodontal involvement.
[1485][Para 006] Basic ‘Hall’ technique
[1486][Para 001] Separators placed a few days before may aid placement.
[1487][Para 001] Check carious 1° molar free from obvious pulpal or periradicular pathology.
[1488][Para 001] Select correct-size crown, fill with a suitable cement (GIC is recommended) and place on tooth.
[1489][Para 001] Advise child and parent that the patient may feel pushing when seating the crown.
[1490][Para 001] Get child to bite down on crown, seating it onto the tooth.
[1491][Para 001] Clear away excess cement.
[1492][Para 001] Crown is likely to be in premature occlusion, but as long as this is not gross, occlusion usually evens out by dento-alveolar compensation within a few weeks.
[1493][Heading 1] Success rates
[1494][Para 004] A number of studies have demonstrated that both conventional and Hall technique crowns have a far superior longevity to conventional restorations in 1° teeth. Initial studies of ‘Hall’ technique SS crowns have also indicated very favourable results probably due to creation of an effective pericoronal seal.14 The UK FiCTION (Filling Children’s Teeth—Indicated Or Not?) trial is nearing completion and aims to provide more information about the relative merits of ‘conventional’ vs ‘biological’ techniques.
[1495][Para 009] Class III, IV, and V in primary teeth
[1496][Para 014] Carious 1° incisors and canines are seen less frequently than molars and are usually indicative of a high caries rate during early infanthood (…… Severe early childhood caries, p. 92).
[1497][Heading 1] Management
[1498][Para 004] Objectives are relief of pain and prevention. Aesthetics are less important.
[1499][Heading 1] Rx options
[1500][Para 004] Include:
[1501][Para 001] Extraction.
[1502][Para 001] Topical 2% sodium fluoride and observation. Intervene if caries progresses.
[1503][Para 001] Make self-cleansing (with flat fissure no. 1 bur) plus topical fluoride.
[1504][Para 001] Restoration with adhesive materials.
[1505][Heading 1] Class III restoration
[1506][Para 004] Similar technique to that used for permanent incisors, but omit incisal retention groove.
[1507][Heading 1] Class IV restoration
[1508][Para 004] If restoration is essential the greater strength of composite is required. Polycarboxylate (strip) crowns are advocated by some paedodontists, for the well-motivated child.
[1509][Heading 1] Class V restoration
[1510][Para 004] Remove caries with a small round bur and restore with GIC/composite.
[1511][Heading 1] Composite strip crowns
[1512][Para 004] Cellulose acetate crown forms for 1° incisors. Enable restoration of 1° incisors using composite resin.
[1513][Para 009] Severe early childhood caries
[1514][Para 022] Aetiology
[1515][Para 004] Frequent ingestion of sugar &/or reduced salivary flow.
[1516][Heading 1] Nursing bottle or bottle mouth caries
[1517][Para 004] Terms used to describe patterns of early childhood caries (ECC) associated with frequent consumption of a sugar-containing drink, especially from a feeding-bottle. Commonly the child falls asleep with the bottle of juice or milk and suckles during the night. Possibly related to the relatively high levels of lactose in breast milk.15 The WHO recommends mothers exclusively breastfeed their child for the first 6 months before introducing nutritious complementary foods.16 Characteristically, starts with the maxillary 1° incisors, but in more severe cases the first 1° molars are also involved. The mandibular incisors are relatively protected by the tongue and saliva.
[1518][Para 008] Severe ECC may also be associated with the prolonged and frequent intake of sugar-based medications; however, both pharmaceutical companies and doctors are more aware of the problem and the number of alternative sugar-free preparations is i. See Table 3.6 for a list (p. 119). Recent studies have confirmed that ECC may be associated with prolonged breastfeeding beyond age 2yrs. Children >1yr old who suckle frequently during the night may be most at risk. Breastfeeding is considered to be optimal for babies and should be encouraged. Counselling about the possible role of on-demand breastfeeding in ECC should be approached with sensitivity and understanding.
[1519][Heading 1] Rampant caries
[1520][Para 004] A term with no specific definition, but often used to describe extensive, rapidly progressing caries affecting many teeth in the 1° &/or permanent dentition.
[1521][Heading 1] Radiation caries
[1522][Para 004] Radiation for head and neck cancer may result in fibrosis of salivary glands and salivary flow. Patients often resort to sucking sweets to alleviate their dry mouth, which exacerbates the problem. Management of radiation caries requires specialist referral.
[1523][Para 009] Primary molar pulp therapy
[1524][Para 014] NB: 1° molar roots resorb.
[1525][Para 008] Where the carious process has jeopardized pulpal sensibility there are two alternatives: (i) extraction and (ii) pulp therapy.
[1526][Heading 1] Indication and contraindications
[1527][Para 035] See …… Extraction versus restoration of primary teeth, p. 80.
[1528][Para 001] Any medical condition where a focus of infection is potentially dangerous is a C/I to pulp therapy.
[1529][Para 001] Pulp therapy may be preferable to extraction in children with bleeding disorders.
[1530][Para 001] Tooth must be restorable following pulp therapy.
[1531][Para 016] The ∆ of the state of the pulp can be difficult, as not only is a child’s perception of pain less precise than an adult’s, but the clinical picture may also be complicated by death of one root canal while the other(s) remain vital.
[1532][Heading 1] Indicators of possible pulp involvement
[1533][Para 001] Breakdown of marginal ridge.
[1534][Para 001] Symptoms.
[1535][Para 001] Tenderness to percussion, ↑ mobility, and buccal swelling/sinus.
[1536][Para 001] Inter-radicular radiolucency seen radiographically (usually on b/w radiographs).
[1537][Heading 1] Definitions
[1538][Para 001] Indirect pulp Rx: Rx without exposure of the pulp.
[1539][Para 001] Direct pulp capping: management of exposure by direct capping—not usually advocated in 1° molars due to poor outcomes.
[1540][Para 001] Pulpotomy: removal of coronal pulp and Rx of radicular pulp.
[1541][Para 001] Pulpectomy: removal of entire coronal and radicular pulp.
[1542][Para 009] Pulp therapy techniques
[1543][Para 022] Indirect pulp Rx
[1544][Para 004] Indicated for asymptomatic, vital 1° molars with no pulp exposure after removal of all soft caries. In common with the Hall crown, this is considered by some as a ‘biological’ technique and aims to maintain health and vitality of the 1° tooth pulp, which may be more resilient and have greater ability to recover from insult than traditionally thought. Recent studies have shown relatively high rates of success in teeth without evidence of irreversible pulpal damage.
[1545][Para 006] Technique
[1546][Para 005] Removal of all soft caries. Leaving carious, but firm, affected dentine in vital, asymptomatic 1° molars has been shown to be reasonably successful. Margins of cavities should be rendered caries free to ensure an adequate coronal seal. Works best in occlusal cavities, less likely to be successful in approximal caries due to early pulpal involvement and difficulty in achieving a good coronal seal. Setting calcium hydroxide can be used in the deepest portion, with GIC, composite, or a SS crown (see …… Stainless steel crowns, p. 88). If pulp exposure occurs, pulpotomy/pulpectomy are usually more appropriate restorative techniques.
[1547][Heading 1] Pulpotomy (for the vital primary molar pulp)
[1548][Para 004] In 1° molars the relatively larger pulps result in earlier pulpal involvement, therefore amputation of the coronal pulp leaving healthy radicular pulp in situ (pulpotomy) gives more consistent results than techniques that attempt to retain vitality of the whole pulp, e.g. indirect pulp capping.
[1549][Para 006] Materials
[1550][Para 005] The most commonly used medicaments are:
[1551][Para 001] Formocresol—historically widely used for 1° teeth pulpotomy, because of its ease of use and high success rate (70–90%) However, recent concerns about the toxicity and potential mutagenicity of formalin-containing compounds has led many authorities to advise against its use where suitable alternatives exist.
[1552][Para 001] Ferric sulfate—the technique recommended by many authorities as an alternative to formocresol.17 Success rates have been shown to nearly match formocresol, but are more technique sensitive.
[1553][Para 001] Calcium hydroxide—very time-consuming and more technique sensitive, but similar success to ferric sulfate in some studies.
[1554][Para 001] Mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA)—recent studies demonstrate similar success to formocresol. Very expensive.
[1555][Para 001] Bioactive dentine substitutes—recent studies show promising results in 1° tooth pulpotomy.
[1556][Para 001] Devitalizing paste (paraformaldehyde)—has fallen out of favour (for the same reasons as formocresol).
[1557][Para 006] Technique
[1558][Para 001] Give LA and place rubber dam.
[1559][Para 001] Complete cavity preparation and excavate caries.
[1560][Para 001] Remove roof of pulp chamber.
[1561][Para 001] Amputate coronal pulp with a large excavator or sterile round bur.
[1562][Para 001] Wash chamber and arrest bleeding with damp cotton wool.
[1563][Para 001] Place cotton wool pledget dampened with 15.5% ferric sulfate on exposed pulp stumps for at least 1min, then remove. Alternatively, once bleeding arrested, place CaOH or MTA over root stumps.
[1564][Para 001] Apply dressing of reinforced zinc oxide eugenol (ZOE) cement.
[1565][Para 001] Restore tooth, usually with a stainless steel crown (Fig. 3.7).
[1566][Para 023] 
[1567][Para 019] Fig. 3.7 Pulpotomy restored with stainless steel crown.
[1568][Para 006] Problems
[1569][Para 001] Necrotic pulp (i.e. no bleeding)—proceed with non-vital technique or extract.
[1570][Para 001] Profuse haemorrhage—indicates more serious inflammation of the radicular pulp. Intermediate dressing with Ledermix® followed by non-vital technique or extraction.
[1571][Heading 1] Pulpectomy (for non-vital primary molar pulp)
[1572][Para 004] A pulpectomy is often considered difficult in 1° molars because of the complexity of ribbon-shaped canals (although instrumentation is often easier than some texts might suggest). The risk of damage to the permanent successor also needs to be considered, but if conditions are favourable it is the Rx of choice for non-vital pulps. The technique can be carried out in one or two visits.
[1573][Para 001] LA and rubber dam.
[1574][Para 001] Remove the necrotic pulp, locate and file and irrigate canals (sodium hypochlorite 0.1%).
[1575][Para 001] Cleanse to within 2–3mm of apex, but avoid extending beyond.
[1576][Para 001] Fill canal with plain ZOE paste, non-setting calcium hydroxide, or iodoform paste (e.g. Vitapex®) with a spiral filler.
[1577][Para 001] Restore with SS crown.
[1578][Para 001] Arrange clinical and radiographic review.
[1579][Para 016] If there is evidence of any infection a two-stage Rx is recommended, leaving non-setting calcium hydroxide in the canals for 1–2 weeks prior to filling.
[1580][Para 006] Success rate
[1581][Para 005] A success rate of >80% at 3yrs has been reported.
[1582][Heading 1] Pulp therapy for primary anterior teeth
[1583][Para 004] Usual Rx is extraction, as A and B are exfoliated before patient is able to cooperate satisfactorily with more complicated Rx. However, C is exfoliated later and unilateral loss may result in centre-line shift, therefore pulp Rx is indicated for some patients. The root canal morphology is amenable to pulpectomy and the canal should be cleaned using files, with care (remember underlying successor). A resorbable filling material, e.g. calcium hydroxide or ZOE, should be used.
[1584][Para 009] Dental trauma
[1585][Para 014]  If there is evidence of head injury, transfer patient to hospital immediately.
[1586][Heading 1] Note
[1587][Para 001] By 12yrs of age, 33% of boys and 19% of girls have experienced at least one episode of dental trauma.18
[1588][Para 001] Prognosis ↑ with good immediate Rx, therefore see patient as soon as possible.
[1589][Para 001] Avulsed permanent teeth should be replanted immediately.
[1590][Para 001] Child and parent may be upset, therefore handle accordingly and defer any non-urgent Rx.
[1591][Para 001] Take good notes for future reference and medico-legal purposes.
[1592][Para 001] If crown # this will have dissipated most of the energy of impact, therefore root # less likely.
[1593][Para 001] Clinical photos would be beneficial at this stage.
[1594][Heading 1] History
[1595][Para 004] Take a structured history as an aide-memoire and for medico-legal purposes.
[1596][Para 001] Loss of consciousness? Concussion/headache/vomiting (…… Assessing head injury, p. 492)? Refer immediately to hospital.
[1597][Para 001] Accompanied by? Parent/teacher? Consider consent issues.
[1598][Para 001] When? Time interval between injury and Rx affects prognosis.
[1599][Para 001] Where? Does patient need a tetanus booster? If so, refer to a GMP or hospital.
[1600][Para 001] How? Be alert to the possibilities of other injuries and child abuse.
[1601][Para 001] Tooth fragments? These may have been inhaled or embedded in soft tissues (e.g. lip). If fragment/tooth not accounted for &/or loss of consciousness, a chest X-ray (CXR) is mandatory.
[1602][Para 001] Past dental history (PDH)—previous trauma may affect prognosis and cooperation in the dental setting.
[1603][Para 001] Past medical history (PMH)—check for bleeding disorder and allergy to penicillin. Ask about immunosuppression, this may impact your decision on whether or not to reimplant a tooth.
[1604][Heading 1] Aims of Rx
[1605][Para 001] 1° dentition: (i) preserve integrity of permanent successor; (ii) preserve 1° tooth if cooperation good and compatible with first aim.
[1606][Para 001] 2° dentition: (i) preserve vitality of the tooth to allow maturation of the root; (ii) restore the crown to prevent drifting, tilting, and over-eruption.
[1607][Heading 1] Principles of Rx
[1608][Para 017] Emergency Rx
[1609][Para 001] Elimination of pain.
[1610][Para 001] Protection of pulp.
[1611][Para 001] Reduction and immobilization of mobile teeth.
[1612][Para 001] Suturing of soft tissue lacerations (IO—3/0 resorbable suture (Dexon®, Vicryl®); EO—refer to hospital).
[1613][Para 001] ? Antibiotics, ? tetanus, ? analgesics, ? chlorhexidine mouthwash.
[1614][Para 006] Intermediate Rx
[1615][Para 001] Pulp therapy.
[1616][Para 001] Consider orthodontic requirements and long-term prognosis of damaged teeth.
[1617][Para 001] Semi-permanent restorations.
[1618][Para 001] Keep under review, usually 1 month, 3 months, and then 6-monthly for 2yrs.
[1619][Para 006] Permanent Rx
[1620][Para 001] Usually deferred until >16yrs (to allow pulpal and gingival recession and ↓ likelihood of further trauma); e.g. definitive crown.
[1621][Heading 1] Classification of tooth injuries
[1622][Para 004] Several exist; some use roman numerals, others describe the injuries sustained (WHO system):
[1623][Para 001] Complicated #—pulp exposed.
[1624][Para 001] Uncomplicated #—pulp intact.
[1625][Heading 1] Prevention
[1626][Para 001] Prevalence ↑ as the overjet (o/j) ↑ (>9mm prevalence doubles), ? early orthodontics.
[1627][Para 001] Mouthguard for sports (vacuum-formed thermoplastic vinyl best, triple thickness).
[1628][Para 016] Be alert for evidence of child abuse (…… Safeguarding children, p. 100).
[1629][Para 009] Safeguarding children
[1630][Para 014]  All professionals involved with children need to be aware of the principles of safeguarding and alert to the possibility of child abuse or neglect.
[1631][Para 008] NB: the term ‘child abuse’ is now favoured over ‘non-accidental injury’.
[1632][Para 008] The following signs are associated with abuse:
[1633][Para 001] Usually younger children are involved.
[1634][Para 001] The presenting injuries may not match the parent’s account of how they were sustained. The account may change over time.
[1635][Para 001] Delay attending at a surgery or clinic for Rx of the injury.
[1636][Para 001] Bruises/injuries of different vintages are found on examination.
[1637][Para 001] Ear pinches and frenal tears in children <1yr old are highly suspicious.
[1638][Para 001] 50% of abused children will have signs on the head &/or neck.
[1639][Para 016] ‘Child Protection and the Dental Team’ is a detailed and practical web-based resource developed by COPDEND/DOH aimed specifically at dentists and other DCPs and can be accessed at …… http://www.cpdt.org.uk.
[1640][Heading 1] Management
[1641][Para 004] Local guidelines are produced by Local Safeguarding Children Boards (LSCBs) or Area Child Protection Committees. To find yours, type ‘LSCB’ followed by your area into an Internet search engine. A copy of the local LSCB guidance should be kept in every practice.
[1642][Para 006] If abuse is suspected
[1643][Para 001] Take a careful history and keep full records.
[1644][Para 001] Discuss concerns with an experienced/trusted colleague and decide if further action/referral is justified.
[1645][Para 001] Provide any urgent/emergency dental care.
[1646][Para 001] Talk to child and parents—tactfully explain your concerns, seeking consent to sharing of information. Rarely, if you feel informing the parents/carers may put the child or others (including yourself) at risk, you may still share information &/or refer if you believe it is in the child’s best interests to do so. Make sure to arrange review with child and parents before they leave the appointment.
[1647][Heading 1] Where to get help and advice
[1648][Para 004] (Tip: write the telephone numbers of the first three on this list on your copy of the local LSCB guidance.)
[1649][Para 001] Child protection nurse.
[1650][Para 001] Local consultant paediatrician.
[1651][Para 001] Social services.
[1652][Para 001] Child’s health visitor.
[1653][Para 001] Your defence organization.
[1654][Heading 1] Making a referral
[1655][Para 004] Referral should be made directly to social services and followed up in writing within 48h. The child’s medical practitioner should also be informed. If a child presents with serious injuries which are suspicious, they should be referred to the nearest accident and emergency department, with the department informed of the situation before the child’s arrival.
[1656][Para 008] Tact and understanding is required when dealing with the patient’s family. Try to avoid making accusations and concentrate on treating the patient’s injuries, expressing the need to refer them on to experts who will be able to fully evaluate the situation and offer appropriate help.
[1657][Para 009] Injuries to primary teeth
[1658][Para 014] About 30–40% of 5yr-olds have experienced dental trauma,19 most frequently at toddler stage. As alveolar bone is more elastic the younger the child, the most common injuries are luxation or avulsion. Crown and root # are relatively rare.
[1659][Heading 1] Management
[1660][Para 004] For definitions, see …… Definitions, p. 108. If radiographs are required, you may have to get the parent to hold the child and film. Alternatively, try placing a periapical film between the teeth (like an occlusal view) and angle the beam at 45°.
[1661][Para 008] There is a need to consider the effect of any proposed Rx upon the permanent successor.20 Splinting of 1° incisors is exceedingly difficult and not indicated. When in doubt, extract 1° tooth!
[1662][Para 006] Concussion of tooth
[1663][Para 005] Rx: reassurance and soft diet.
[1664][Para 006] Subluxation
[1665][Para 005] If tooth near to exfoliation, extract. Otherwise, soft diet (for about 1 week). May become non-vital, therefore keep under observation. Give appropriate advice regarding possible complications.
[1666][Para 006] Lateral luxation/extrusion
[1667][Para 005] Extraction if loose and tooth in danger of being inhaled, or if tooth interferes with occlusion. If crown displaced labially, ↑ risk of damage to underlying 2° incisor.
[1668][Para 006] Intrusion
[1669][Para 005] Most common injury (>60%). If X-ray confirms that tooth has been forced into follicle of 2° tooth, extract 1° incisor. Otherwise leave tooth and wait to see if spontaneous eruption will occur (between 1 and 6 months). Unfortunately, pulpal necrosis often follows, necessitating either pulp Rx (…… Pulp therapy for primary anterior teeth, p. 96) or extraction. Should the tooth fail to erupt, then extraction is indicated. It is prudent to warn parents about possible damage to underlying permanent tooth.
[1670][Para 006] Avulsion
[1671][Para 005] Replantation not recommended due to risk of damage to permanent successor.
[1672][Para 006] Crown fracture
[1673][Para 005] Rare. Minimal # can be smoothed and left under observation. Larger # either restore with composite &/or RCT if pulp involved, or extract.
[1674][Para 006] Root fracture
[1675][Para 005] Provided it is not displaced and there is little mobility, advise a soft diet and keep under review. If coronal fragment is displaced or mobile, extract, but leave the apical portion as it will usually resorb.
[1676][Heading 1] Sequelae of trauma
[1677][Para 017] Primary dentition
[1678][Para 056] Discoloration
[1679][Para 025] If tooth becomes grey/reddish in early post-trauma period, pulp may be vital and discoloration reversible.
[1680][Para 008] Greying later indicates pulp necrosis. Yellowing of tooth is suggestive of calcification of pulp—no Rx required.
[1681][Para 028] Ankylosis
[1682][Para 025] Rx: extraction to prevent displacement of 2° incisor.
[1683][Para 028] Pulp death
[1684][Para 025] Rx: RCT or extraction.
[1685][Para 006] Permanent dentition
[1686][Para 005] In >50% of children <4yrs, trauma to a 1° tooth affects the underlying developing successor.21 The effect depends upon stage of development, type of injury and severity, Rx, and pulpal sequelae. Trauma can cause hypomineralization, hypoplasia (likelihood ↑ if <4yrs &/or injury more severe), dilaceration, severe malformation, and arrest of development.
[1687][Para 009] Injuries to permanent teeth—crown fractures
[1688][Para 014] Prevalence: 26–76% of injuries.
[1689][Heading 1] Enamel only
[1690][Para 004] For small enamel #, smooth with white stone.
[1691][Heading 1] Enamel and dentine
[1692][Para 004] Need to protect exposed dentine, preferably with a hard-setting calcium hydroxide cement and an acid-etch retained composite. If time permits, this can be done with a crown former to restore tooth contour. Keep under review. Veneer or porcelain jacket crown (PJC) can be considered later. If # near to pulp, treat as for pulp involvement.
[1693][Para 006] Acid-etch composite tip technique
[1694][Para 001] Place rubber dam, if possible.
[1695][Para 001] Place hard-setting calcium hydroxide on exposed dentine. No need to bevel enamel.
[1696][Para 001] Using contralateral tooth as guide, select a cellulose acetate crown former.
[1697][Para 001] Trim crown former to within 1–2mm of # line.
[1698][Para 001] Etch enamel for 20sec, wash, and dry.
[1699][Para 001] Place bonding resin and cure.
[1700][Para 001] Put sufficient composite and a little extra into crown former and position.
[1701][Para 001] Allow to cure and remove crown former.
[1702][Para 001] Trim, using soflex discs.
[1703][Para 001] Check occlusion.
[1704][Heading 1] Enamel, dentine, and pulp
[1705][Para 004] Rx depends upon size of exposure, state of root development (1 root radiographically complete 10–11yrs, histologically 14–15yrs), time since injury, and other injuries (e.g. root #). If apex open, there is an ↑ blood supply to pulp, therefore likelihood of pulp death d. This is advantageous as Rx should be directed towards retaining vitality of radicular pulp to allow root closure to continue. If pulp non-vital, see …… Root canal treatment—rationale, p. 338. Otherwise, Rx alternatives are as follows:
[1706][Para 006] Pulp cap
[1707][Para 005] Indications: exposure <1mm; <24h; complete or incomplete root development; pulp still vital. Cover exposure with calcium hydroxide (e.g. Dycal®), and place composite tip. Review vitality.
[1708][Para 006] Partial (Cvek) pulpotomy
[1709][Para 005] Indications: exposure >1mm; >24h; complete or incomplete root development, pulp still vital.
[1710][Para 001] LA and rubber dam.
[1711][Para 001] Slightly enlarge access at site of exposure with high speed and amputate pulp to a depth of 2–4mm into healthy pulp tissue.
[1712][Para 001] Arrest bleeding with sterile, moist cotton wool (usually takes several minutes).
[1713][Para 001] Cover amputation site with non-setting calcium hydroxide.
[1714][Para 001] Seal with GIC.
[1715][Para 001] Restore crown.
[1716][Para 006] Full coronal pulpotomy
[1717][Para 005] Indications: large, contaminated exposures; long duration; incomplete root development; coronal pulp demonstrates impaired vascularity.
[1718][Para 001] LA and rubber dam.
[1719][Para 001] Open up pulp chamber and amputate coronal pulp to cervical construction with sterile bur/sharp excavator.
[1720][Para 001] Wash with sterile water.
[1721][Para 001] Place non-setting calcium hydroxide and restore tooth with polycarboxylate or GIC and composite.
[1722][Para 001] Leave 6–8 weeks, then review symptoms and vitality. No need to investigate for presence or not of a calcific barrier.
[1723][Para 001] If tooth becomes non-vital, see …… Root canal treatment—rationale, p. 338.
[1724][Para 016] All pulpotomized teeth should be kept under long-term review as pulp necrosis and calcification are common sequelae. Success rates of 72% for cervical pulpotomies and 96% for minimal (Cvek) pulpotomies have been reported.22
[1725][Para 009] Root fractures
[1726][Para 022] Prevalence
[1727][Para 004] Account for <10% of injuries to permanent dentition.
[1728][Para 001] Where root # is suspected, two X-ray views at different angulations in the vertical plane are advisable to improve chances of visualizing the # line.
[1729][Para 001] The prognosis for this type of injury depends upon whether the # line communicates with the gingival crevice. Actual Rx depends on position of #. The prognosis is also affected by the degree of dislocation of apical and coronal fragments and mobility/displacement.
[1730][Heading 1] Apical third
[1731][Para 004] Usually no Rx is required unless mobility ↑ significantly. However, the tooth should be kept under observation as death of coronal two-thirds of pulp may occur. Only need to prepare canal to # line as apical third usually retains vitality. Prognosis good. If extraction required, apical third can be left in situ to preserve bone.
[1732][Heading 1] Middle third
[1733][Para 004] In the majority of cases the tooth is loosened, therefore rigid splinting is advisable to attempt to achieve hard-tissue union of # line. 12 weeks of rigid splinting was previously advocated, but recent evidence suggests flexible splinting for 4 weeks may give a similar outcome.23 If coronal part is not displaced, loss of vitality is unlikely. Where coronal fragment is displaced, re-position, splint, and if loss of vitality occurs, RCT to # line. Calcium hydroxide should be used as an interim dressing to limit inflammation and resorption. Delay in Rx ↓ prognosis. If extraction required, consider leaving apical portion in situ.
[1734][Heading 1] Coronal third
[1735][Para 004] In this group there is a high risk of direct communication with the gingival crevice, allowing ingress of bacteria into pulp. Where no obvious risk, flexible splinting for a prolonged period (up to 4 months) is advocated.24 Where the # line extends coronally, emergency Rx is either (i) temporary stabilization or (ii) extraction of the coronal fragment. Definitive Rx usually is extraction of both parts of tooth or, preferably, removal of the coronal fragment, and appropriate RCT of remainder, followed by placement of a dressing which will prevent gingival tissues overgrowing root surface. Can use a temporary post-retained crown, but repositioning of the coronal fragment using a dentine-bonding agent and composite has been described. Permanent Rx is post and core crown.
[1736][Para 008] If # extends below alveolar crest, need improved access for crown fabrication. There are two alternatives, shown in Table 3.5.
[1737][Para 008] An orthodontic extrusion will need either an upper removable appliance (URA) or a sectional fixed appliance (FA) with an attachment bonded on to the labial surface of a temporary post and core crown or any available enamel. Gentle forces of 50–100g should be used. When sufficient extrusion has been achieved, retain for at least 3–6 months before fabricating a permanent restoration.
[1738][Para 036] Table 3.5 Improving access for crown fabrication
[1739][Heading 1] Oblique
[1740][Para 004] Provided # does not extend above alveolar crest, can treat as coronal #. Otherwise, consider extraction of coronal portion only, leaving apical portion in situ to preserve bone.
[1741][Heading 1] Vertical
[1742][Para 004] Extraction is often the only option.
[1743][Para 008] If tooth extracted, a P/− will need to be fabricated (…… Treatment planning for patients with missing teeth, p. 274).
[1744][Para 009] Luxation, subluxation, intrusion, and extrusion
[1745][Para 014] Prevalence: 15–40% of injuries.
[1746][Heading 1] Definitions
[1747][Para 017] Concussion
[1748][Para 005] Injury to supporting tissues of tooth, without displacement.
[1749][Para 006] Lateral luxation
[1750][Para 005] Displacement of tooth (laterally, labially, or palatally).
[1751][Para 006] Subluxation
[1752][Para 005] Actually means partial displacement, but commonly used to describe loosening of a tooth without displacement.
[1753][Para 006] Intrusive luxation
[1754][Para 005] Displacement of tooth into its socket. Often accompanied by # of alveolar bone.
[1755][Para 006] Extrusive luxation
[1756][Para 005] Partial displacement of tooth from its socket.
[1757][Heading 1] Rx
[1758][Para 017] Concussion
[1759][Para 005] Reassurance and soft diet.
[1760][Para 006] Luxation
[1761][Para 005] Need to reposition tooth as soon as possible. Give LA and use fingers to push back into place. Then tooth should be splinted flexibly for 2–3 weeks. If there has been a delay of >24h since the injury, manual reduction is unlikely to be successful. In these cases the tooth can be repositioned orthodontically. If the displaced tooth is interfering with the occlusion a URA, with buccal capping, should be fitted as soon as possible. If root development is complete, loss of vitality is a common sequelae following luxation (~70%), leading to inflammatory resorption (…… Pulpal sequelae following trauma, p. 112). Teeth with immature apices have a much better chance of pulp survival. External or internal resorption and pulp canal obliteration may also occur, therefore keep under review.
[1762][Para 006] Subluxation
[1763][Para 005] If minor, no Rx other than advising a soft diet is necessary. If mobile, splint for 1–2 weeks and watch vitality.
[1764][Para 006] Intrusion
[1765][Para 005] Current UK guidelines25 advise passive repositioning, with commencement of orthodontic repositioning within 3 weeks for all teeth with open apices and for teeth intruded <3mm with closed apices. For intrusions of 3–6mm in teeth with a closed apex, consider orthodontic or surgical repositioning, and if intrusion exceeds 6mm with a closed apex, surgically reposition. Surgically repositioned teeth require flexible splinting for 1–2 weeks. Pulp death &/or root resorption can ensue rapidly after injury and early pulp extirpation and placement of the calcium hydroxide dressing is advisable. Pulp death is virtually certain in teeth with closed apices, and occurs in two-thirds of immature teeth. Replacement resorption is also a common sequel.
[1766][Para 006] Extrusion
[1767][Para 005] The affected tooth should be repositioned under LA with digital pressure and splinted for 1–2 weeks. Again, loss of vitality is a common sequel, so the tooth should be observed for any signs of resorption or pulp death.
[1768][Para 008] If any of these situations occur in conjunction with # of the alveolar bone, the splinting period should be ↑ to 3–4 weeks to aid bony healing. If, however, the socket is comminuted, splinting may need to be extended to 6–8 weeks.
[1769][Para 009] Splinting
[1770][Para 022] Indications
[1771][Para 001] To stabilize a loosened tooth to allow periodontal healing and improve patient comfort. In order to promote fibrous rather than bony healing (ankylosis), a short splinting time with a flexible splint is recommended: avulsion 7–10 days; luxation <3 weeks; middle third root # 4 weeks.
[1772][Para 001] To stabilize a cervical-third root # and encourage healing with calcified tissue, flexible splinting for up to 4 months is indicated.
[1773][Heading 1] Methods
[1774][Para 017] Direct
[1775][Para 005] Constructed on patient. An almost infinite variety has been described, but the following are the most popular:
[1776][Para 001] Acid-etch splint with composite/acrylic/epimine resin &/or wire.
[1777][Para 001] Orthodontic attachments and sectional archwire.
[1778][Para 001] Preformed metal (titanium trauma splint).
[1779][Para 001] Lone standing teeth can be supported by sling suture.26
[1780][Para 001] Lead foil &/or cement. Useful in Australian Outback, but better alternatives available in most dental surgeries!
[1781][Para 006] Indirect
[1782][Para 005] This type of splint is removable, which can cause trauma with insertion and removal, and therefore less preferable. It does, however, allow an assessment of mobility or firmness, which may be of value in cases of reimplantation. The more common types are:
[1783][Para 001] URA with cribs 6|6 and occlusal coverage.
[1784][Para 001] Vacuum-formed thermoplastic polyvinylacetatepolyethylene ‘Essix’ type.
[1785][Para 016] This approach requires an impression of a traumatized mouth and involves some delay (few hours/days) before the splint can be fitted; in practice, direct splinting is preferred.
[1786][Heading 1] Factors affecting choice of splint
[1787][Para 001] Type of injury and therefore length of time splint required. For example, coronal-third root # will need up to 4 months of splinting, therefore composite and wire splint is advisable. For a replanted tooth, prolonged splinting should be avoided as it may lead to ankylosis.
[1788][Para 001] Number of teeth injured and availability of uninjured adjacent teeth, e.g. if both 1|1 traumatized and no adjacent teeth, a full coverage acrylic splint or sling-suture may be indicated.
[1789][Para 001] Facilities and time available.
[1790][Para 009] Management of the avulsed tooth
[1791][Para 014] Exarticulation = avulsion. Prevalence: 0–16% of injuries.
[1792][Heading 1] Factors affecting prognosis
