[4067][Para 009] Treatment planning for patients with missing teeth
[4068][Para 014] Solutions for missing teeth will vary depending on the number, their location and function, and the patient’s wishes. A minimally invasive approach is preferable where possible. Twenty-one or more is considered the minimum number of teeth consistent with a functioning dentition but this may vary depending on the patient’s age, pattern of tooth loss, and incisal relationship. Replacement of missing teeth, therefore, isn’t always necessary. The Adult Dental Health Survey in 2009 showed that 86% of dentate adults had 21 or more natural teeth but this proportion ↓ significantly as age i.1 In 2009, 6% of adults aged 16yrs or over were edentulous compared with 37% in 1968. These edentulous patients are also in the older age groups.
[4069][Para 008] For those with insufficient teeth for satisfactory function and aesthetics, fixed or removable prosthodontic solutions will be needed. The use of bonding techniques and implants can help minimize unnecessary destruction of valuable tooth tissue.
[4070][Heading 1] Indications for the replacement of missing teeth
[4071][Para 001] ↑ masticatory efficiency.
[4072][Para 001] Improve speech.
[4073][Para 001] Preserve or improve health of the oral cavity by preventing unwanted tooth movements (vertical/rotational/tipping/drifting).2
[4074][Para 001] Improve distribution of occlusal loads.
[4075][Para 001] Space maintenance.
[4076][Para 001] Restore aesthetics.
[4077][Para 001] Prepare patient for complete dentures.
[4078][Heading 1] Treatment planning for the replacement of missing teeth
[4079][Para 017] History
[4080][Para 005] Active listening in order to clarify the patient’s aims and expected outcomes is essential.
[4081][Para 016] It is important to enquire about previous denture history (just because a patient is not wearing a denture does not mean that they have not had one) and assess the reasons for failure or success.
[4082][Para 006] PMH
[4083][Para 005] Medical factors can impact upon availability for Rx and ability to cope with dentures. Some drugs may ↓ salivary flow.
[4084][Para 006] Social history
[4085][Para 005] Other considerations may affect Rx, e.g. transport arrangements.
[4086][Para 006] Clinical examination
[4087][Para 005] EO and IO examinations, including a thorough assessment of any pathology, remaining teeth, existing restorations, periodontium, and edentulous areas (ridge form and extent, compressibility of mucosa). Assess tongue size, tonicity of the lips, and the volume and viscosity of saliva. An evaluation of any current dentures: what to copy and what to correct. Some patients present with a collection of unsuccessful dentures!
[4088][Para 006] Special investigations
[4089][Para 005] Radiographs/sensibility testing (especially of potential bridge abutments). Mounted study models and wax-up in partly dentate cases.
[4090][Para 006] Diagnoses
[4091][Para 005] These are then listed and will allow appropriate Rx planning after considering the Rx options. If pre-existing denture problems are diagnosed, some could be addressed via modifications to the existing dentures prior to embarking on the construction of replacement prostheses.
[4092][Heading 1] Options for the replacement of missing teeth
[4093][Para 017] No replacement
[4094][Para 005] First consider whether benefits of replacing missing teeth (improved mastication, speech, occlusal stability, and aesthetics) outweigh disadvantages (↑ oral stagnation, tooth preparation, cost). If not, then replacement is C/I. An occlusion with the second premolar to the second premolar present in each jaw (shortened dental arch) is usually functionally adequate.
[4095][Para 006] Bridges
[4096][Para 005] (…… Bridges, p. 278.) These have the advantage that they are fixed. Resin-bonded cantilever design is minimally invasive. Conventional bridges can have good appearance, but are destructive of tooth tissue, moderately expensive, and require lengthy clinical time.
[4097][Para 006] Implant-supported prostheses
[4098][Para 005] These can be fixed or removable and have the advantage of avoiding preparation of natural teeth but involve surgical procedures and are expensive. They help maintain supporting bone and have a high level of predictability if carefully planned and carried out.
[4099][Para 006] Removable partial dentures
[4100][Para 005] (…… Removable partial dentures—principles, p. 292.) These can be minimally invasive as only minor (or no) tooth preparation is required but ↑ plaque accumulation/changes in composition. Damage to soft tissues and remaining teeth is exacerbated by poor denture design and/or lack of patient care. Can be a good option when there are multiple edentulous areas or as a training/interim appliance prior to F/F. Can be used to replace missing soft tissue and aesthetics can be very good but patients often dislike removable prostheses.
[4101][Para 006] Complete immediate dentures
[4102][Para 005] These are indicated for patients who have already mastered wearing a partial denture and whose remaining teeth have a poor prognosis.
[4103][Para 006] Complete dentures
[4104][Para 005] These require patient compliance as well as good clinical and technical management for success. They can replace hard and soft tissue, but patients tend to dislike them and successful denture control can be difficult for patients to master.
[4105][Para 008] In the older, partially dentate patient it is important to assess whether the patient is likely to retain some functional teeth for the remainder of their lifespan. If this is improbable, some advocate providing F/F dentures while the patient is still young enough to adapt.
[4106][Para 006] Orthodontic space closure
[4107][Para 005] This is an option that is seldom used but may be appropriate, particularly in the imbricated dentition.
[4108][Heading 1] Treatment planning
[4109][Para 004] If replacement is indicated: consider fixed or removable prosthesis. A number of factors affect this decision (Table 7.1).
[4110][Para 008] These factors need to be favourable if expensive and complex bridge-work is required. Removable prostheses are indicated if general or local factors are less than ideal. Always consider implants or shortened dental arch therapy.
[4111][Para 006] Treatment options
[4112][Para 005] These must be clearly explained to the patient with the advantages and disadvantages of each. This is essential in the management of expectations and to allow informed consent.
[4113][Para 006] Initial treatment
[4114][Para 001] Relief of pain and any emergency Rx including temporary modification of existing dentures, if indicated.
[4115][Para 001] Unless immediate dentures are planned, extract any teeth with hopeless prognosis. Consider extraction of teeth with poor prognosis.
[4116][Para 001] OHI and periodontal Rx.
[4117][Para 001] Preliminary design of partial denture.
[4118][Para 001] Carry out restorations required.
[4119][Para 001] Modify design if necessary and commence prosthetic Rx (…… Removable partial dentures—clinical stages, p. 300).
[4120][Para 001] Removal of pathological abnormalities (e.g. retained roots), and pre-prosthetic surgery, if required.
[4121][Para 001] Carry out definitive prosthetic Rx.
[4122][Para 036] Table 7.1 Fixed or removable prosthesis?
[4123][Para 009] Bridges
[4124][Para 022] Definitions
[4125][Para 017] Bridge (fixed partial denture)
[4126][Para 005] A prosthetic appliance that is definitively attached to remaining teeth and replaces a missing tooth or teeth.
[4127][Para 006] Abutment
[4128][Para 005] A tooth which provides attachment and support for a bridge.
[4129][Para 006] Retainer
[4130][Para 005] The part of the fixed prosthesis that is cemented or bonded to an abutment tooth in order to provide retention. In the case of an implant, this may be screw or cement retained.
[4131][Para 006] Pontic
[4132][Para 005] The artificial tooth that is suspended from the abutments.
[4133][Para 006] Connector
[4134][Para 005] The component that joins the pontic to the retainer. May be rigid or non-rigid.
[4135][Para 006] Saddle
[4136][Para 005] The area of edentulous ridge over which the pontic will lie.
[4137][Para 006] Units
[4138][Para 005] Number of units = number of pontics + number of retainers.
[4139][Para 006] Retention
[4140][Para 005] Prevents removal of the restoration along the path of insertion or vertical direction of the preparation.
[4141][Para 006] Support
[4142][Para 005] The ability of the abutment teeth to bear the occlusal load on the restoration.
[4143][Para 006] Resistance
[4144][Para 005] The features of tooth preparation that enhance the stability of a restoration and resists dislodgement along an axis other than the path of placement.
[4145][Heading 1] Types of bridge
[4146][Para 017] Fixed–fixed
[4147][Para 005] The pontic is anchored to the retainers with rigid connectors at either end of the edentulous span. Both abutments provide retention and support. Both preparations must have at least one common path of insertion to allow the prosthesis to be fully seated.
[4148][Para 006] Fixed–movable
[4149][Para 005] The pontic is anchored rigidly to the major retainer at one end of the span and via a movable joint to the minor retainer at the other end (Fig. 7.1). The major abutment provides retention and support while the minor abutment provides support only. This design allows some independent movement of the minor abutment and has the advantage that the preparations need not be parallel.
[4150][Para 006] Direct–cantilever
[4151][Para 005] Pontic is anchored at one end of the edentulous span only.
[4152][Para 006] Spring cantilever
[4153][Para 005] A tooth-retained, mucosal-supported bridge. The retainer and pontic are remote from each other and connected by a metal bar which runs along the palate. Usually an upper incisor is replaced from the premolars or a molar. It is useful where there is an anterior diastema or if the posterior teeth are heavily restored; however, they are often poorly tolerated. These are rarely used now.
[4154][Para 006] Minimal or no preparation resin-bonded bridges
[4155][Para 005] Retained by resin composite (…… Resin-bonded bridges, p. 288). May be adhered by glass ionomer adhesives when considered for temporary purposes.
[4156][Para 006] Compound/hybrid
[4157][Para 005] Combination of more than one of the types listed.
[4158][Para 006] Removable
[4159][Para 005] Can be used to describe screw-retained implant bridges and removable partial dentures. Can be removed by dentist for maintenance.
[4160][Para 023] 
[4161][Para 019] Fig. 7.1 Fixed movable bridge replacing the lower left first permanent molar.
[4162][Heading 1] Types of retainers
[4163][Para 001] Full coverage crown.
[4164][Para 001] Three-quarter crown.
[4165][Para 001] Onlay.
[4166][Para 001] Inlay.
[4167][Para 016] All of these restorations have been used as retainers in conventional bridgework. They are listed in order from most retentive to least retentive. Wherever possible, one of the first two should be used, as the failure rate of the last three is much higher. Post crowns should be avoided if possible, and onlays or inlays should only ever be used as minor retainers in fixed–movable bridges. It is ideal to aim for equal retention on abutments unless deliberately trying to ‘build in’ a failure point.
[4168][Heading 1] Selection of abutment teeth
[4169][Para 004] General factors must be taken into account, e.g. caries status and existing restorations. Also, two other considerations specifically relate to bridgework—retention and support.
[4170][Para 006] Assessment of retention
[4171][Para 005] Retention offered by a potential abutment tooth depends on clinical crown height and the available surface area. It is important to assess the amount of enamel present for retention for resin-bonded bridges. Obviously, larger teeth offer more retention and should be chosen in preference to smaller ones. The teeth of both arches are listed in Table 7.2 in order of the amount of retention offered (if a full coverage restoration is used).
[4172][Para 036] Table 7.2 Assessment of retention
[4173][Para 083] 
[4174][Para 155] 
[4175][Para 006] Assessment of support
[4176][Para 005] Three factors are important:
[4177][Para 001] Crown–root ratio. Ideally should be 2:3 but 1:1 is acceptable. As bone is lost, the lever effect on the supporting tissues is i.
[4178][Para 001] Root configuration. Widely splayed roots provide more support than fused ones.
[4179][Para 001] Periodontal surface area. Ante’s law, ‘the combined periodontal area of the abutment teeth must be at least as great as that of the teeth being replaced’, has no scientific basis and no longer has a place in contemporary bridgework design. It does not take into account that we are dealing with a biological system—as the load is ↑ on the abutment teeth, a biofeedback mechanism operates to cause a reduction in this load.
[4180][Para 085] The teeth of both arches are listed in Table 7.3 in order of the support offered, assuming that the periodontal tissues are intact.

[4184][Para 006] Taper and parallelism
[4185][Para 001] For most designs, abutments should be prepared with a common path of insertion.
[4186][Para 001] Opposing walls of abutments should have a 6° taper or a total degree of convergence of 12°.
[4187][Para 001] Checking parallelism: direct vision, with one eye; survey mirror with parallel lines inscribed.
[4188][Para 001] Management of tilted abutments (…… Tilted abutments, p. 282).
[4189][Heading 1] Types of pontic
[4190][Para 017] Modified ridge lap
[4191][Para 005] This type of pontic should make (minimal) contact with the buccal aspect of the ridge. Gives good aesthetics and is the most popular type.
[4192][Para 006] Bullet
[4193][Para 005] Makes point contact with the tip of the ridge. Can be used for posterior bridgework.
[4194][Para 006] Ovate
[4195][Para 005] Aims to address the issue of emergence profile in the maxillary anterior region. Has greater mucosal contact and applies light pressure to the underlying mucosa. Needs a smooth, convex surface to allow flossing. The patient must have excellent OH. The ‘modified ovate pontic’ lies slightly more labial to the ovate pontic, so tends to be used more in aesthetic areas.
[4196][Para 006] Hygienic
[4197][Para 005] Does not contact saddle, therefore supposedly easy to clean but can still be challenging and may lead to food packing if insufficient clearance. Unaesthetic, therefore limited to molar replacement.
[4198][Para 006] Saddle (ridge lap)
[4199][Para 005] Extends over ridge buccally and lingually, therefore difficult to clean. Should not be used.
[4200][Para 009] Bridges—design
[4201][Para 022] Designing bridges
[4202][Para 001] Assess prognosis of all teeth in vicinity to ↓ risk of another tooth requiring extraction in the near future.
[4203][Para 001] Assess possible abutment teeth (check restorations, endodontic status, periodontal condition, mobility, and take periapical radiographs).
[4204][Para 001] Select design of retainers, e.g. full or partial crown. Full coverage is preferred.
[4205][Para 001] Consider pontics and connectors.
[4206][Para 001] With this information compile a list of possible bridge designs.
[4207][Para 001] Consideration of the advantages and disadvantages of each design combined with a diagnostic wax-up should help to narrow down the choice. Where possible, try the least destructive alternative first.
[4208][Heading 1] Specific design problems
[4209][Para 017] Periodontally involved abutments
[4210][Para 005] First control periodontal disease. Then consider whether a bridge is indicated. A fixed–fixed type of design is preferable to splint teeth together. Consider fibre-reinforced resin composite fixed partial dentures for this specific indication.
[4211][Para 006] Pier abutments
[4212][Para 005] This is the central abutment in a complex bridge that supports pontics on either side, which are in turn anchored to the terminal abutments. In this situation, the pier abutment can act as a fulcrum and when one part of the bridge is loaded the retainer at the other end experiences an unseating force which can lead to cementation failure. To overcome this a stress-breaking element must be introduced, e.g. fixed–movable joint, or avoid pier abutments by simplifying the design.
[4213][Para 006] Tilted abutments
[4214][Para 005] Occurs most commonly following loss of a molar. There are several approaches if bridgework is planned:
[4215][Para 001] Orthodontic Rx to upright abutments.
[4216][Para 001] Two-part bridge, e.g. fixed–movable.
[4217][Para 001] Telescopic crowns—placement of individual gold shell crowns on abutments, over which the telescopic sleeves of the bridge fit.
[4218][Para 001] Precision attachments—a precision screw and screw tube can be incorporated into a two-part bridge. After cementation the screw is inserted, which effectively converts the bridge to a fixed–fixed design.
[4219][Para 006] Canines
[4220][Para 005] The canine is often the keystone of the arch, and a very difficult tooth to replace. The adjacent teeth are poor in terms of the amount of retention and support that they offer and the canine is often subject to enormous stresses in lateral excursion (in a canine-guided occlusion). If a canine is to be replaced with a bridge, the occlusal scheme should be designed to provide group function in lateral excursion—never canine guidance.
[4221][Para 009] Bridges—practical stages
[4222][Para 014] As always, a thorough history and examination are required (…… Treatment planning for patients with missing teeth, p. 274). It is essential to clarify the patient’s attitude to and expectation of Rx. They must be assessed for active disease due to poor OH or diet and for pre-existing TMD. The response to initial Rx to stabilize active disease should be monitored before embarking on definitive Rx. If bridgework is planned, the following stages are carried out:
[4223][Para 001] Diagnostic mounting—take accurate impressions of both arches, a facebow record, and have the models mounted on a semi-adjustable articulator. The mounting can be carried out either in ICP (best fit) or in RCP, for which a precentric record will be necessary. If a reorganized approach to reconstruction is being considered, or if the clinical examination has revealed significant occlusal interferences, an RCP mounting should be performed. Carefully examine the occlusion and consider what occlusal consequences the proposed restoration will have.
[4224][Para 001] Diagnostic waxing—in effect, this is a mock-up of the final restoration on the mounted models. Wax can be added to the teeth to simulate the effect that the restoration will have on the final occlusion and aesthetic result. In the anterior part of the mouth a denture tooth can be used. In addition to assessing aesthetics and occlusion, the diagnostic wax-up can serve as a template from which the temporary bridge can be constructed. An impression is taken of the wax-up in a silicone putty and saved for later. At this stage, the design of the prosthesis must be finalized.
[4225][Para 001] Preparations—before the preparations are carried out, any suspect restorations in the abutment teeth are replaced. Preparations are carried out in accordance with basic principles (see Chapter 6) and care is taken to ensure that a single path of insertion is established. When checking for parallelism, one eye should be kept closed and the use of a large mouth mirror is very helpful. Custom-made paralleling devices can be used but they are very cumbersome.
[4226][Para 001] Temporary bridge—this is normally constructed using the matrix which has been formed from the diagnostic wax-up; in this way the temporary bridge should reproduce the aesthetics and occlusion of the final bridge (if the wax-up was done properly!). The matrix is filled with one of the proprietary temporary crown and bridge resins (e.g. Protemp®) and seated over the preparations. After it has set it is removed, trimmed, polished, and cemented with a temporary cement (e.g. TempBond®). Or a laboratory-made temporary bridge may be used. The pontic should be contoured so that it is hygienic (e.g. to a modified ridge lap design).
[4227][Para 001] Impressions—an impression is taken using an elastomeric material. Ideally, all of the preparations should be captured on one impression, but this can be very difficult if multiple preparations are involved. If difficulties are encountered in this respect, they can often be overcome by using the transfer coping technique. In this technique, acrylic (DuraLay®) copings are made on dies of the preparations for which a successful impression has been achieved. These are then taken to the mouth and seated on the appropriate tooth, and the impression repeated to capture the other preparations. On removal, the coping will be removed in the impression and the dies can be reseated in the copings and a new model poured around them. CAD/CAM digital techniques can also be used.
[4228][Para 001] Occlusal registration—under most circumstances the models will be mounted in ICP in the position of best fit, and therefore an occlusal registration will not be necessary. Where numerous preparations have been carried out and it is difficult to locate this position, or where there is a lack of AP stability in the models, some form of inter-occlusal record will be necessary. A popular technique involves the use of transfer copings, and is described in the section on occlusion (…… Occlusal records, p. 237).
[4229][Para 001] Metal work try-in—if a porcelain fused to metal bridge is being constructed, it is advisable to try-in the metal work before the porcelain is added, particularly for larger span bridges. At this stage the fit of the framework can be evaluated and the occlusion adjusted. On occasions it will be found that one retainer seats fully while the other does not. This can occur if there has been some minor movement of the abutments since the impression was taken. If this is the case the bridge should be sectioned, and hopefully both retainers will then seat. The two parts are then secured in their new position with acrylic resin (DuraLay®) and sent back to the laboratory for soldering.
[4230][Para 001] Trial cementation—the finished bridge is tried in and any necessary adjustments made. The bridge should then be temporarily cemented (with modified TempBond®) for a period of a week or so. The advantage of a trial cementation period is that if any further adjustments are necessary they can be carried out outside the mouth and the restoration repolished and reglazed. The patient is instructed in how to clean the bridge (use of Super Floss® or an interdental brush).
[4231][Para 001] Permanent cementation—after the period of trial cementation, the bridge is re-evaluated and the patient asked if they are happy with it. If all is well the bridge is removed and cemented with a permanent cement (usually traditional or RMGIC).
[4232][Para 001] Follow-up—arrangements are made to recall the patient to check that the bridge is still functioning satisfactorily.
[4233][Para 009] Bridge failures
[4234][Para 014] Patients should be warned about these prior to Rx.
[4235][Heading 1] Most common reasons for failure
[4236][Para 001] Loss of retention.
[4237][Para 001] Mechanical failure, e.g. # of casting.
[4238][Para 001] Problems with abutment teeth, e.g. 2° caries, periodontal disease, loss of vitality.
[4239][Heading 1] Management of failures
[4240][Para 004] Depending upon type and extent of problem:
[4241][Para 001] Keep under review.
[4242][Para 001] Adjust or repair in situ.
[4243][Para 001] Replace.
[4244][Heading 1] Replacement
[4245][Para 004] Before replacement of a bridge is embarked upon, a careful analysis of the reasons for failure is necessary. Minor problems in an otherwise satisfactory bridge should be repaired if at all possible. Fractured porcelain can be repaired with one of the specialized repair kits available (e.g. CoJet™). 2° caries or marginal deficiencies, if small, can be restored with traditional GIC. Failure may be due to loss of vitality. This is not necessarily an indication for removal of the bridge because RCT can often be carried out through the retainer of the abutment.
[4246][Heading 1] Removing old bridges
[4247][Para 004] To remove intact, try a sharp tap at the cervical margin with a chisel or preferably a slide hammer. Orthodontic band-removing pliers can also be used but these require a small hole to be cut in the occlusal surface. If only one retainer is loose, support the bridge in position while trying to remove it so that it does not bind.
[4248][Para 008] Retainers can be cut through, but this will destroy the bridge.
[4249][Para 009] Resin-bonded bridges
[4250][Para 014] This technique involves bonding a cast metal framework, carrying the pontic tooth, to abutment teeth using an adhesive resin. This type of bridge is almost exclusively used for cantilever adhesive bridgework, i.e. one abutment and one pontic (Fig. 7.2). Fixed–fixed designs have been problematic, with one retainer debonding being a common clinical finding. The resin bonds to the abutment tooth using the acid-etch technique and to the metal framework by either mechanical or chemical means. Fibre-reinforced bridges are also available.
[4251][Heading 1] Classification
[4252][Para 017] Position
[4253][Para 001] Anterior.
[4254][Para 001] Posterior.
[4255][Para 006] Retention
[4256][Para 001] Macromechanical:
[4257][Para 001] Perforated (Rochette).
[4258][Para 001] Mesh (Klett-O-Bond®).
[4259][Para 001] Particular (Crystalbond™).
[4260][Para 001] Micromechanical:
[4261][Para 001] Electrolytically etched (Maryland).
[4262][Para 001] Chemically etched.
[4263][Para 001] Chemical:
[4264][Para 001] Sandblasted.
[4265][Para 001] Tin-plated.
[4266][Para 016] Chemical retention to a sandblasted metal surface is now used virtually exclusively. A dual-affinity cement (e.g. Panavia™ 21) is used, which chemically bonds to both enamel and non-precious alloys.
[4267][Heading 1] Advantages
[4268][Para 001] Less expensive than conventional bridge or cobalt chromium partial denture or implant in the shorter term.
[4269][Para 001] Minimal or no tooth preparation required.
[4270][Para 001] No LA required as preparation is in enamel.
[4271][Para 001] Potential for rebond if debond occurs.
[4272][Heading 1] Disadvantages
[4273][Para 001] Tendency to debond especially if planning and preparation and placement technique is poor.
[4274][Para 001] Metal may show through abutments.
[4275][Para 001] Creation of a natural emergence profile can be challenging especially in very resorbed ridges. Use of an ovate pontic can be helpful.
[4276][Heading 1] Indications
[4277][Para 001] Short span-single tooth edentulous space.
[4278][Para 001] Sound abutment teeth (or only minimal restoration) and sufficient crown height to ensure sufficient surface area for acid etch bonding.
[4279][Para 001] Favourable occlusion.
[4280][Para 023] 
[4281][Para 019] Fig. 7.2 Adhesive cantilever bridgework replacing missing upper canines.
[4282][Heading 1] Treatment planning
[4283][Para 004] This is as for conventional bridgework. If orthodontic Rx is needed to localize space or upright adjacent teeth, it is advisable to retain with a removable retainer for at least 3 months prior to bridge placement.
[4284][Heading 1] Design
[4285][Para 004] The design is usually cantilever. If a fixed–fixed design is used and there is a debond of one retainer, caries can develop quickly and undetected under this retainer. Fixed–fixed design may be used if periodontal splinting is required or retention required following orthodontics.
[4286][Heading 1] Tooth preparation
[4287][Para 004] There is debate as to what is the ‘ideal’ preparation and some advocate no preparation. The need for preparation will be defined by the individual clinical situation.
[4288][Heading 1] Guidelines for preparation
[4289][Para 001] Give a single path of insertion. Provide near-parallel guiding planes eliminating undercuts, which allow coverage of maximal surface area for bonding.
[4290][Para 001] Provide space in occlusion to accommodate bridge. Need at least 0.7mm for wings.
[4291][Para 001] ↑ retention, e.g. using a wrap-around design (covering >180° of tooth circumference) to resist lateral displacement and reduce stress on the cement bond.
[4292][Para 001] Mesial and distal grooves enhance resistance form.
[4293][Para 001] To prevent gingival displacement a minimal chamfer is recommended.
[4294][Para 001] Provide axial loading of the abutments—prepare cingulum or occlusal rests.
[4295][Para 001] A connector height of at least 2mm is required.
[4296][Para 016] NB: tooth preparation should usually be confined to enamel, and the framework should be designed with maximal coverage (to ↑ surface area available for bonding).
[4297][Heading 1] Technique
[4298][Para 017] Chemical method using Panavia™ 21
[4299][Para 005] Following tooth preparation an elastomeric impression of the abutment teeth is taken plus an alginate impression of the opposing arch. At the try-in stage the bridge should be assessed for fit, aesthetics, etc., and then the fitting surface thoroughly cleaned with alcohol (assessment of occlusion may not be possible until after cementation). Contamination of the fitting surface with saliva must be avoided and cementation is best done under a rubber dam. Following etching and washing of the abutment(s), and placement of a dentine adhesive system, the wings of the bridge are coated with Panavia™ 21 and the bridge seated into place and held firmly until set. Use of acetate strips and Super Floss® at this stage will clear most of the excess cement and prevent it adhering to the adjacent teeth. The cement must then be covered with a substance known as OxyGuard®, which prevents O2 inhibition of the surface layer. After 3min the rubber dam is removed and any excess cement removed.
[4300][Heading 1] Problems
[4301][Para 076] Dentine exposed during preparation. Use a dentine adhesive system.
[4302][Para 001] Metal shining through abutments. Cut wings away incisally before cementation or use a more opaque cement. May have to consider conventional bridge or placing veneer on labial surface.
[4303][Para 001] Debonds. If one flange only, can usually detach other by a sharp tap with a chisel or by using ultrasonic scaler tips. If a persistent problem, consider conventional bridge. The trend is for these bridges to be used for cantilevered bridgework and it is not usual for fixed–fixed adhesive bridgework to be prescribed due to problems with unilateral debonding.
[4304][Para 076] Caries occurring under debonded wings. Remove bridge and repair.
[4305][Para 059] Further reading
[4306][Para 066] D. S. Thomas, et al. 2017 Article I. A systemic review of the survival and complication rates of resin-bonded fixed dental prostheses after a mean observation period of at least 5 years. Clin Oral Implants Res28 11.
[4307][Para 009] Removable partial dentures—principles
[4308][Para 022] Definitions
[4309][Para 017] Saddle
[4310][Para 005] That part of a denture which rests on and covers the edentulous areas and carries the artificial teeth and gumwork.
[4311][Para 006] Connector (major and minor)
[4312][Para 005] Joins together component parts of a denture.
[4313][Para 006] Support
[4314][Para 005] Resistance to vertical forces directed towards mucosa.
[4315][Para 006] Retainers
[4316][Para 005] Components which resist displacement of denture.
[4317][Para 006] Indirect retention
[4318][Para 005] Resistance to rotation about fulcrum axis by acting on the opposite side to the displacing force. Retention of the denture may be possible through other means as opposed to clasping, such as guide planes.
[4319][Para 006] Fulcrum axis
[4320][Para 005] Axis around which a tooth- and mucosa-borne denture tends to rock when saddles are loaded.
[4321][Para 006] Bracing
[4322][Para 005] Resistance to lateral movement.
[4323][Para 006] Reciprocation
[4324][Para 005] The mechanism by which lateral forces generated by a retentive clasp passing over a height of contour are counterbalanced by a reciprocal clasp passing along a reciprocal guiding plane.3
[4325][Para 006] Guide planes
[4326][Para 005] Two or more parallel surfaces on abutment teeth used to limit the path of insertion, and improve retention and stability.
[4327][Para 006] Survey line
[4328][Para 005] This indicates the maximum bulbosity of a tooth in the plane of the path of withdrawal.
[4329][Para 006] Free-end saddle
[4330][Para 005] Edentulous area posterior to the natural teeth.
[4331][Para 006] Stress-breaker
[4332][Para 005] A device allowing movement between the saddle and the retaining unit of partial denture.
[4333][Para 006] Gum-stripper
[4334][Para 005] A tissue-borne partial denture which can ‘sink’.
[4335][Para 006] Swinglock denture
[4336][Para 005] Has a labial retaining bar or flange which is hinged at one side of the mouth and locks at the other.4
[4337][Para 006] Sectional denture
[4338][Para 005] Made in two or more sections which are then fixed together with screws or other devices.
[4339][Heading 1] Classification
[4340][Para 017] Kennedy
[4341][Para 005] Describes the pattern of tooth loss (Fig. 7.3):
[4342][Para 001] Bilateral free-end saddles.
[4343][Para 001] Unilateral free-end saddle.
[4344][Para 001] Unilateral bounded saddle.
[4345][Para 001] Single, anterior bilateral bounded saddle. Must cross the midline.
[4346][Para 085] Any additional saddles are referred to as modifications (except Class IV), e.g. Class I modification 1 has bilateral free-end saddles and an anterior saddle.
[4347][Para 006] Craddock
[4348][Para 005] Describes the denture type:
[4349][Para 001] Tooth-borne.
[4350][Para 001] Mucosa-borne.
[4351][Para 001] Mucosa- and tooth-borne.
[4352][Para 023] 
[4353][Para 019] Fig. 7.3 Kennedy classification.
[4354][Heading 1] Acrylic versus metal dentures
[4355][Para 004] Approximately 75% of the dentures provided in the UK have an acrylic connector and base. Although metal bases are generally preferred because the greater strength of metal permits a more hygienic design, an acrylic base is indicated for:
[4356][Para 001] Temporary replacement, e.g. following trauma or in children.
[4357][Para 001] Where there is inadequate support from the remaining teeth for a tooth-borne denture.
[4358][Para 001] When additions to the denture are likely in the near future.
[4359][Para 016] However, where financial constraints C/I a metal base, attention to the following may avoid the production of a gum-stripper:
[4360][Para 001] Wide mucosal coverage to provide maximum support.
[4361][Para 001] Keep base clear of the gingival margins wherever possible.
[4362][Para 001] No interdental extensions of acrylic.
[4363][Para 001] Point contact and wide embrasures between natural and artificial teeth.
[4364][Para 001] Labial flanges for extra retention and bracing.
[4365][Para 001] Additional support from wrought SS rests.
[4366][Para 009] Removable partial dentures—components
[4367][Para 022] Saddles
[4368][Para 004] These can be made entirely of acrylic or have a sub-framework of metal overlaid by acrylic.
[4369][Heading 1] Rests
[4370][Para 004] These are an extension of the denture onto a tooth to provide support &/or prevent over-eruption. Occlusal rests are used on posterior teeth (usually over either the mesial or distal marginal ridge and fossa) and cingulum rests on anterior teeth. Rests may be wrought or cast; the latter is preferred for strength and fit.
[4371][Heading 1] Clasps
[4372][Para 004] These provide direct retention by engaging the undercut portion of a tooth (Fig. 7.4 and Fig. 7.5). The action of a clasp must be resisted either by a non-retentive clasp arm above the maximum bulbosity of the tooth or by a reciprocal connector. Clasps can be classified by their position (occlusally approaching or gingivally approaching) or by their construction and material. A minimum length of 14mm is generally advocated for cobalt–chrome clasps to prevent rapid distortion.
[4373][Para 006] Cast
[4374][Para 005] Cast (cobalt–chrome) clasps are stiff, easily distorted, and liable to #. However, provided they are limited to undercuts of 0.25mm, the advantage of being able to cast them as an integral part of a denture framework offsets these drawbacks.
[4375][Para 006] Wrought
[4376][Para 005] Wrought clasps are usually attached by insertion into the acrylic of a saddle. SS is the most commonly used alloy, but gold clasps are more flexible and easily adjusted (and distorted).
[4377][Para 008] The stiffer the wire, the smaller the undercut that can be engaged. This can be offset by reducing the diameter of the wire to ↑ flexibility (but ↑ the likelihood of #) or by ↑ the length of the clasp arm (e.g. gingivally approaching clasp). Cast cobalt–chrome can be too stiff for occlusally approaching clasps on premolar teeth. The actual design used depends upon:
[4378][Para 001] Depth of undercut: 0.25mm—cast cobalt–chrome; 0.5mm—SS wire; <0.75mm—wrought gold.
[4379][Para 001] Position of undercut on tooth and relative to saddle, e.g.:
[4380][Para 001] High survey line: gingivally approaching clasp or modify tooth shape by grinding.
[4381][Para 001] Diagonal survey line, (i) sloping down from saddle: gingivally or occlusally approaching (ring or recurved) clasp; (ii) sloping up from saddle: gingivally or occlusally (circumferential) approaching clasp.
[4382][Para 001] Medium survey line: as for previous bullet point.
[4383][Para 001] Low survey line: modify tooth shape, e.g. with resin composite.
[4384][Para 001] Position of tooth. Gingivally approaching clasps are less conspicuous and are therefore preferred for anterior teeth.
[4385][Para 001] Occlusion: adequate inter-occlusal space should be present or created for a clasp arm to cross a contact point between two natural teeth, to prevent occlusal disruption.
[4386][Para 001] Shape of sulcus: fraenal attachments and alveolar undercuts may prevent use of gingivally approaching clasps.
[4387][Para 001] Periodontal health: reduced periodontal support requires more flexible clasps to avoid overload.
[4388][Para 001] Material of denture base. Cast clasp arms are easily cast as part of the framework but for acrylic dentures wrought clasps are more usual.
[4389][Para 006] Connectors
[4390][Para 005] In addition to joining parts of the denture together, the connector can also contribute to support and retention (Table 7.4).
[4391][Para 006] −/P connectors
[4392][Para 001] Lingual bar should only be used if there is >7mm between floor of mouth and gingival margin to give 3mm clearance from gingivae. Does not contribute to indirect retention. Usually cast. C/I if incisors are retroclined. If insufficient space can use sublingual bar.
[4393][Para 001] Sublingual bar lies horizontally in anterior lingual sulcus, but opinions differ as to patient tolerance. More rigid than lingual bar.
[4394][Para 001] Lingual plate is well tolerated and provides good support, bracing, and indirect retention if used in conjunction with rests but covers gingival margins. Can be made of cast metal or acrylic.
[4395][Para 001] Continuous clasp is really a bar which runs along the cingulum of the lower anterior teeth and is usually used in conjunction with a lingual bar. Poorly tolerated.
[4396][Para 001] Dental bar is similar to continuous clasp, but of ↑ cross-sectional area and without lingual bar. Useful for teeth with long clinical crowns. Provides support and indirect retention. May not be well tolerated.
[4397][Para 001] Buccal/labial bar is indicated when the lower incisors are retroclined.
[4398][Para 016] Fig. 7.4 and Fig. 7.5 show the two most commonly used types of clasp.
[4399][Para 036] Table 7.4 P/− connectors
[4400][Para 023] 
[4401][Para 019] Fig. 7.4 Occlusally approaching three-arm clasp. One arm is the bracing reciprocal arm. One arm is the retentive component. One arm is the occlusal rest.

[4404][Para 009] Removable partial dentures—design
[4405][Para 014] P/P design is carried out after assessment of the patient and with reference to any previous dentures. A set of accurately articulated study models is essential.
[4406][Heading 1] Surveying
[4407][Para 004] Objectives:
[4408][Para 001] Establish path of insertion.
[4409][Para 001] Define those undercuts which may be used to retain the denture.
[4410][Para 001] Define those undercuts which require blocking out prior to finish.
[4411][Para 016] If the path of insertion is at 90° to the occlusal plane, insertion of the denture will be straightforward; however, where the teeth are tilted or few undercuts exist, an angled path of insertion may be advantageous. Whether this provides more resistance to displacement during function is controversial.
[4412][Para 008] A survey line can then be marked on the teeth to indicate their maximum bulbosity in the plane of the path of withdrawal. This is done using a dental surveyor.
[4413][Heading 1] Design
[4414][Para 001] Outline saddles. Usually straightforward. If less than half a tooth width or if in doubt of the need to replace a missing tooth, omit.
[4415][Para 001] Plan support. Support can be tooth only, mucosa only, or both. Tooth-borne support (occlusal and cingulum rests) should be used wherever possible, as teeth are better able to withstand occlusal loading and support will not be compromised following resorption. Tooth and mucosa support are inevitable with large or free-end saddles and where plate designs are used. Tissue-only support should be utilized when no suitable teeth are available, and is less damaging in the upper than the lower arch, because of the palatal vault.
[4416][Para 001] Need to assess the role of the denture, length of the saddles, the amount of support required (? denture opposed by natural or artificial teeth), and the potential of remaining teeth to provide support (root area in bone), before a final decision is made.
[4417][Para 001] Obtain retention. Retention can be:
[4418][Para 001] Direct. E.g. clasps, guide planes, soft tissue undercuts, or precision attachments. Of these, clasps are the most commonly used. The best arrangement is to use three clasps as far away from each other as possible. Guide planes help to establish a precise path of insertion and withdrawal. Need be only 2–3mm in length, reducing reliance on clasps. Composite resin can be added to abutment teeth to maximize undercuts.
[4419][Para 001] Indirect. This is derived by placing components so as to resist ‘rocking’ of the denture around direct retainers, e.g. by the position of clasps and rests and the type of connector. Particularly important with free-end and large anterior saddles.
[4420][Para 001] Assess bracing required. Bracing is provided by the connector, maximum saddle extension, and the reciprocal arms of clasps. Elimination of occlusal interferences ↓ need for bracing.
[4421][Para 001] Choose connector. After consideration of earlier listed points. Is there space in the occlusion to accommodate the chosen connector? Where possible, the connector should be cut away from the gingival margins.
[4422][Para 001] Reassess. ? As simple as possible. ? Aesthetic.
[4423][Para 001] Instructions to technician. Should include written details and diagram. Where some confusion may arise over the precise position of a component, it may be helpful to mark this directly on the cast. CAD programs are now available for design, communication, and production of prostheses.
[4424][Heading 1] Some design problems
[4425][Para 017] The lower bilateral free-end saddle (Class I)
[4426][Para 005] This presents a particular problem because of a lack of tooth support and retention distally, small saddle area compared to force applied, and distal leverage on abutment tooth in function (which ↑ with resorption). Possible solutions include:
[4427][Para 001] Maximize indirect retention by placing rests and clasps on mesial aspect of the abutment tooth and using lingual plate design.
[4428][Para 001] Using a muco-compressive impression of saddle area to ↓ displacement in function—the altered cast technique.
[4429][Para 001] Use fewer, smaller teeth and maximize base extension.
[4430][Para 001] RPI system for distal abutment teeth—mesial Rest, distal guiding Plate, and mid-buccal I bar. During function the saddle moves tissue-ward and rotates around the mesial rest. The plate and I bar are constructed in such a way as to disengage from the tooth and avoid potentially harmful loading.
[4431][Para 001] Stress-breaker design (advantages more theoretical than practical).
[4432][Para 001] Use precision attachments (beware of overloading abutments).
[4433][Para 006] Class IV
[4434][Para 005] Can sometimes avoid unsightly clasps anteriorly by the use of:
[4435][Para 001] A flange engaging a labial alveolar undercut.
[4436][Para 001] Avoiding distal facing clasps. A mesial-facing clasp will engage more as the anterior saddle tries to drop/rotate out.
[4437][Para 001] A rotational path of insertion5 utilizing rigid minor connectors that are rotated into proximal undercuts anteriorly.
[4438][Para 001] Interproximal undercuts, which may allow minimal display of clasps—‘hidden clasps’ (Fig. 7.6).
[4439][Para 001] An acrylic spoon denture held in place by the tongue.
[4440][Para 006] Multiple bounded saddles
[4441][Para 005] A horseshoe design, which utilizes guide planes for retention, may be indicated.
[4442][Para 023] 
[4443][Para 019] Fig. 7.6 Sectional partial denture (Implant bar retained).
[4444][Para 009] Removable partial dentures—clinical stages
[4445][Para 057] Assessment and treatment plan. …… Treatment planning for patients with missing teeth, p. 274.
[4446][Para 001] Take first impressions. These are usually taken using alginate in a stock tray. For free-end saddles modify the tray first with compound or silicone putty.
[4447][Para 001] Record occlusion. If ICP is obvious, the occlusion can be recorded conventionally (…… Occlusal examination, p. 236) at the same visit as first impressions. If ICP is not obvious, wax record blocks will be required and a separate visit. Where there are no teeth in occlusal contact, the steps involved are the same as for recording the occlusion for F/F (…… Complete dentures—recording the occlusion, p. 308). If there is an occlusal stop, but insufficient standing teeth to produce a stable relationship of the casts, the procedure is as follows:
[4448][Para 001] Determine the occlusal vertical dimension (OVD) and mark the position of two index teeth with pencil.
[4449][Para 001] Define the occlusal plane using the record block on which this is easiest, e.g. tooth to tooth in a bounded saddle, tooth to retromolar pad in a free-end saddle.
[4450][Para 001] Check the record blocks in the mouth, using the mark on the index teeth as a guide, and adjust blocks if necessary.
[4451][Para 001] Record occlusion with bite-recording paste.
[4452][Para 001] Check the relationship of the index teeth on the articulated casts corresponds to that in the mouth.
[4453][Para 057] Mounted casts are surveyed and denture designed (…… Occlusal considerations for restorative procedures, p. 236).
[4454][Para 001] Tooth preparation may be required to:
[4455][Para 001] Accommodate rest seats. Rests need to be >1mm for strength, therefore if insufficient room in occlusion to accommodate this bulk, tooth reduction is required.
[4456][Para 001] Establish guide planes.
[4457][Para 001] Accommodate clasp arms passing over contact points.
[4458][Para 001] Modify unfavourable survey line, e.g. ↓ bulbosity.
[4459][Para 001] ↑ retention, e.g. by the addition of resin composite to create undercuts.
[4460][Para 001] Consider crowning teeth with a poor long-term prognosis prior to denture construction.
[4461][Para 001] Record second impressions using a special tray. Alginate is the most commonly used material, but elastomers are preferable. It is helpful to have a wax try-in before the framework is made. This enables you to confirm the tooth position so that the retentive elements for the acrylic are placed appropriately.
[4462][Para 076] Try-in of framework:
[4463][Para 001] Check extension, adaptation, and position of clasp, and rests. If casting does not fit, use of correcting fluid may reveal which areas to relieve.
[4464][Para 001] Check upper and lower separately for OVD and occlusion, and then together.
[4465][Para 001] Major faults: repeat second impressions.
[4466][Para 001] Minor faults: adjust at finish.
[4467][Para 001] Re-record occlusion, if required.
[4468][Para 001] Select tooth mould and shade.
[4469][Para 001] Altered cast technique, if required.
[4470][Para 076] Try-in of waxed denture on framework:
[4471][Para 001] Check position of denture teeth.
[4472][Para 001] Check flange extensions/thickness.
[4473][Para 001] Check OVD and occlusion.
[4474][Para 001] Check aesthetics with patient and only proceed when patient is satisfied.
[4475][Para 001] Prescribe post-dam relief areas and management of undercuts.
[4476][Para 001] Finish. Once any fitting surface roughness is eliminated, the dentures are tried in separately, adjusting undercuts and contacts as required. The extension, occlusion, and articulation are then adjusted if necessary. Give the patient written and verbal instructions, and a further appointment.
[4477][Heading 1] Rebasing P/P
[4478][Para 004] Acrylic mucosa-borne dentures can be rebased at the chair-side with self-cure materials, but difficulty may be experienced in removing the denture in the presence of undercuts, and the materials are generally inferior to the original denture base. Alternatively, P/P can be rebased in the laboratory by means of a technique similar to that used for F/F (…… Rebasing, p. 314). Alternatively, make a new denture. For cast metal dentures an impression can be recorded of the saddle area using an elastomer or ZOE, while holding the denture by the framework. In all cases care must be taken to avoid the introduction of occlusal errors, e.g. ↑ OVD.
[4479][Para 009] Immediate complete dentures
[4480][Para 014] When the remaining teeth have a poor prognosis, the transition from the partly dentate to edentulous state must be managed carefully. Patients must be warned about the effects of resorption and the need for early rebasing/replacement. Rx planning must be thorough.
[4481][Heading 1] Rx alternatives for partial denture wearer
[4482][Para 001] A gradual transition towards being edentulous via additions to a transitional P/P can ↑ the chances of successful adaptation to F/F especially for the older patient.
[4483][Para 001] Immediate complete denture. This has the advantage that the form and position of the natural teeth can be copied and is said to promote better healing and reduce resorption, but frequent adjustments and early replacement are necessary.
[4484][Para 001] Overdenture (…… Overdentures, p. 324); may retain alveolar bone.
[4485][Heading 1] Rx alternatives for patients with no previous denture experience
[4486][Para 001] Provide a partial denture and allow the patient to adapt before progressing to an immediate complete denture—the best solution.
[4487][Para 001] Extract the majority of posterior teeth leaving sufficient only to maintain OVD and occlusal relationship, and then make immediate complete dentures when resorption has slowed.
[4488][Para 001] Extraction of the remaining teeth and provision of a denture after healing has occurred (post-immediate denture). Avoid if possible as considerable guesswork is involved in the subsequent denture and the chances of the patient coping successfully are d.
[4489][Heading 1] Types of immediate complete denture
[4490][Para 001] Flanged. Either full or part (extended 1mm beyond maximum bulbosity of ridge).
[4491][Para 001] Open face. No flange, artificial teeth sit over (or just into) the socket of the natural predecessor.
[4492][Para 016] Flanged dentures are preferable as they afford better retention and make subsequent rebasing easier. However, where a deep labial undercut exists into which it would be impossible to extend a flange, the choice is either surgical reduction or an open-face denture. Most patients choose the latter.
[4493][Heading 1] Clinical procedures
[4494][Para 057] 1° impressions (as for P/P, …… Removable partial dentures—clinical stages, p. 300).
[4495][Para 001] 2° impressions in alginate or silicone.
[4496][Para 001] Recording occlusion. Where there are sufficient posterior teeth remaining, a hand articulation should suffice, and this can be taken at the same visit as impressions are recorded. Otherwise, record blocks will be required.
[4497][Para 001] Try-in. This will be limited to those teeth that are already missing. Check fit, extension, and stability, etc. In addition, need to prescribe:
[4498][Para 001] Type of flange required.
[4499][Para 001] Any proposed changes in position of anterior artificial teeth compared to natural teeth.
[4500][Para 001] Extraction of remaining teeth as atraumatically as possible.
[4501][Para 001] Finish. Repeated removal and insertion of the denture should be avoided, therefore adjustments should be limited to making the patient comfortable. They should be instructed not to remove the denture before the review appointment in 24h.
[4502][Para 001] Review. The fitting and occlusal surfaces are adjusted as required. If dentures are unretentive they will require temporary reline (…… Denture problems and complaints, p. 318).
[4503][Para 001] Recall. Regular inspection of immediate dentures is important as rapid bone resorption means that they will require rebasing early. However, this should be deferred, if feasible, for at least 3 months after the extractions. A possible regimen is 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, and then yearly.
[4504][Heading 1] Laboratory procedures
[4505][Para 004] These are similar to F/F except that the plaster teeth are removed and the cast trimmed to mimic the changes that will occur in the hard and soft tissues following extraction, before final processing.
[4506][Heading 1] Surgical procedures
[4507][Para 035] See …… The extraction of teeth, p. 383 and …… Minor pre-prosthetic surgery, p. 426.
[4508][Heading 1] Problems
[4509][Para 001] Denture unretentive. Use a temporary reline material (replaced regularly) to tide patient over initial 3 months and then reline with heat-cure acrylic.
[4510][Para 001] Gross occlusal error. Adjust occlusal surface of one denture until even contact attained. This denture can then be replaced after initial resorption has occurred.
[4511][Para 009] Complete dentures—principles
[4512][Para 022] Retention
[4513][Para 004] The resistance of a denture to displacement. It is dependent upon (i) peripheral seal, (ii) contact area between denture and tissues, (iii) close fit, and (iv) viscosity/volume of saliva. Neuromuscular control has more to do with stability than retention.
[4514][Heading 1] Stability
[4515][Para 004] The ability of a denture to resist displacing forces during function. Influenced by forces acting on polished and occlusal surfaces, as well as the form of the supporting tissues.
[4516][Heading 1] Neutral zone
[4517][Para 004] The area where the muscular displacing forces are in balance.
[4518][Heading 1] Ways to optimize retention and stability
[4519][Para 001] Maximum extension of denture base (as far as the surrounding musculature will allow). The upper denture should extend distally over the tuberosities and onto the compressible tissue just anterior to the vibrating line on the palate. The lower denture should extend the full depth and width of the lingual pouch, and halfway across the retromolar pad. NB: over-extension will result in a denture that is easily displaced in function.
[4520][Para 001] As close an adaptation of denture base to mucosa as possible, to maximize the surface tension effects of saliva.
[4521][Para 001] Placement of the teeth in the neutral zone. More important in −/F. The better retention of F/− often allows some latitude in this respect.
[4522][Para 001] Correct shape of the polished surfaces so that muscle action tends to re-seat the denture.
[4523][Para 001] A good border seal. This is achieved by ensuring that the flanges fill the entire sulcus width and by placing a post-dam on compressible tissue.
[4524][Para 001] Balanced occlusion free from interfering contacts.
[4525][Heading 1] Common denture faults
[4526][Para 001] Lack of freeway space (FWS).
[4527][Para 001] Failure to reproduce closely enough the features of previous successful dentures.
[4528][Para 001] Occlusal errors.
[4529][Para 001] Incorrect adaptation and extension.
[4530][Para 009] Complete dentures—impressions
[4531][Para 014]  Tissues must be healthy before final impressions are recorded. If necessary, use tissue conditioner in present F/F (…… Tissue conditioners, p. 314).
[4532][Para 008] Classically, two sets of impressions are recorded of the edentulous mouth. The purpose of the first is to record sufficient information for a special tray to be made in which to record the second or master impression.
[4533][Heading 1] Preliminary impressions
[4534][Para 004] These are recorded using an (edentulous) stock tray and alginate, elastomer (both preferable for undercut or flabby ridges), or impression compound. A line should be marked on the impression to indicate to the technician the desired extension of the special tray. In the upper, the posterior limit should be the hamular notches and the vibrating line, and in the lower the retromolar pads.
[4535][Para 006] Special trays
[4536][Para 005] These can be made in self-cure or light-cure acrylic. The space left for the impression depends upon the material to be used: ZOE = 0.5mm; elastomer = 0.5–1.5mm (depending on viscosity); alginate = 3mm. For trays with >1mm space use greenstick stops clinically to aid positioning.
[4537][Heading 1] Master impressions
[4538][Para 004] These aim to record the maximum denture-bearing area, and to develop an effective border seal, the functional width and depth of the sulcus. The special tray should be modified by reducing any over-extension and the peripheries adapted by the addition of greenstick tracing compound. Non-perforated trays ensure that a peripheral seal with the upper tray can be demonstrated before taking the impression. However, a perforated tray reduces the compression of tissue leading to a more mucostatic impression. Gently manipulate the patient’s soft tissues and ask them to slightly protrude their tongue to imitate functional movements.
[4539][Para 006] Muco-compressive versus muco-static
[4540][Para 005] A muco-compressive impression technique is sometimes advocated to give a wider distribution of loading during function and to compensate for the differing compressibility of the denture-bearing area, thus preventing # due to flexion. ZOE or composition is used. However, dentures made by this method are less well retained at rest, which is the greater proportion of time. Alginate is said to be more muco-static. Tissue adaptation following a period of use probably reduces the clinical difference between the two techniques.
[4541][Heading 1] Special techniques
[4542][Para 017] Neutral zone impression technique
[4543][Para 005] This is used for recording the neutral zone in patients with limited natural retention for −/F.
[4544][Para 001] Record second impressions and occlusion.
[4545][Para 001] A fully extended acrylic baseplate is made on the lower cast, with wire loops added which do not extend above the occlusal plane.
[4546][Para 001] The upper trial denture or record block is inserted.
[4547][Para 001] Tissue conditioner is placed on the baseplate and around loops, and inserted.
[4548][Para 001] Ask patient to swallow, purse lips and say ‘Ooh’ and ‘Eee’.
[4549][Para 001] The impression is removed and trimmed down until it can be fitted onto the articulator to replace the lower occlusal rim.
[4550][Para 001] A mould of the impression is made into which wax is poured.
[4551][Para 001] The wax is cut away so that each denture tooth can be positioned within the zone recorded to make the trial denture. The polished surfaces should replicate the impression.
[4552][Para 006] Flabby (displaceable) ridge
[4553][Para 005] Classically occurs under a F/− opposed by natural lower teeth. If mild, then an impression recorded with alginate or elastomer in a tray perforated over the flabby area may suffice. For more severe cases a two-stage technique is required, using a special tray with a window cut out over the flabby tissue. First, an impression is recorded in the tray with ZOE and the paste trimmed away from the flabby area. This is then re-seated and low-viscosity elastomer or impression plaster placed into the window to complete the impression. NB: combination type cases should have the dentures constructed on a semi-adjustable articulator to minimize occlusal displacing forces.
[4554][Para 006] Functional impression
[4555][Para 005] Tissue conditioner is placed inside the patient’s existing denture. After several days of wear a functional impression is produced.
[4556][Heading 1] Common impression problems and faults
[4557][Para 001] A feather edge indicates under-extension. This can be corrected by the addition of greenstick to the tray and repeating.
[4558][Para 001] Tray border shows through impression material. Reduce tray in the area of over-extension and repeat the impression.
[4559][Para 001] Air blows. If small, can be filled in with a little soft wax. If large, retake the impression, or if using silicones or ZOE the impression may be added to.
[4560][Para 001] Tray not centred. Often partially due to using too much material so that it is difficult to see what is where. Remember to line up the tray handle with the patient’s nose (except for ex-boxers).
[4561][Para 001] Retching. A calm and confident manner is necessary for successful impressions. Gain the patient’s confidence by attempting the lower first and use a fast-setting, viscous material. Distraction techniques may help, e.g. wriggling the toes on the left foot and the fingers of the right hand at the same time (the patient, not the operator).
[4562][Para 001] Patient with dry mouth: ZOE is C/I; use elastomer instead.
[4563][Para 001] Areas where tray shows through in otherwise good impression. Can be overcome by prescribing a tin-foil relief when dentures are being processed.
[4564][Para 009] Complete dentures—recording the occlusion
[4565][Para 014] When recording the occlusion with wax rims mounted on rigid acrylic or shellac bases, the aim is to provide the technician with information for constructing trial dentures.
[4566][Para 016] As head posture can affect FWS, position the patient so that the Frankfort plane is horizontal. A wax trimmer and a heat source are required to adjust the rims.
[4567][Para 001] Check fit of bases. If poor, can either repeat second impressions, or take a ZOE or low-viscosity elastomer impression with the base and proceed.
[4568][Para 001] Adjust upper rim to give adequate lip support.
[4569][Para 001] Trim occlusal plane of upper rim.
[4570][Para 001] Position of the occlusal plane. This should be placed so that ~1–2mm (↓ with age) of tooth are visible below the patient’s upper lip at rest. The occlusal plane should lie midway between the ridges parallel to the inter-pupillary and the ala-tragal lines. At rest, the tongue should rise just above the lower occlusal plane posteriorly. Centre lines, canine lines, and smile line should be marked.
[4571][Para 001] Trim lower record block to obtain correct lip support and bucco-lingual position of posterior teeth.
[4572][Para 001] Adjust lower rim so that it meets upper evenly in RCP, with 2–4mm of FWS:
[4573][Para 001] Vertical dimension. The FWS is the space between the occlusal surfaces of the teeth when the mandible is in the rest position. In the majority of patients it is 2–4mm. The OVD for an edentulous patient can therefore be determined by measuring their resting face height and subtracting a FWS. Resting face height is assessed using:
[4574][Para 001] A Willis gauge, to measure the distance between the base of nose and the underside of the chin. Is only accurate to ±1mm.
[4575][Para 001] Spring dividers, to measure the distance between a dot placed on both the chin and the tip of the patient’s nose. This method is less popular with patients and is C/I for those with a beard.
[4576][Para 001] The patient’s appearance and speech.
[4577][Para 001] Mark the centre lines.
[4578][Para 001] Locate rims in RCP, e.g. with bite-recording paste:
[4579][Para 001] Horizontal jaw relationship. Record the more reproducible RCP. In the natural dentition, ICP is ~1mm forward of RCP; some prosthetists advise adjusting the finished dentures to allow the patient to slide comfortably between the two positions.
[4580][Para 001] Prescribe mould and shade of artificial teeth for try-in.
[4581][Para 001] Consider using a facebow registration to mount the maxillary cast on the articulator.
[4582][Heading 1] Position of the anterior and posterior teeth
[4583][Para 004] Ideally, the artificial teeth should lie in the space occupied by the natural dentition. The extent to which it is possible to compensate for a Class II or III malocclusion depends upon the retention afforded by the ridges. In the natural dentition the upper incisors lie ~10mm anterior to the posterior border of the incisive papilla. With resorption this comes to lie on the ridge crest, therefore the artificial teeth should be placed labial and buccal to the ridge, to give adequate lip support and a nasolabial angle of ~90°.
[4584][Para 008] Posterior teeth should be narrow to ↑ masticatory efficiency. Low-cusped teeth are preferred, but cuspless teeth are useful for patients with poor natural retention or a ‘wandering’ ICP. When considering the colour, mould, and arrangement of the anterior teeth, the patient’s age, facial appearance, and most importantly their opinion, must be considered. If you disagree about the suitability of their choice, document it.
[4585][Heading 1] Type of articulator to be used for setting up the teeth
[4586][Para 004] Most textbooks advocate semi-adjustable or average value articulators for F/F dentures. However, most dentures are made on simple hinge articulators to the satisfaction of the majority of patients, probably because they are able to adapt to the occlusion that results. An average value type is the preferred method. It will give some degree of balanced articulation which can then be refined in the mouth and will help avoid the introduction of occlusal interferences.
[4587][Heading 1] Common pitfalls
[4588][Para 001] Inaccuracies caused by poorly fitting bases.
[4589][Para 001] Rims contacting prematurely posteriorly and flipping-up anteriorly, or vice versa.
[4590][Para 001] Failure to provide adequate FWS. This is less likely to occur if the rest position is recorded with only one denture or rim in position.
[4591][Para 001] Attempting to correct too much when replacing old worn dentures and exceeding the adaptive capacity of the patient.
[4592][Para 009] Complete dentures—trial insertion
[4593][Para 014] Trial dentures are constructed by setting-up the prescribed teeth in wax on acrylic or shellac bases. Both the dentist and patient must be satisfied before the dentures are processed in acrylic.
[4594][Heading 1] Clinical procedures
[4595][Para 017] Check the trial dentures
[4596][Para 001] On and off the articulator. Comparison with the patient’s existing dentures is helpful to see if the features to be copied or modified have been successfully incorporated.
[4597][Para 001] Singly in the mouth. To check extension, stability, and the position of the teeth relative to the soft tissues.
[4598][Para 001] Together in mouth. Examine vertical dimension, occlusion, aesthetics, and phonetics (‘S’ sound will be affected by ↑ or ↓ FWS).
[4599][Para 006] Seek the patient’s opinion
[4600][Para 005] Some advocate getting patients to sign an acceptance slip before going to finish.
[4601][Para 006] Prepare post-dam
[4602][Para 005] This should be placed just anterior to the vibrating line on the palate, which can be assessed by asking patient to say ‘Aah’. The degree of compressibility of the tissues is assessed and the depth of the post-dam cut accordingly (usually ~1mm). The post-dam is recorded by marking the master impression with indelible pen and prepared on the upper cast with a wax knife in the shape of a Cupid’s bow.
[4603][Para 006] Complete prescription to the technician
[4604][Para 005] This should include:
[4605][Para 001] Any changes in posterior tooth position or anterior tooth arrangement.
[4606][Para 001] For fibrous undercuts >4mm and bony undercuts >2mm, decide whether they are to be plastered out or the flange thickened for adjustment at finish.
[4607][Para 001] Tin-foiling for relief of hard or nodular areas, if required.
[4608][Para 001] Gingival colour and contour.
[4609][Para 001] Denture base material. This is usually heat-cure acrylic; however, metal bases are indicated for patients with a history of fractured dentures.
[4610][Para 001] Identification marker, which is preferably legible.
[4611][Heading 1] Common problems and possible solutions
[4612][Para 001] Over-extension of flanges. Reduce.
[4613][Para 001] Under-extension of flanges. Try a temporary wax addition to flange first, to check effect of extending it. If this is satisfactory a new impression is required.
[4614][Para 001] Teeth outside neutral zone. Remove offending teeth and replace with wax which can be trimmed until correct.
[4615][Para 001] Incorrect OVD. If too small, can ↑ by adding wax to the occlusal surfaces of teeth, but if too large, will need to replace lower teeth with wax and re-record OVD.
[4616][Para 001] Occlusal discrepancy or anterior open bite or posterior open bite. Replace lower posterior teeth with wax and re-record OVD.
[4617][Para 001] Too little of upper anterior teeth visible. Reset anterior teeth to correct position and ask the laboratory to adjust occlusal plane accordingly.
[4618][Para 001] Too much of upper anterior teeth showing. The effect of reducing the length of the incisors can be judged by colouring the incisal region with a black wax pencil and then indicating desired change in position to lab.
[4619][Para 001] Inadequate lip support. An ↑ in support can be assessed by adding wax to the labial aspect of the upper try-in.
[4620][Para 016] A new try-in will be required if large errors are being corrected or if any doubt still exists about the occlusion.
[4621][Para 009] Complete dentures—fitting
[4622][Para 014] Some adjustment of completed dentures is inevitable following processing. On average, a 0.5mm ↑ in height occurs and a slight shift in tooth contact posteriorly. The main steps are:
[4623][Heading 1] Adjustment of fitting surface
[4624][Para 004] First, smooth any roughness and if necessary gradually reduce the bulk of the flanges in areas of undercut until the denture can be easily inserted without compromising retention.
[4625][Heading 1] Check occlusion
[4626][Para 004] The vertical dimension of the dentures is maintained by contact between the upper palatal and lower buccal cusps, therefore adjustment of these should be avoided if possible.
[4627][Para 001] Get patient to occlude and check contact with articulating paper. If contact uneven, or heavy contacts seen, adjust the fossae.
[4628][Para 001] For cusped teeth only, place articulating paper between occlusal surfaces and ask patient to make small lateral movements and adjust buccal upper and lower lingual (‘BULL’ rule) cusps only to remove any interferences.
[4629][Para 001] Remove any interferences to protrusive movements.
[4630][Para 001] Balancing contacts are desirable, but not essential unless they can be established easily by minor adjustments to working side contacts. Some authorities suggest providing even occlusal contact only at the time of fitting, allowing the patient to adapt to their new dentures before trying to achieve balanced articulation.
[4631][Heading 1] Advice to the patient
[4632][Para 004] Verbal and written instructions should be given.
[4633][Para 001] Most patients take some time to adapt to their new dentures. During this time a softer diet is advisable.
[4634][Para 001] If pain is experienced, the patient should try to continue wearing their dentures and return for adjustment as soon as possible so that affected areas can easily be seen. If this is not possible, they should stop wearing the dentures until 24h prior to the next visit.
[4635][Para 001] Although patients should be encouraged not to wear their dentures at night, adaptation may be speeded up if they are worn full-time for the first 1–2 weeks.
[4636][Para 001] When the dentures are not being worn they should be stored in water to prevent them drying out and warping. Plastic denture boxes are cheap, and safer than a glass of water at the bedside.
[4637][Para 001] Cleaning (…… Cleaning dentures, p. 316).
[4638][Heading 1] Review
[4639][Para 004] The patient should be seen 1–2 weeks after fitting to ease the dentures and adjust the occlusion. Localization of the cause of any irritation due to a flaw on the fitting surface can be helped by:
[4640][Para 001] Pressure relief cream which is painted onto the fitting surface of the denture.
[4641][Para 001] Indelible pencil, or denture fixative powder mixed with zinc oxide, which is applied carefully to the area thought to be responsible and the denture inserted. On removal, the mark will have been transferred to the adjacent mucosa and should correspond with the damaged area.
[4642][Para 001] If there is no obvious cause relating to the fitting surface remember that occlusal faults can cause displacement and mucosal trauma, and an excessive OVD is a common cause of generalized soreness under −/F (…… Denture problems and complaints, p. 318).
[4643][Para 016] Stress the importance of regular review to all patients with dentures.
[4644][Para 009] Denture maintenance
[4645][Para 014]  Review patients with F/F annually. Regular maintenance will help prevent damage due to ill-fitting dentures and will ↑ the likelihood of early detection of oral pathology.
[4646][Heading 1] Problems caused by lack of aftercare of F/F
[4647][Para 004] As a result of resorption all dentures become progressively ill-fitting, → loss of retention and stability. Movement of dentures in function may result in:
[4648][Para 001] Resorption.
[4649][Para 001] Predisposition to candidal infection.
[4650][Para 001] Denture irritation hyperplasia (…… Problems in denture wearers, p. 426).
[4651][Para 001] Inflammatory papillary hyperplasia of the palate.
[4652][Para 016] All of these are exacerbated by wear of the occlusal surfaces.
[4653][Heading 1] Rebasing
[4654][Para 004] The terms ‘rebasing’ and ‘relining’ are commonly used interchangeably. Strictly speaking, relining is replacement of the fitting surface (e.g. with a temporary material) and rebasing is replacement of most or all of the denture base.
[4655][Para 008] Rebasing is indicated where the only feature of F/F that requires improvement is the fitting surface; otherwise consider replacement F/F using the copy method. For rebasing, the material of choice is heat-cure acrylic (…… Denture materials—rebasing, p. 682), but this necessitates the patient being without their dentures while the addition is being made. Self-cure acrylic applied at the chair-side appears attractive, but its properties are inferior. For a heat-cure rebase, a wash impression (ZOE or low-viscosity elastomer) must be recorded inside the denture.
[4656][Para 006] Technique
[4657][Para 005] To avoid an ↑ in OVD, record the impression for one denture at a time.
[4658][Para 001] Check occlusion and adjust if required. Note OVD.
[4659][Para 001] Remove undercuts from fitting surface.
[4660][Para 001] Correct extension and place post-dam in greenstick.
[4661][Para 001] Apply impression material and insert in mouth. Get patient to close into contact with opposing denture. Check OVD and occlusion.
[4662][Para 001] Remove and examine impression; if unsatisfactory (or if in doubt) repeat.
[4663][Para 016] An alternative method for inflamed tissues is to record a functional impression (…… Functional impression, p. 307) over several days with a tissue conditioner (e.g. Visco-gel®), in which case the resulting impression needs to be cast immediately.
[4664][Heading 1] Tissue conditioners (e.g. Coe-Comfort™, Visco-gel set®)
[4665][Para 004] These are r0esilient materials which give a more even distribution of loading and thus promote tissue recovery. They are particularly useful where ill-fitting dentures have caused trauma, as it is important to allow the tissues to recover before impressions for replacement dentures or a rebase are taken.
[4666][Para 006] Technique
[4667][Para 005] Relieve any areas of pressure on the fitting surface and reduce any over-extension. A minimum thickness of 2mm is required and the material should not be left for >1 week. Repeated applications may be necessary.
[4668][Para 008] Tissue conditioners can also be used after pre-prosthetic surgery. They become less soft with time therefore they should be replaced at least weekly.
[4669][Para 008] For patients who have very atrophic ridges and who struggle with denture wearing, a definitive soft lining aimed at distributing stresses more evenly to the denture bearing area may be helpful, e.g. GC reline™ or Permasoft®. GC reline™ may also be used to engage bony undercuts.
[4670][Para 006] Soft linings
[4671][Para 005] These are indicated for:
[4672][Para 001] Older patients with a thin atrophic mucosa. Usually for −/F.
[4673][Para 001] Following prosthetic surgery.
[4674][Para 001] To utilize soft tissue undercuts for ↑ retention, e.g. following hemimaxillectomy, clefts.
[4675][Para 016] It is wise to make a new denture first in acrylic and adjust the occlusion, before placing soft lining. A minimum thickness of 2mm is required, which may significantly weaken a lower denture necessitating placement of a metal strengthener on the lingual aspect. No material is ideal and soft linings are best avoided (…… Soft liners, p. 682).
[4676][Para 009] Cleaning dentures
[4677][Para 014] When new dentures are fitted, the importance of regular, thorough cleaning, especially of fitting surfaces, with soap, water, and a brush to prevent the build-up of plaque, stain, and calculus should be emphasized. Unfortunately, few patients are sufficiently diligent, due in part to being conditioned by advertising, to expect to use a denture cleaner.
[4678][Para 008] Advise patients to clean their dentures over a basin of water to act as a safety net (Table 7.5).
[4679][Heading 1] Practical tips
[4680][Para 004] Hypochlorite solutions are effective for acrylic dentures when used overnight, but if used with hot water are liable to cause bleaching, therefore warn patient.6 The peroxide cleaners are popular but are ineffective if used for only 15–30min as the manufacturers advise. See Table 7.6.
