[8666][Para 040] Principal sources
[8667][Para 043] J. F. McCabe & A. W. G. Walls 2008 Applied Dental Materials, Blackwell Publishing.
[8668][Para 009] Properties of dental materials
[8669][Para 022] Definitions
[8670][Para 017] Coefficient of thermal expansion
[8671][Para 005] The extent to which a material expands upon heating. The fractional ↑ in length for each degree of temperature i.
[8672][Para 006] Creep
[8673][Para 005] The slow plastic deformation that occurs with the application of a static or dynamic force over time, after the material has set.
[8674][Para 006] Elastic modulus
[8675][Para 005] A measure of the rigidity of a material, defined by the ratio of stress to strain (below elastic limit).
[8676][Para 006] Fatigue
[8677][Para 005] When cyclic forces are applied, a crack may nucleate and ↑ by small increments each time the force is applied. In time the crack will ↑ to a length at which the force results in # through the remaining material.
[8678][Para 006] Hardness
[8679][Para 005] Resistance to penetration. A number of hardness scales are in use (e.g. Vickers, Rockwell, Mohs’). Between these scales, hardness values are not interchangeable.
[8680][Para 006] Resilience
[8681][Para 005] The energy absorbed by a material undergoing elastic deformation up to its elastic limit.
[8682][Para 006] Stiffness
[8683][Para 005] An indication of how easy it is to bend a piece of material without causing permanent deformation or #. It is dependent upon the elastic modulus, size, and shape of the specimen.
[8684][Para 006] Strain
[8685][Para 005] Change in size of a material that occurs in response to a force. It is the change in length divided by the original length.
[8686][Para 006] Stress
[8687][Para 005] Internal force per unit cross-sectional area acting on the material. Can be classified according to the direction of the force: tensile (stretching), compressive, or shear.
[8688][Para 006] Thermal conductivity
[8689][Para 005] Ability of a material to transmit heat.
[8690][Para 006] Thermal diffusivity
[8691][Para 005] Rate at which temperature changes spread through a material.
[8692][Para 006] Toughness
[8693][Para 005] The amount of energy absorbed up to the point of #. A function of the resilience of the material and its ability to undergo plastic deformation rather than #.
[8694][Para 006] Wear
[8695][Para 005] The abrasion (mechanical or chemical) resistance of a substance.
[8696][Para 006] Wettability
[8697][Para 005] Ability of one material to flow across the surface of another, determined by the contact angle between the two materials and influenced by surface roughness and contamination. The contact angle is the angle between solid/liquid and liquid/air interfaces measured through the liquid.
[8698][Para 006] Yield strength
[8699][Para 005] (Or elastic limit.) The stress beyond which a material is permanently deformed when a force is applied.
[8700][Heading 1] Evaluation of a new material
[8701][Para 004] Before it reaches the dental supply companies a new material should have undergone the following tests:
[8702][Para 001] Standard specifications (i.e. physical properties), e.g. compressive strength, hardness, etc. The actual values obtained are mainly of value in comparing the new material with those already in use and which are performing satisfactorily. Compliance with an international (International Organization for Standardization (ISO)) standard indicates fitness for dental use.
[8703][Para 001] Laboratory evaluation. Should be relevant to the clinical situation, but this is easier said than done!
[8704][Para 001] Clinical trials. Usually conducted under optimal conditions. Many materials have been less successful under the conditions imposed by clinical practice, particularly those with demanding placement techniques.
[8705][Para 016] Clinically, the important questions to ask a representative selling or promoting any dental material include:
[8706][Para 001] Details of the chemical constituents.
[8707][Para 001] Handling characteristics, e.g. presentation, mixing, working time, setting time, and dimensional changes on setting.
[8708][Para 001] Performance in service.
[8709][Para 001] Cost.
[8710][Para 001] Shelf life.
[8711][Para 001] Does the material meet the relevant ISO standard?
[8712][Para 016] Then decide whether this new material has any significant advantages over the material you are familiar with.
[8713][Heading 1] Restoration of teeth
[8714][Para 004] When restoring or replacing teeth it should be remembered that the teeth themselves are composed of enamel, dentine, and pulpal tissues each with quite different properties that must be taken into account when selecting a material with which to restore them. In addition, the teeth emerge from a complex dentogingival junction and are supported in alveolar bone by the viscoelastic periodontal ligament. All of these features are difficult to reproduce with current dental materials and most likely will not be until teeth themselves or their individual tissues are able to be bioengineered.
[8715][Para 009] Amalgam
[8716][Para 014] Dental amalgam is made by mixing together mercury (Hg) with a powdered silver–tin alloy (mercury around 50% by weight) to produce a soft mass that can be packed into a preparation before setting.
[8717][Heading 1] Types of amalgam
[8718][Para 004] There are two ways of classifying amalgam:
[8719][Para 001] Particle shape—can be lathe-cut (irregular), spheroidal, or a mixture of the two. Spheroidal particles give a more fluid mix which is easy to condense, can be carved immediately, and take 3h to reach occlusal strength (compared to >6h for lathe-cut amalgams). Spheroidal amalgams are preferable for pinned restorations.
[8720][Para 001] Particle composition—the first (conventional) alloys introduced had a low copper content (5%). The weakest (Sn–Hg or λ-2) phase of the set amalgam could be eliminated by ↑ the proportion of copper, so a variety of high copper (10–30%) amalgams have been introduced that react to eliminate it. These are more expensive, but superior in terms of corrosion resistance, creep, strength, and durability of marginal integrity. There are two types of high-copper alloy: (i) a single composition alloy of silver–tin–copper; (ii) a blended (dispersion) mix of silver–tin and copper–silver alloys. Of these, (i) is the most resistant to tarnishing.
[8721][Para 006] Types of amalgam currently available
[8722][Para 005] Conventional lathe-cut, conventional spherical, high-copper dispersion lathe + spherical, high-copper single spheroidal, and high-copper single lathe-cut amalgam (Table 16.1).
[8723][Heading 1] Handling characteristics
[8724][Para 017] Mixing or trituration
[8725][Para 005] This is carried out mechanically, in one of two ways:
[8726][Para 001] Pre-encapsulated by manufacturer, with automatic vibrator—preferred method.
[8727][Para 001] Using an amalgamator that dispenses Hg and alloy in correct proportions and mixes them. However, the amalgamator requires refilling by hand which ↑ likelihood of Hg spillage occurring. The duration of trituration varies from 5 to 20sec.
[8728][Para 006] Condensation
[8729][Para 005] Carry out incrementally by hand instruments (lathe-cut or spheroidal). Preparations should be overfilled so that the Hg-rich surface layer is removed by carving.
[8730][Para 006] Carving
[8731][Para 005] With spherical alloys this can be commenced immediately; burnishing is recommended in an attempt to prevent marginal leakage.
[8732][Para 006] Polishing
[8733][Para 005] Polished amalgams look good, but whether polishing is necessary is still the subject of debate. NB: maximum strength takes 24h to develop, so it is advisable to recommend patients do not chew on the restored tooth for this time where possible.
[8734][Heading 1] Marginal leakage
[8735][Para 004] While amalgam corrosion products will form a marginal seal in time, microleakage can be ↓ by the use of either a conventional cavity varnish (e.g. Copalite®) or a bonding agent (e.g. Amalgambond® or Panavia-21™) in the interim. The latter (an anaerobic resin adhesive) also bonds to set amalgam.1 Alternatively, sealing over the completed restoration with a fissure sealant has been suggested, and this is a possible solution to the ‘ditched’, but caries-free amalgam.
[8736][Heading 1] Toxicity
[8737][Para 004] Despite toxicity scares and the introduction of posterior composites, amalgam is still widely used, mainly because of its ease of handling. In Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, dental amalgam is banned for environmental reasons. The Control of Mercury (Enforcement) Regulations 2017 stipulate there should be no use of amalgam in the treatment of deciduous teeth, in children under 15yrs or pregnant or breastfeeding women, except when strictly deemed necessary by the practitioner on the grounds of specific medical needs of the patient.2 It is likely further phasing down will occur (possibly to a full ban!). These regulations aim to reduce mercury in the environment and are not a reflection on any specific safety concerns about amalgam.
[8738][Para 008] In addition, there is a link between allergy to constituents of dental amalgam and lichenoid eruptions in the oral cavity in certain individuals.
[8739][Para 008] The greatest actual risk appears to be related to the inhalation of Hg vapour and as such, the dental team as well as patients are theoretically at risk.
[8740][Para 008] Attention should be paid to the following:
[8741][Para 001] Avoid spilling Hg if non-encapsulated system employed.
[8742][Para 001] Waste amalgam should be stored appropriately to prevent mercury vapour release.
[8743][Para 001] When removing old amalgams, safety glasses, masks, and high-volume aspiration are a wise precaution.
[8744][Para 001] Amalgam separation devices should be in use as per Hazardous Waste Directive (91/689/EEC). Should comply with British Standard Dental Equipment—amalgam separators (BS EN ISO 11143:2008) (…… http://www.bsigroup.com).
[8745][Para 036] Table 16.1 Composition of amalgams
[8746][Para 009] Composite resins—constituents and properties
[8747][Para 014] The modern composite resin is a mixture of resin and particulate filler, the handling characteristics of which are determined largely by the size of the filler particles and method of cure.
[8748][Heading 1] Constituents
[8749][Para 017] Resin
[8750][Para 005] Most composite resins are based on either Bis-GMA (addition product of bisphenol A and glycidylmethacrylate) or urethane dimethacrylate plus a diluent monomer, triethylene glycol dimethacrylate (TEGMA).
[8751][Para 006] Filler
[8752][Para 005] (E.g. quartz, fused silica, glasses such as aluminosilicate and borosilicate.) Confers the following benefits on the composite resin:
[8753][Para 001] Compressive strength, abrasion resistance, modulus of elasticity, and # toughness.
[8754][Para 001] Thermal expansion and setting contraction.
[8755][Para 001] Aesthetic qualities.
[8756][Para 016] Composite resins can be subdivided according to particle size:
[8757][Para 028] Macrofilled
[8758][Para 025] (Or conventional.) Contains particles of radio-opaque barium or strontium glass 2.5–5µm in size, to give 75–80% by weight of filler. Good mechanical properties, but hard to polish and soon roughens.
[8759][Para 028] Microfilled
[8760][Para 025] Contains colloidal silica particles 0.04µm in size and 30–60% by weight. Retains a good surface polish, but is unsuitable for load-bearing situations, has poor wear resistance, and ↑ contraction shrinkage.
[8761][Para 028] Nanofilled
[8762][Para 025] By combining nanometric particles and nanoclusters in a conventional resin matrix, manufacturers claim to offer ↑ wear resistance as well as polishability and lustre.
[8763][Para 028] Hybrid
[8764][Para 025] Contains a mixture of conventional and microfine particles designed to optimize both mechanical and surface properties. Contains 75–85% by weight of filler, of which the bulk is conventional (1–50µm). Some manufacturers achieve up to 90% filler loadings by using blended sizes of filler particles.
[8765][Para 028] Packable (condensable)
[8766][Para 025] Developed to simulate the ‘condensation’ of amalgam although no ↓ in volume as compressed therefore not strictly condensed. Resin and ceramic fillers are incorporated into a network of ceramic fibres. Claim to have ↑ wear resistance and less polymerization shrinkage.
[8767][Para 006] Initiator/activator
[8768][Para 001] Chemically cured: benzoyl peroxide (or sulfinic acid) initiator + tertiary amine activator.
[8769][Para 001] Light cured: amine + diketone activated by blue light (460–70nm).
[8770][Para 006] Other constituents
[8771][Para 005] These include pigments, stabilizers, and silane coupler to produce bond between particles and filler.
[8772][Para 008] Composites may also be classified as:
[8773][Para 001] Microfilled.
[8774][Para 001] Posterior composite.
[8775][Para 001] All-purpose.
[8776][Para 001] Flowable.
[8777][Para 001] Condensable/packable.
[8778][Heading 1] Important properties of composites
[8779][Para 001] Polymerization shrinkage of 1–4%.
[8780][Para 001] Thermal expansion is significantly greater than enamel or dentine, and without an acid-etch bond can result in marginal leakage.
[8781][Para 001] Elastic modulus should be high to resist occlusal forces. Modulus of hybrid type is greater than other composite resins, amalgam, or dentine. However, composite resins are still brittle and # if used in thin section.
[8782][Para 001] Wear resistance is greatest in hybrids.
[8783][Para 001] Radio-opacity is particularly useful, especially for posterior resin composites.
[8784][Para 001] ? Toxicity. Resins have been found to be toxic in cell culture. Also controversy surrounding the oestrogenicity of composite resins.
[8785][Para 016] Newer developments include hydroxyl ion-releasing composite resin to counteract demineralization during periods of low pH in the restoration. Also use of fibre reinforcement to fabricate posts and cores as well as bridges/splints.
[8786][Para 009] Composite resins—practical points
[8787][Para 022] Method of polymerization
[8788][Para 017] Chemical (self-cure)
[8789][Para 005] No additional equipment required, but mixing of two components introduces porosity and the working time is limited.
[8790][Para 006] Light activation
[8791][Para 005] Provides long working time, command set, and better colour stability, but requires a light source, has a limited depth of cure, and the temperature ↑ during setting can be as high as 40°C. Three types of light source are currently available: quartz tungsten halogen (QTH), plasma arc light (PAC), and light-emitting diode (LED). PAC and LED lights confer theoretical advantages in, e.g. speed and depth of cure, portability (not PAC), lifetime, and reliability of light source. LED models are becoming most widely used replacing QTH. PAC light sources claim quicker curing times due to ↑ intensity but are more expensive.
[8792][Para 006] Dual-cure
[8793][Para 005] Curing is initiated by a conventional light source, but continues chemically to help ensure polymerization throughout the restoration.
[8794][Para 006] Practical tips for light activation
[8795][Para 001] Replace bulbs every 6–12 months. Some lights correct for the effects of bulb ageing.
[8796][Para 001] Air attenuates light beam, ∴ position as close to tooth as possible.
[8797][Para 001] Preparations >2mm depth should be cured incrementally.
[8798][Para 001] Precautions are necessary to protect eyes from glare, ∴ use safety shield, get the patient to close their eyes, and the DN to look away.
[8799][Para 001] The efficiency of the light source can be tested by curing a block of composite. Practical depth of cure is half the thickness of set material.
[8800][Para 001] The greater the intensity of the light source, the greater the depth of cure.
[8801][Para 006] Finishing
[8802][Para 005] Ideally, a mylar strip to produce the contour of the restoration. Then refine with microfine diamond or multi-bladed tungsten carbide finishing burs (under water spray), finishing strips, and then polish with aluminium oxide-coated discs (e.g. Sof-Lex™). Shofu points or finishing pastes (Shofu CompoSite™ finishing kit) are useful for inaccessible concave surfaces.
[8803][Heading 1] Problems with composite resins
[8804][Para 001] Difficult to obtain satisfactory contact points and occlusal stops. Modern placement techniques have made improvements in this regard, e.g. using sectional contoured matrix bands.
[8805][Para 001] Post-operative sensitivity.
[8806][Para 001] Polymerization shrinkage.
[8807][Para 001] The C-factor (configuration) is the ratio of bonded to unbonded surfaces in a cavity. The higher the C-factor, the more likely the risk of effects of polymerization shrinkage (bond failure, cuspal deflection, post-operative sensitivity).
[8808][Para 001] Depth of cure of light-cured materials is limited. This is a particular problem in posterior teeth.
[8809][Para 016] Indirect composite inlays may circumvent the last two problems (…… Indirect resin composite or porcelain inlays/onlays, p. 225).
[8810][Heading 1] Fissure sealants
[8811][Para 004] Composite resins containing little or no filler, which are either self- or light-cured. Clear or opaque types are available, the former having better flow characteristics (whether this is an advantage depends upon the position of the tooth). Success depends upon being able to achieve good moisture control for the acid-etch bond.
[8812][Heading 1] Flowable composite resins
[8813][Para 004] Predominantly resin with a reduced percentage of filler particles, and consequently shrink considerably on curing. Some advocate using them as liners or in the bottom of proximal preparations, but the high shrinkage precludes this. RMGIC is preferable in proximal preparations, which are below the cemento-enamel junction (bonded-base approach); however, they have a place in the marginal repair of restorations and some advocate their use for facial cervical margin restorations.
[8814][Para 008] Flowable technology has led to further developments in the ability to bulk fill with the addition of several new materials such as SDR® flow+ from Dentsply with a 4mm depth of cure. In addition, the data from this material and similar suggests ↓ polymerization shrinkage and cusp deflection.
[8815][Heading 1] Pink composite
[8816][Para 004] (E.g. Amaris® Gingiva by Voco.) These pink-coloured composite restoratives can be used chairside and some, e.g. GC Gradia® gum shades, are compatible with their laboratory microceramic composite namesake.
[8817][Para 009] Enamel and dentine bonding
[8818][Para 014] Research would suggest that:
[8819][Para 001] Success depends upon adequate moisture control, as contact with saliva for as little as 0.5sec will contaminate the etch pattern.
[8820][Para 001] A prophylaxis prior to etching is not required unless abundant plaque deposits are present.
[8821][Para 001] 30–50% buffered phosphoric acid provides the best enamel etch pattern.
[8822][Para 001] An etching time of 15–20sec is adequate for both 1° and permanent enamel, and 15sec for dentine is recommended.
[8823][Para 001] The etch pattern is easily damaged; using a probe to aid etchant penetration of pits and fissures, or applying etchant by rubbing vigorously with a pledget of cotton wool, is C/I.
[8824][Para 001] There is no difference in bond strength whether an etchant solution or gel is used. Gels take twice as long to rinse away but have the advantage of greater viscosity and colour contrast.
[8825][Para 001] Rinse for at least 15sec.
[8826][Para 001] Remineralization of etched enamel occurs from the saliva, and after 24h it is indistinguishable from untreated enamel.
[8827][Para 001] Etched enamel is porous and has a high surface energy.
[8828][Para 016] The etch pattern consists of three zones (from surface inwards):
[8829][Para 001] Etched zone (enamel removed): 10µm.
[8830][Para 001] Qualitative zone: 20µm.
[8831][Para 001] Quantitative porous zone: 20µm.
[8832][Para 016] Composite resin tags may penetrate up to 50µm into enamel to give micromechanical retention.
[8833][Para 008] NB: many of the newer dentine adhesive systems do not have a separate acid-etch stage. These systems use a combination of acidic primers and bonding resins, either as a single stage or applied separately (…… Dentine-adhesive systems (dentine bonding agents), p. 658).
[8834][Para 009] Dentine-adhesive systems (dentine bonding agents)
[8835][Para 014] The advantages of bonding to dentine (e.g. preservation of tooth tissue) have fuelled considerable research effort. The problems that have had to be overcome include the high water and organic content of dentine; the presence of a ‘smear layer’ after dentine is cut; and the need for adequate strength immediately following placement, to withstand the polymerization contraction of composite resin. These difficulties have been approached in a number of ways, making the topic of dentine bonding confusing, a situation that has been exacerbated by the pace of new developments and by the claims of the manufacturers.
[8836][Heading 1] Indications
[8837][Para 001] Marginal seal where preparation margin is in dentine or cementum, e.g. cervical (Class V), proximal (Class II) box.
[8838][Para 001] Retention and seal of direct resin-composite restorations.
[8839][Para 001] Retention and seal of indirect porcelain and composite inlays.
[8840][Para 001] Dentine adhesives have also been used for repairing # teeth, cementing ceramic crowns and veneers, and as an endodontic sealer.
[8841][Para 006] The smear layer
[8842][Para 005] This consists of an amorphous layer of organic and inorganic debris, produced by cutting dentine. It ↓ sensitivity by occluding the dentine tubules and prevents loss of dentinal fluid. The smear layer is partially or completely removed &/or modified during dentine bonding.
[8843][Heading 1] Mechanism of dentine bonding
[8844][Para 004] Most dentine adhesive systems aim to modify and partially remove the smear layer, by the application of an acidic primer. This demineralizes the underlying surface, exposing the collagen and opening up the dentinal tubules. It is important to keep this surface moist to prevent the collagen becoming flattened (not with saliva, though!). This layer is then infiltrated using a resin with bi-functional ends: one hydrophilic end, which is able to bond to wet dentine, and one hydrophobic end capable of bonding to the composite resin. In this infiltrated hybrid layer molecular entanglement of the collagen and resin occurs, providing the basis for the bonding system.
[8845][Heading 1] Practical points
[8846][Para 001] Follow manufacturer’s instructions.
[8847][Para 001] For better results, use a matched resin-composite and adhesive system.
[8848][Para 001] When a dentine adhesive is used, polymerization shrinkage of composite resin is more likely to result in cuspal deformation and post-operative pain. An incremental filling and curing technique will help to solve this problem.
[8849][Para 001] Pre-curing the adhesive bonding agent before placing the composite ↑ bond strength to dentine.3
[8850][Para 001] No technique produces zero microleakage.
[8851][Heading 1] Techniques
[8852][Para 017] Etch and rinse
[8853][Para 001] Three step (acid etch, primer, and adhesive)—37% phosphoric acid usually used to remove the smear layer and demineralize the surface dentine. A primer is then applied, often containing a solvent such as acetone to eliminate water in the dentine that is then filled by resin tags. Another method is to use an aqueous primer solution. Benefit of ease of use as well as stronger acid etching of the enamel.
[8854][Para 001] Two step (etchant and primer/adhesive).
[8855][Para 006] Self-etching
[8856][Para 001] Two step—a weaker acid is used to solubilize the smear layer and at the same time act as the difunctional primer (hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends). Second stage is adhesive.
[8857][Para 076] One step:
[8858][Para 001] Self-etching one-step mix. The resin bonding agent is mixed in the same liquid as the etch and primer. Often unidose presentation.
[8859][Para 001] Self-etching, no mix ‘one-bottle system’.
[8860][Para 016] If enamel is present, it is usually better to undertake etch and rinse whereas at the other extreme when dentine only is present, e.g. a crown preparation, then the weaker acid of the self-etching technique may be preferable. Self-etching possibly leads to less post-operative sensitivity.
[8861][Heading 1] Bonding to metals and ceramics
[8862][Para 004] The described bonding systems may be used in conjunction with preparation of metal or ceramic surfaces to allow bonding of materials other than composite resin to the tooth surface. Metal surfaces are usually sandblasted to provide roughness for micromechanical retention then prepared with a 4-META-derived conditioner before application of a composite luting cement. Ceramic surfaces are usually etched then silanated before luting. This allows for a great variety of clinical uses including orthodontics as well as fixed prosthodontics.
[8863][Para 009] Glass ionomers
[8864][Para 014] Glass ionomer = polyalkenoate.
[8865][Heading 1] Setting reaction
[8866][Para 004] Alumino-silicate glass powder + polyalkenoic acid → calcium + aluminium polyalkenoates (base + polyacid → polysalt + water).
[8867][Para 008] The set material consists of unreacted spheres of glass surrounded by a silicaeous gel, embedded in metal polyalkenoates. Fluoride is uptaken and released from the cement to give theoretical cariostatic properties.
[8868][Heading 1] Presentation
[8869][Para 001] Powder + liquid.
[8870][Para 001] Powder (with anhydrous acid) + water.
[8871][Para 001] Encapsulated.
[8872][Para 016] Tartaric acid is added to lengthen working time. In some products, polymaleic acid replaces polyacrylic and Diamond Carve™ is hand-mixed glass polyphosphonate.
[8873][Para 008] ‘High-viscosity’ or reinforced GIs, e.g. GC Fuji IX GP™, are claimed to have improved earlier physical properties and resistance to dissolution.
[8874][Heading 1] Properties
[8875][Para 017] Adhesion
[8876][Para 005] To enamel and dentine by: (i) ionic displacement of calcium and phosphate with polyacrylate ions; (ii) possible absorption of polyalkenoic acid onto collagen. Some authors recommend pre-conditioning the dentine, e.g. with 10% polyalkenoic acid (GC Dentin Conditioner™) for 30sec. Whether this ↑ adhesion is controversial. GIC also bonds to the oxide layer on SS and tin.
[8877][Para 006] Cariostatic
[8878][Para 005] Due to fluoride release throughout the lifetime of the restoration. GIs are also able to take up fluoride when the IO concentration is raised, the ‘reservoir effect’. However, the therapeutic benefit of fluoride release has yet to be proven to be clinically significant.
[8879][Para 006] Thermal expansion
[8880][Para 005] Similar to enamel and dentine.
[8881][Para 006] Strength
[8882][Para 005] Brittle material. Tensile strength is only 40% of composite resin.
[8883][Para 006] Radiolucent
[8884][Para 005] Except for the cermets, which are rarely used.
[8885][Para 006] Abrasion/erosion resistance
[8886][Para 005] Poor, but improving with newer materials, especially with the high-viscosity versions.
[8887][Para 006] Biocompatibility
[8888][Para 005] This has been questioned following reports of pulpal inflammation when used as a luting cement and pulp response studies have shown conflicting results. However, literature has demonstrated no such reports of pulp reactions after cementation of cast restorations with GIC.4
[8889][Heading 1] Applications
[8890][Para 004] GIs are unable to match the aesthetics and abrasion resistance of the composite resins, and brittleness limits their use to non-load-bearing situations. However, their adhesive and fluoride-releasing properties have resulted in a range of applications and matching formulations.
[8891][Para 006] Type I
[8892][Para 005] Luting cements for crowns, bridges, and orthodontic bands.
[8893][Para 006] Type II
[8894][Para 005] Restorative cements. There are two subtypes: (i) aesthetic and (ii) reinforced. Can also be used as a fissure sealant, for the restoration of 1° teeth (…… Material selection for intracoronal restorations, p. 84) and for repairing defective restorations.
[8895][Para 006] Type III
[8896][Para 005] Fast-setting lining materials. Defer placement of amalgam for at least 15min and composite for 4min. In load-bearing situations or where lining is exposed to the oral environment (e.g. in sandwich technique), use of a type II reinforced cement or RMGIC is preferable.
[8897][Para 006] Type IV
[8898][Para 005] Includes the light-cure and dual-cure GI (use of a light source optimizes the properties of the dual-cure materials, although they will self-polymerize without). 3M Vitremer™ is an example of a so-called tri-cure GI where, in addition to the acid–base reaction and the photoinitiated free radical methacrylate cure there is also a further dark methacrylate cure that can occur in the absence of light.
[8899][Para 008] Forms of true GI can also be used for fissure sealants, orthodontic cements, core build-ups, and for restoration of deciduous teeth.
[8900][Heading 1] Practical tips
[8901][Para 001] A dry field is essential.
[8902][Para 001] Encapsulated systems ensure optimal mixing and allow placement via a syringe tip, e.g. Ketac-Fil™.
[8903][Para 001] Cement should be inserted before its sheen is lost.
[8904][Para 001] GI sticks to instruments, ∴ use powder as a separator if powder-liquid.
[8905][Para 001] Cellulose or soft metal strips provide the best finish.
[8906][Para 001] Water balance during setting is critical. Absorption of water results in dissolution, and dehydration leads to crazing, ∴ cement must be protected with waterproof material, e.g. light-cured bonding resin, which acts as a lubricant for finishing and can then be cured.
[8907][Para 001] Although most manufacturers claim that trimming can be started 10–15min after placement, it is better to defer for >24h.
[8908][Para 009] Other glass ionomer/composite-based products
[8909][Para 022] Resin-modified glass ionomers
[8910][Para 004] These allow ‘command’ setting and help overcome the moisture sensitivity and low early mechanical strength associated with conventional GI. The acid–base reaction of GI is supplemented by the addition of 75% resin (hydroxyethyl methacrylate Bis-GMA). The initial set of the material is due to the formation of a polymerization matrix, which is strengthened by the acid–base reaction. They are easier to handle than conventional GIs and may be polished immediately after light-curing. Aesthetics approach those of resin-based materials, plus the advantage of fluoride release (although this is still of unproven clinical significance). These materials can be used in conjunction with composite resin for placement in deep proximal preparation where the deepest parts of the preparation are below the cemento-enamel junction. This type of open sandwich restoration fell into disrepute when restorations were placed with traditional GIC. Single-surface glass ionomer restorations have a relatively poor survival of <40% across 10yrs.5 Also widely used as lining materials and luting cements.
[8911][Heading 1] Compomer
[8912][Para 004] Polyacid-modified composite resin. It combines the adhesive and fluoride-releasing properties of GI with the abrasion resistance of composite resin and is called, with a touch of originality, ‘compomer’. Composed of a single hydrophobic resin filled with acid-leachable glass particles. Bonded with a bi-functional primer and light-cured. It is claimed that the chemical reaction takes place through uptake of water from saliva leading to fluoride ions leaching out. Popular in general practice due to ease of technique and especially useful for restoration of deciduous teeth.
[8913][Heading 1] Giomers
[8914][Para 004] This group of materials may be described as composite resins with active (GI) filler particles. The filler particles are based on pre-reacted surface or fully reacted GI filler particles (S-PRG) whereas the acid–base reaction process occurs after initial setting in acid-modified composites. Have been shown to be capable of sustained fluoride ion release in the absence of water (unlike GI and compomers that require water absorption before fluoride recharge can occur). Possibly useful for high-caries-risk individuals. E.g. Shofu Beautifil II™.
[8915][Heading 1] Ormocers
[8916][Para 004] Organically modified ceramics, e.g. Admira®. Made up of three components: organic polymers, ceramic glasses, and polyvinylsiloxane. Claimed to confer less polymerization shrinkage, good handling, marginal integrity, and biocompatibility (less free diluent monomer). Lack of clinical trials to date.
[8917][Heading 1] Cermets
[8918][Para 004] These are similar to GIs, except that the ion-leachable glass is fused with fine silver powder. Mixing with a polymeric acid gives a cement consisting of unreacted glass particles to which silver is fused, held together by a metal–salt matrix with the benefit of ↑ wear resistance. Cermets have been largely superseded by the RMGICs and are now generally discouraged.
[8919][Heading 1] Ceromers
[8920][Para 004] Ceromers are second-generation indirect composite resins. Their main components are silanized microhybrid inorganic fillers embedded in a light-curing organic matrix. Ceromers have high filler content and so improved mechanical properties compared to traditional composites. They are, however, less wear resistant than enamel with potential problems in the long term in high loading sites. The material may be used as indirect onlays with benefits over porcelain in ‘camouflaging’ of shade as well as a fibre-reinforced crown or bridge material (Targis Vectris®) with variable success.
[8921][Para 009] Cements
[8922][Para 022] Types of cement
[8923][Para 017] Based on zinc oxide eugenol (ZOE)
[8924][Para 005] Powder of pure zinc oxide is mixed (in a ratio of 3:1) with eugenol liquid to give zinc eugenolate and unreacted powder. Setting time is 24h. This is the weakest cement, but the eugenol acts as an obtundent and analgesic, ∴ used as a sedative dressing. The following modifications change the properties for various indications.
[8925][Para 006] Accelerated ZOE
[8926][Para 005] (E.g. Sedanol®.) Addition of zinc acetate to the powder ↑ setting time to 5min.
[8927][Para 006] Resin-bonded ZOE
[8928][Para 005] (E.g. Kalzinol®.) Addition of 10% hydrogenated resin to the powder ↑ strength.
[8929][Para 006] EBA
[8930][Para 005] Addition of ortho-ethoxybenzoic acid (62%) to the liquid ↑ strength.
[8931][Heading 1] Zinc phosphate
[8932][Para 004] (E.g. DeTrey® Zinc.) The powder consists of zinc and magnesium oxides, and the liquid 50% aqueous phosphoric acid. The working time is ↑ by adding the powder in small increments. Popular in the past because of its strength. Although low setting pH theoretically C/I its use for vital teeth, in practice this does not seem to be a problem.
[8933][Heading 1] Zinc polycarboxylate
[8934][Para 004] (E.g. Poly-F Plus®, DurelonTM.) The powder is a mixture of zinc and magnesium oxides and the liquid is 40% aqueous polyacrylic acid. Anhydrous acid formulations have been introduced, which are mixed with water or encapsulated. The powder should be added quickly to the liquid. The temptation to remove excess cement should be resisted until it has reached a rubbery stage. Adheres to dentine, enamel, tin, and SS. Often used as temporary cement where ↑ adherence required.
[8935][Heading 1] Calcium hydroxide
[8936][Para 004] Chemically curing types comprise two pastes which are mixed together in equal quantities. One paste contains the calcium hydroxide plus fillers in a non-reacting carrier, and the other polysalicylate fluid. The set material consists of an amorphous calcium disalicylate complex plus calcium hydroxide and has a pH of 11. In addition to being bacteriostatic, calcium hydroxide can induce mineralization of adjacent pulp. Light-cured formulations which are resin-based are available. Have ↓ bactericidal properties, but ↑ strength.
[8937][Heading 1] RMGIC
[8938][Para 004] This is a popular luting cement used for indirect cast restorations and for cavity lining.
[8939][Para 006] Strength
[8940][Para 005] Phosphate > EBA or polycarboxylate > resin-bonded ZOE > accelerated ZOE > calcium hydroxide.
[8941][Para 006] Practical points
[8942][Para 001] Generally, the thicker the mix, the greater the strength.
[8943][Para 001] Heat ↓ setting time, ∴ a cooled slab is advisable.
[8944][Para 001] To stop cement sticking to the instruments during placement, dip in cement powder (except calcium hydroxide) or use non-stick instruments.
[8945][Para 001] When luting, apply cement to crown or inlay before tooth.
[8946][Heading 1] Choice of cement
[8947][Para 017] Temporary restorations
[8948][Para 005] Choice depends upon how long the dressing needs to last and whether any therapeutic qualities are required. Pure ZOE is useful for a tooth with a reversibly inflamed pulp, but resin-bonded ZOE is stronger. GI is preferable for semi-permanent dressings and endodontic provisionalization because it seals the preparation margins.
[8949][Para 006] Luting cement
[8950][Para 005] Zinc phosphate, GI, and polycarboxylate are all popular as luting cements. EBA cement is C/I because of ↑ solubility. Composite-based luting systems are often used in conjunction with dentine adhesive systems. Mandatory for cementing ceramic or porcelain inlays/onlays and ceramic veneers. Now available as one-step luting cements with no etching or bonding required.
[8951][Para 006] Lining cement
[8952][Para 005] Choice of lining depends upon the depth of the preparation and the material being used to restore it:
[8953][Para 001] Amalgam—minimal: preparation sealer (Gluma® Desensitizer); moderate: RMGIC (Vitrebond™); deep: use a sub-lining of calcium hydroxide (direct or indirect pulp capping) and any of the cements listed. Typically RMGIC is recommended as it seals as well as lines the preparation.
[8954][Para 001] Composite resin—dentine adhesive system with direct or indirect pulp capping as indicated.
[8955][Para 006] Pulp capping
[8956][Para 005] Hard-setting calcium hydroxide or MTA.
[8957][Para 006] Sedative dressing
[8958][Para 005] ZOE &/or calcium hydroxide.
[8959][Para 006] Bacteriostatic dressing
[8960][Para 005] Calcium hydroxide plus GI (stepwise excavation).
[8961][Para 009] Impression materials
[8962][Para 022] Classification
[8963][Para 035] See Table 16.2.
[8964][Heading 1] Elastomers
[8965][Para 004] Indicated when accuracy is paramount, e.g. crown and bridge work, and implants.
[8966][Para 006] Condensation-cured silicone
[8967][Para 005] These materials are relatively cheap compared with other elastomers, but prone to some shrinkage and should be cast immediately. Addition-cured silicones are preferred.
[8968][Para 006] Addition-cured silicone
[8969][Para 005] This type of silicone is very stable, which means that impressions can be posted or stored prior to casting. A perforated tray or rim lock tray is advisable as the adhesives supplied are not very effective. Up to five viscosities are manufactured, allowing a range of impression techniques. NB: powdered latex gloves (now rarely used) can retard setting of putty materials.6 Can also be used for registering occlusion.
[8970][Para 006] Polysulfide
[8971][Para 005] Messy to handle, but useful when a long working time is required. Use with a special tray and, although stable, cast within 24h. Not recommended except in complete denture cases.
[8972][Para 006] Polyether
[8973][Para 005] (e.g. Impregum™) Popular because it uses a single mix and a stock tray. The set material is stiff, although newer products (e.g. Penta Soft™) have addressed this and removal can be stressful in cases with deep undercuts or advanced periodontitis. Absorbs water, ∴ do not store with alginate impressions. Can cause allergic reactions. Routinely used for implant cases and crown and bridge work, especially when there are multiple preps.
[8974][Heading 1] Hydrocolloids
[8975][Para 017] Reversible hydrocolloid
[8976][Para 005] This is accurate, but liable to tear. Requires the purchase of a water bath and is not infection-control friendly.
[8977][Para 006] Irreversible hydrocolloid (alginate)
[8978][Para 005] Setting is a double decomposition reaction between sodium alginate and calcium sulfate. Popular because it is cheap and can be used with a stock tray. However, it is not sufficiently accurate for crown and bridge work. Impressions must be kept damp and cast within 24h. Alginate can retard the setting of gypsum and affect the surface of the model.
[8979][Heading 1] Impression compound
[8980][Para 004] Available in either sheet form for recording preliminary impressions, or in stick form for modifying trays. The sheet material is softened in a waterbath with warm water (55–60°C) and used in a stock tray to record edentulous ridges. The viscosity of compound results in a well-extended impression, but limited detail. Admix impression material (mix of greenstick and impression compound) is useful for denture cases with severe resorption.
[8981][Heading 1] Zinc oxide pastes
[8982][Para 004] Dispensed 1:1 and mixed to an even colour. Used for recording edentulous ridges in a special tray or the patient’s existing dentures, but C/I for undercuts. Setting time is ↓ by warmth and humidity. Fared worse in one particular RCT.7
[8983][Para 036] Table 16.2 Classification of impression materials
[8984][Para 009] Impression techniques
[8985][Para 014] (For crown and bridge work.)
[8986][Para 008] 2Time spent recording a good impression is an investment, as repeating laboratory work is costly.
[8987][Heading 1] Special trays
[8988][Para 004] These help the adaptation of impression material and ↓ the amount required, i.e. ↑ accuracy and ↓ cost. Can be made in cold-cure acrylic or light-activated tray resin. Special trays are rarely used for crown and bridge work impressions, with stock trays used routinely. Usually the palate does not need to be included, so design the special tray accordingly or use a lower stock tray. For the opposing arch, alginate in a stock tray will suffice.
[8989][Heading 1] Monophase technique
[8990][Para 004] (E.g. polyether.) The same mix of medium-viscosity material is used for both a stock tray and syringe. Although less accurate than other methods, it is adequate for most tasks.
[8991][Heading 1] Double-mix technique
[8992][Para 004] (E.g. polysulfide, addition-cured silicone.) A single-stage technique necessitating the mixing of heavy- and light-bodied materials at the same time, and use of a special or stock tray.
[8993][Para 001] Apply adhesive to tray.
[8994][Para 001] Mix light- and heavy-bodied viscosities simultaneously for 45–60sec.
[8995][Para 001] Remove retraction cord or preferably leave in place and dry preparation, while nurse loads syringe with light-bodied material.
[8996][Para 001] Syringe light-bodied mix around prep. A gentle stream of air helps to direct material into crevice.
[8997][Para 001] Position tray containing heavy-bodied material.
[8998][Para 001] Support tray with light pressure until 2min after apparent set.
[8999][Heading 1] Putty and wash technique
[9000][Para 004] (E.g. silicone.) The putty and light-bodied viscosities can be used with a stock tray, either:
[9001][Para 001] Single stage—similar to the double-mix technique, or
[9002][Para 001] Two stage—this involves taking an impression of the prep with the putty, using a polythene sheet as a spacer. This is then relined with the light-bodied material, which is also syringed around the prep. Depending on circumstances and clinician preferences, different impression techniques and materials may be favoured, however there is limited evidence to prove superiority, particularly regarding denture fabrication. More high quality RCTs are needed to determine if any material or technique is advantageous.8
[9003][Heading 1] Cost
[9004][Para 004] In decreasing order:
[9005][Para 001] Addition-cured silicone using putty/reline.
[9006][Para 001] Polyether with special tray.
[9007][Para 001] Addition-cured silicone using double mix and special tray.
[9008][Para 001] Polysulfide with special tray.
[9009][Para 001] Condensation-cured silicone using putty/reline.
[9010][Para 001] Hydrocolloid.
[9011][Heading 1] Automixing dispensers
[9012][Para 004] This double-cartridge presentation is exceptionally popular. The two pastes are extruded and mixed in the nozzle when the trigger is pressed. Appears expensive, but ↓ waste and the mixture is void free. Many manufacturers are now producing their materials in this format.
[9013][Heading 1] Disinfection of impressions
[9014][Para 004] Impressions should be rinsed to remove debris and then immersed in a solution of sodium hypochlorite (1000ppm available chlorine) or a glutaraldehyde-free proprietary disinfectant such as Perform® for 10min. In general, dimensional stability of impressions seems unaffected by current protocols.9
[9015][Heading 1] Intraoral scanning
[9016][Para 004] Various systems are now available that record impressions digitally and miss out messy conventional impressions altogether, digitally relaying the detail of a conventional impression. Current scanners are sufficiently accurate in capturing details required to fabricate most restorations including inlays/onlays, crowns, fixed bridgework, fixed partical dentures, copings, and frameworks.10 These are becoming more commonplace in general practice and have the advantage that sections can be rescanned without the additional expense of a repeat impression. Other advantages include direct receipt by the laboratory reducing transportation costs and time as well as being better for the environment due to the lack of printed laboratory tickets, labels, and postage/packaging. They are often tolerated well by patients who find conventional impressions difficult to cope with and can be useful for patient education purposes.
[9017][Para 008] Tips for IO scanning:
[9018][Para 001] Scan systematically to ensure no areas are missed.
[9019][Para 001] Use retraction cord around preparations unless supra-gingival margins.
[9020][Para 001] Ensure area being scanned is dry and the soft tissues are not obstructing the image.
[9021][Para 001] Practise scanning technique to ensure as efficient and comfortable for the patient as possible.
[9022][Para 001] Ensure a bite registration is recorded.
[9023][Para 001] Communicate clearly with the laboratory what is required.
[9024][Para 009] Casting alloys
[9025][Para 014] An alloy is a mixture of two or more metallic elements. The chemistry of alloys is too complicated for this book chapter (and its author), so for a fuller understanding, the reader is referred to the source text.
[9026][Para 008] The properties of an alloy depend upon:
[9027][Para 001] The thermal treatments applied to the alloy (including cooling).
[9028][Para 001] The mechanical manipulation of the alloy.
[9029][Para 001] The composition of the alloy.
[9030][Para 016] NB: the properties of an alloy may differ significantly from that of its constituents.
[9031][Para 008] The main examples of alloys in dentistry include amalgam (…… Amalgam, p. 650), steel burs and instruments, metallic denture bases, inlays, crowns and bridges, NiTi endodontic instruments, and orthodontic wires.
[9032][Para 008] A warm, moist mouth provides the ideal environment for corrosion. To overcome this problem, dental casting alloys comprise an essentially corrosion-resistant metal (usually gold), with the addition of other constituents to enhance its properties. However, with the possible exception of titanium, all have the potential to affect hypersensitive individuals.
[9033][Heading 1] Additions to gold alloys
[9034][Para 017] Copper
[9035][Para 005] i strength and hardness, but ↓ ductility.
[9036][Para 006] Silver
[9037][Para 005] i hardness and strength, but ↑ tarnishing and ↑ porosity.
[9038][Para 006] Platinum/palladium
[9039][Para 005] (As in type III/IV gold alloys.) ↑ melting point (which confers advantage for soldering).
[9040][Para 006] Zinc or indium
[9041][Para 005] Scavenger, preventing oxidation of other metals during melting and casting.
[9042][Heading 1] Traditional dental casting gold alloys
[9043][Para 017] ISO standard
[9044][Para 005] ISO standard is that the noble metal (gold, platinum, palladium, iridium, ruthenium, rhodium) content must be >75% with no less than 65% gold. Four types are defined by proof stress (stress required to cause a permanent deformation of a particular value (e.g. 0.2%)—similar to elastic limit) and elongation (ductility) values from type I (low strength for castings subject to low stress) to type IV (extra-high strength).
[9045][Para 008] Clinically this means the type I and II alloys are used in low load-bearing situations such as inlays; type III where demands are higher such as full cuspal coverage onlays, crowns, and bridges; and type IV where rigidity is required for removable partial denture bases or clasps.
[9046][Heading 1] Dental casting semi-precious alloys
[9047][Para 004] These have 25–74% noble metal content.
[9048][Para 006] Low gold alloys
[9049][Para 005] Similar to the traditional gold alloys, four types are defined by proof stress and elongation properties. High palladium content imparts ‘whiteness’. Popularity ↑ with ↑ cost of gold.
[9050][Para 006] Silver palladium
[9051][Para 005] Palladium (generally >25%), silver, gold, indium, and zinc. Cheaper than gold alloys and of equivalent hardness, but less ductile, more difficult to cast, and prone to porosity.
[9052][Heading 1] Base metal casting alloys
[9053][Para 004] Contain no gold, platinum, or palladium.
[9054][Para 006] Nickel chromium
[9055][Para 005] 75% nickel, 20% chromium. Used in crowns and bridge work. In latter, ↑ rigidity compared to gold alloys is an advantage. However, castings are less accurate than gold, and nickel sensitivity can C/I its use.
[9056][Para 006] Cobalt chromium
[9057][Para 005] 35–65% cobalt, no less than 25% chromium. Modulus of elasticity (rigidity) twice that of type IV gold alloys ∴ good for denture base but not as good for clasps. Proportional limit (ability to withstand stress without permanent deformation) high. A good polish is difficult to achieve, but durable. Used mainly for P/–.
[9058][Heading 1] Titanium
[9059][Para 004] Good biocompatibility; used for implants and their superstructure and in patients with allergies to other materials as a denture base material. In its use for implants, the titanium can be subjected to post-manufacture heat treatment to optimize the grain structure (small α grain size and well-dispersed β phase with a small α–β interfacial zone). This improves the properties with regard to cyclic fatigue and crack propagation. (Also see Chapter 6.)
[9060][Heading 1] Alloys for porcelain bonding
[9061][Para 004] Requirements:
[9062][Para 001] Higher melting point than porcelain.
[9063][Para 001] Similar coefficient of thermal expansion to porcelain (leucite used in the porcelain to bring it closer to that of the metal).
[9064][Para 001] Will not discolour the porcelain.
[9065][Para 001] High modulus of elasticity (rigidity) to avoid flexure and # of porcelain.
[9066][Para 001] Ability to bond to the porcelain to avoid detachment.
[9067][Para 016] Indium is usually added to facilitate bonding to porcelain. Copper is C/I as it discolours the porcelain. A matched alloy and porcelain should be used.
[9068][Para 006] High gold
[9069][Para 005] i palladium or platinum content (to ↑ melting point) compared to non-porcelain alloys but need thick copings for strength ∴ bulky. Also costly.
[9070][Para 006] Medium gold
[9071][Para 005] 50% gold, 30% palladium. Good properties and economical. Widely used.
[9072][Para 006] Silver palladium
[9073][Para 005] Cheap, but care required to avoid casting defects.
[9074][Para 006] Nickel chromium
[9075][Para 005] Very high melting point and modulus of elasticity, but casting more difficult due to shrinkage, voids. Also bond strength to porcelain via ceramic oxide weak. NB: some patients are sensitive to nickel.
[9076][Heading 1] Casting
[9077][Para 004] For gold (melting point <950°C):
[9078][Para 001] Wax pattern and sprue are invested in gypsum-bonded material.
[9079][Para 001] Wax burnt out by slowly heating investment mould to 450°C.
[9080][Para 001] Alloy melted either by gas/air torch or electric induction heating and cast with centrifugal force.
[9081][Para 001] Casting allowed to cool to below red-heat.
[9082][Para 001] Quenched. Some alloys are used as cast and others heat-hardened.
[9083][Para 001] Cleaned with ultrasonics and acid immersion.
[9084][Para 016] For nickel chromium and cobalt chromium alloys (melting points 1200–1500°C), need silica or phosphate bonded investment and either oxyacetylene torch or electric induction heating.
[9085][Para 006] Casting faults
[9086][Para 005] A casting may:
[9087][Para 001] Be dimensionally inaccurate (depends on balancing out of casting contraction and investment expansion on setting).
[9088][Para 001] Display finning (due to overheated and cracked investment material) and bubbling (due to surface porosities in the investment material).
[9089][Para 001] Be porous/contaminated (broken pieces of investment or dirt falling down the sprue) or incomplete (sprue problem, premature solidification of the molten metal, insufficient centrifugal force, back pressure effects from poor escape of gases, cooling shrinkage).
[9090][Para 009] Wrought alloys
[9091][Para 014] Wrought alloys are hammered, rolled, drawn, or bent into the desired shape when they are solid.
[9092][Heading 1] Stainless steel
[9093][Para 004] Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. The addition of chromium (>12%) produces a passive surface oxide layer which gives SS its name. The SS used in dentistry is also known as austenitic steel (because the crystals are arranged in a face-centred cubic structure) or 18:8 steel (due to the chromium and nickel content). Available as:
[9094][Para 001] Preformed sheets for denture bases. The SS is swaged onto the model by explosive or hydraulic pressure. This produces a thin (0.1mm), light denture base resistant to #. Rarely used today.
[9095][Para 001] Wires are produced by drawing the SS through dies of ↓ diameter until the desired size is achieved. This work-hardens the wire, but heat treatments are carried out to give soft, hard, or extra-hard forms. Manipulation of SS wire also work-hardens the wire in the plane of bending, ∴ trying to correct a bend is more likely to result in #. Main applications are orthodontics and partial denture clasps. SS can be welded and soldered.
[9096][Heading 1] Soldering SS
[9097][Para 004] Requires use of a flux (e.g. Easy-flo™ flux) to remove the passive oxide layer (this reforms after soldering). Do not overheat as this can anneal and soften the components.
[9098][Para 001] Melt a small bead of low fusing silver solder (e.g. Easy-flo™ solder) onto the wire.
[9099][Para 001] Mix up the flux with water to a thick paste and apply to the item to be added.
[9100][Para 001] Heat up the solder so that wire underneath is a cherry red.
[9101][Para 001] Bring the fluxed wire into the molten solder and remove the flame at the same time.
[9102][Para 016] This is not easy and requires practice, which explains the popularity of electrical soldering.
[9103][Heading 1] Cobalt chromium
[9104][Para 004] This has a similar composition to the cast form (…… Casting alloys, p. 670).
[9105][Para 006] Cobalt chromium alloys
[9106][Para 005] These are used in orthodontics as an archwire material. It has the advantage that it can be hardened by heat treatment after being formed. Also used for post fabrication in post and core crowns (Wiptam wire).
[9107][Heading 1] Titanium alloys
[9108][Para 004] Nickel and titanium alloy (nitinol) is useful in orthodontics as it is flexible, has good springback, and is capable of applying small forces over a long period of time. However, it is not easy to bend without #. Titanium molybdenum alloy (TMA) is also used for archwires and has properties midway between SS and nitinol.
[9109][Heading 1] Gold
[9110][Para 004] Mainly historical as expense limits the application of wrought gold alloys to partial denture clasp fabrication.
[9111][Heading 1] Alloys for dentures
[9112][Para 004] Cast cobalt chromium is the material of choice for partial denture connectors because of its high proof stress and modulus of elasticity: thin castings are strong, rigid, and lightweight. Although wrought gold alloys are more suitable for clasps, the advantage of being able to cast connector and clasps in one means that cobalt chromium is more commonly used (…… Removable partial dentures—components, p. 294). Be aware of nickel allergy.
[9113][Para 009] Dental ceramics
[9114][Para 014] Ceramics are simple compounds of both metallic and non-metallic oxides. Although many of the materials used in dentistry are ceramics, the term is commonly used to refer to porcelain and its derivatives.
[9115][Para 008] Dental porcelain has three basic requirements: function (durability, strength, and biocompatibility), form (ability to form complex shapes), and aesthetics (colour, translucency, and transmission of light).
[9116][Para 008] Dental ceramics exist in a spectrum from exclusively non-crystalline amorphous glasses through a combination of glass and crystalline mixtures to all-crystalline. In general, the ‘glassier’ the ceramic: ↑ translucence, ↑ aesthetics, but ↓ fracture resistance.
[9117][Heading 1] Properties
[9118][Para 001] Firing shrinkage 30–40%, ∴ crown must be overbuilt.
[9119][Para 001] Chemically inert provided the surface layer is intact.
[9120][Para 001] Low thermal conductivity.
[9121][Para 001] Good aesthetic properties.
[9122][Para 001] Brittle. The main cause of failure is crack propagation which almost invariably emanates from the unglazed inner surface. This can be ↓ by:
[9123][Para 001] Fusion of the inner surface to metal, as in the platinum foil and metal-bonded techniques.
[9124][Para 001] The use of a strengthened porcelain core.
[9125][Para 001] High resistance to wear.
[9126][Para 001] Glazed surface resists plaque accumulation.
[9127][Heading 1] Porcelain jacket crown (PJC)
[9128][Para 004] Now considered somewhat old-fashioned. For strength, a minimum porcelain thickness of 0.8mm is required and a 90° butt joint at the margin.
[9129][Para 008] Conventional PJC construction involves placement of a platinum matrix on the die onto which a core of aluminous porcelain is laid down. First ‘dentine’ then ‘enamel’ porcelains are built up in layers, using porcelain powder and water mixed to form a slurry, until the desired shape is achieved. This is then compacted by water removal to ↓ firing shrinkage and then fired to ↓ porosity, which ↑ strength and ↑ translucency. Glazing produces a glossy outer skin which resists cracking and plaque accumulation. It can be added as a separate layer or by firing at a higher temperature after the addition of surface glazes. The platinum foil lining is unaffected by the firing and so should maintain accuracy of fit throughout. It is removed prior to cementation to give space for the cement lute (725µm).
[9130][Heading 1] Metal ceramic
[9131][Para 004] The porcelains used for bonding to a metal substructure have additional leucite added to ↑ the coefficient of thermal expansion to almost match the alloys used. Also, porcelain that fuses below the melting point of the alloy is required. Bonding to the metal occurs by a combination of:
[9132][Para 001] Mechanical retention.
[9133][Para 001] Chemical bonding to the metal oxide layer on the surface of the alloy.
[9134][Para 016] The greater strength of porcelain bonded to metal crowns allows use in load-bearing areas and is due to:
[9135][Para 001] The metal substructure supporting the porcelain.
[9136][Para 001] ↓ crack propagation by bonding the inner surface of the porcelain to metal.
[9137][Para 001] The outer surface of porcelain being under tension, thus ↓ crack propagation.
[9138][Para 016] But drawbacks are ↓ aesthetics, gingival staining, over-contouring cervically, and in some patients it may cause allergy.
[9139][Para 008] Good success rates reported (94% at 8yrs).11
[9140][Heading 1] All-ceramic alternatives to metal ceramic restorations
[9141][Para 004] Glass ceramic—glasses usually derived from silicone dioxide and with various amounts of aluminium form aluminosilicates or feldspaths. With addition of low levels of leucite they are commonly labelled as feldspathic porcelains.12
[9142][Para 008] With high-leucite variants, extra strength is attained. Can be powder-liquid, machined, or pressed.
[9143][Para 008] A specific popular variant has the usual aluminosilicate glass enhanced with lithium dioxide to give lithium disilicate glass in the form of IPS e.max®. The manufacturer claims ↑ flexural strength as well as ↑ optical properties via light transmission.
[9144][Para 008] A further category of dental ceramics is a crystalline system infiltrated with lanthanum glass known as VITA In-Ceram®. This again provides ↑ strength. It is used as a core that is then layered with veneering porcelain to add characterization. VITA In-Ceram®, like many of its competitors, offers a wide range of applications ranging from aesthetics for anterior work to strength required for multiple unit bridges.
[9145][Para 008] The final category is the polycrystalline form of dental ceramic. Unable to be pressed, the zirconium oxide used in this technique must be oversized initially to compensate for firing shrinkage. This is either done by machining an oversized framework for firing (e.g. 3M ESPE Lava™) or fabrication of an oversized die on which the framework is constructed for firing (Nobel Procera™).
[9146][Heading 1] Porcelain repairs
[9147][Para 004] Can be carried out using composite and a silane coupling agent. A number of proprietary kits (e.g. Cojet™) are available.
[9148][Para 009] CAD/CAM
[9149][Para 014] CAD—computer-aided design. CAM—computer-aided manufacture.
[9150][Para 008] Implant dentistry has speeded the progress of ‘digital solutions’. Intraoral scanners can be utilized to provide information pertaining to a preparation and the adjacent teeth and opposing arch to allow a laboratory scanner to allow for CAD. This then can be progressed to CAM and a prosthesis formed (or its substructure). Dental ceramics may be constructed in this way to provide all-ceramic solutions for fixed prostheses.
[9151][Heading 1] Porcelain veneers
[9152][Para 004] A thin shell of porcelain or castable ceramic ~0.5–0.8mm thick (…… Veneers, p. 258). Their thin section limits their ability to hide underlying tooth discoloration. Amenable to CAD/CAM fabrication. Newer ceramics claim thicknesses of 0.3–0.4mm (e.g. Lumineers™) to be possible without ↑ fracture.
[9153][Heading 1] Porcelain inlays
[9154][Para 004] Useful material for specific inlay/onlay treatment indications. Only limited long-term studies available. Also amenable to CAD/CAM fabrication.
[9155][Para 009] Denture materials—acrylic resins
[9156][Para 014] Acrylic is the most commonly used polymer for denture bases. Not only can it be relined, repaired, and added to comparatively easily, but it is also aesthetic and lightweight. Acrylic is composed of a chain of methacrylate molecules linked together to give PMMA.
[9157][Heading 1] Presentation
[9158][Para 004] Usually comprises a liquid and a powder mixed together (Table 16.3). The liquid is stored in a dark bottle to ↑ shelf life.
[9159][Heading 1] Manipulation
[9160][Para 004] The powder and liquid should be mixed in a ratio of ~2.5:1 by weight. The mix passes through several distinct stages: sandy–string–dough–rubbery–hard (set). The dough stage is the best for handling and packing.
[9161][Para 008] In denture fabrication, the wax pattern and teeth are invested in plaster. The wax is then boiled out and the plaster coated with sodium alginate as a separator. The resultant space is then filled to excess (to allow for contraction shrinkage of 7%) with acrylic dough under pressure. The acrylic is then polymerized.
[9162][Heading 1] Mode of activation
[9163][Para 017] Self-cure
[9164][Para 005] Self-cure acrylics show less setting contraction, but more water absorption than heat-cure acrylics. This may result in the final item being slightly over-sized, thus ↓ retention. Self-cure acrylics are more porous, only 80% as strong, less resistant to abrasion, and contain a greater level of unreacted monomer compared to heat-cure acrylics. The main applications of self-cure acrylics are for denture repairs and relines, and orthodontic appliances, although for the latter the greater strength of heat-cure acrylics is preferable.
[9165][Para 006] Heat-cure
[9166][Para 005] Conventionally, polymerization requires heating in a hot-water bath for 7h at 70°C, then 3h at 100°C. The flask should be cooled slowly to minimize stresses within the acrylic. However, resins with different curing cycles (fast heat-cure) are now available. Microwave energy can be used to cure acrylic resin, but (apart from lunchtime) has no advantage over a water bath.
[9167][Para 006] Light-cure
[9168][Para 005] Light-cure resins are supplied as mouldable sheets. Used for denture bases or special trays.
[9169][Heading 1] Properties
[9170][Para 001] The glass transition (or softening) temperature of self-cure acrylic is 90°C, and for heat-cure acrylic 105°C.
[9171][Para 001] Poor impact strength and low resistance to fatigue #.
[9172][Para 001] Abrasion resistance not very good, but usually adequate.
[9173][Para 001] Good thermal insulator—undesirable as it can lead to the patient swallowing foods which are too hot.
[9174][Para 001] Low specific gravity (i.e. not too heavy).
[9175][Para 001] Radiolucent. Attempts to ↑ radio-opacity have not been very successful.
[9176][Para 001] Absorbs water, resulting in expansion. Drying out of acrylic should be avoided.
[9177][Para 001] Residual monomer (due to inadequate curing) weakens acrylic and can cause sensitivity reaction.
[9178][Para 001] Good aesthetics.
[9179][Para 006] The strength of a denture depends upon:
[9180][Para 001] Design, e.g. adequate thickness, avoidance of notches.
[9181][Para 001] Strength of the acrylic, i.e. low monomer content, ↓ porosity, adequate curing. Can be ↑ by using high-impact resin.
[9182][Para 016] Researchers are still evaluating methods of ↑ strength of denture resins. The addition of high-performance fibres (e.g. glass fibres) appears promising.
[9183][Para 036] Table 16.3 Presentation of acrylic
[9184][Para 009] Denture materials—rebasing
[9185][Para 014] Rebasing a denture base involves replacement of the fitting surface. Rebases can be either:
[9186][Para 001] Hard: heat- or self-cure, or
[9187][Para 001] Soft:
[9188][Para 001] Permanent: heat-, self-, or light-cure.
[9189][Para 001] Temporary:
[9190][Para 001] Tissue conditioner: self-cure.
[9191][Para 001] Functional impression material: self-cure.
[9192][Para 016] The properties of self-cure materials are generally inferior, ∴ they should only be used as a temporary measure.
[9193][Heading 1] Hard rebases
[9194][Para 004] Heat-cure PMMA is preferred, but requires the patient to do without the denture while it is being added. A self-cure material has obvious advantages, but even the higher acrylics, e.g. butylmethacrylate, should only be used as a temporary measure as they are weaker than PMMA and discolour.
[9195][Heading 1] Soft liners
[9196][Para 004] These require a material with a glass transition temperature below or at that of the mouth so that it is soft and resilient. The majority of soft liners are either based on silicone or acrylic (polyethylmethacrylate or PMMA powder plus alkyl methacrylate monomer and a plasticizer) or polyphosphazene fluoroelastomer13 (Table 16.4).
[9197][Para 008] Heat-, light-, or self-cure types are available. The self-cure materials have inferior properties, but all require replacement during the lifetime of the denture.14
[9198][Heading 1] Tissue conditioners
[9199][Para 004] These usually comprise powdered polyethylmethacrylate to which a plasticizing mix of esters and alcohol is added. No chemical reaction takes place, the liquids merely soften the powder to form a gel and leach out over time, resulting in hardening. To ensure maximum tissue recovery the lining should be a minimum thickness of 2mm and replaced every few days, e.g. Coe-Soft®, Coe-Comfort™, Viscogel®. May be used when relining denture after implant placement for minimal loading during osseointegration.
[9200][Heading 1] Functional impression materials
[9201][Para 004] The tissue-conditioning materials are usually used for this purpose, an impression being cast of the fitting surface after a few days of wear.
[9202][Para 036] Table 16.4 Rebasing—soft liners
[9203][Para 009] Safety of dental materials
[9204][Para 014] Before a new material can be marketed it must successfully pass both laboratory and clinical trials to evaluate its safety. It is worth remembering that laboratory tests for cytotoxicity cannot always be extrapolated clinically and even cytotoxic materials can be utilized in the correct indication based on assessment of risk. Think of materials such as sodium hypochlorite, ZOE, and amalgam. In Europe, a CE mark would be issued to accredit its use in a certain clinical situation. Yet, some adverse effects only become apparent after the material has been in clinical use. Unless used with care, many materials may prove a hazard to the patient or the dental team.
[9205][Heading 1] Hazards to the patient
[9206][Para 017] Systemic effects
[9207][Para 056] Allergic reactions
[9208][Para 001] Amalgam—although genuine cases of amalgam allergy exist, these are rarer than the tabloid press would suggest. For proven cases, composite resin or cast restorations should be used.
[9209][Para 001] Nickel—as a constituent of some alloys can cause contact eczema. Sensitive patients often have a history of allergy to jewellery or watch casings. Alternative alloys are available.
[9210][Para 001] Acrylic monomer—can cause an allergic reaction and should be considered in a patient complaining of a ‘burning mouth’. The concentration of monomer is ↑ in poorly cured acrylic and greater in self- than heat-cure. Extended curing, e.g. 24h, may ↓ concentration of monomer to an acceptable level; if not a cobalt chrome or SS denture base will be required.
[9211][Para 001] Epimine—in polyether impression material.
[9212][Para 016] If an allergy is suspected, consider referral to a dermatologist.
[9213][Para 028] Directly toxic
[9214][Para 001] Beryllium, present in some nickel alloys, is known to be a carcinogen. Provided the alloy is not ground, any risks are confined to the production laboratory. Beryllium-free alloys are becoming ↑ available.
[9215][Para 001] Fluoride in excess can be toxic (…… Safety and toxicity of fluoride, p. 28).
[9216][Para 016] Ingestion or inhalation of air-borne dust/aerosols must be avoided.
[9217][Para 006] Local effects
[9218][Para 056] Eye damage
[9219][Para 025] Curing lamps can cause eye damage due to the glare. The simplest solution is to ask the patient to close their eyes and use a shield.
[9220][Para 028] Thermal injury
[9221][Para 025] Can result in injury:
[9222][Para 001] To the pulp, e.g. caused by exothermic setting reactions.
[9223][Para 001] To the mucosa, e.g. caused by dentures which are thermal insulators, as the patient may swallow drink/food that is too hot; or by the setting reaction of self-cure denture reline materials; or by overzealous heating of thermoplastic impression materials, e.g. greenstick.
[9224][Para 001] To the soft tissues, e.g. by hot instruments.
[9225][Para 028] Chemical injury
[9226][Para 025] Can be caused by noxious chemicals (e.g. etchant, hydrogen peroxide) being allowed to come into direct contact with the tissues.
[9227][Para 028] Hypersensitivity reactions
[9228][Para 025] Can occur in response to the materials that cause systemic allergy.
[9229][Heading 1] Hazards to staff
[9230][Para 017] In the surgery
[9231][Para 001] Allergic reactions, e.g. topical anaesthetics, latex gloves, methyl methacrylate monomer, dentine adhesive systems.
[9232][Para 001] Eye damage from light sources. Use eye protection or shielding.
[9233][Para 001] Alginate dust.
[9234][Para 001] Mercury vapour.
[9235][Para 001] Nitrous oxide.
[9236][Para 006] In the laboratory
[9237][Para 001] Cyanide solution for electroplating.
[9238][Para 001] Vapours from low-fusing metal dies.
[9239][Para 001] Siliceous particles in investment materials.
[9240][Para 001] Fluxes containing fluoride.
[9241][Para 001] Hydrofluoric acid used for etching porcelain veneers.
[9242][Para 001] Beryllium in some alloys.
[9243][Para 001] PMMA powders.
[9244][Para 001] Methyl methacrylate monomer.
[9245][Para 001] Casting machines.

[9265][Para 094] Claimant
